question: How good are LLMs at solving traditional tabular ML datasets using ICL?

sections.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) show mixed performance on traditional tabular machine learning datasets using in-context learning (ICL), with notable strengths in few-shot scenarios but significant limitations compared to traditional methods. While LLMs demonstrate surprising competence in handling tabular data through text serialization approaches, they generally underperform established methods like gradient boosting decision trees (GBDT) and XGBoost, especially as sample sizes increase or problem dimensionality grows.

### Few-Shot Learning Advantages LLMs excel in extremely few-shot scenarios, particularly with 8 or fewer examples. Research demonstrates that TabLLM shows advantages over traditional gradient boosting methods when training samples are severely limited (Huertas, 2024)^[1]. In these very-few-shot settings, LLMs outperform classical methods by considerable margins, leveraging their pre-trained knowledge to make reasonable predictions with minimal examples. The FeatLLM framework, which employs LLMs as feature engineers, significantly outperforms alternatives like TabLLM and STUNT by 10% on average across numerous tabular datasets (Han et al., 2024)^[2]. This approach demonstrates that LLMs can contribute meaningfully to tabular learning by generating high-quality features rather than directly making predictions. ### Memorization and Data Contamination Issues A critical concern with LLM performance on tabular datasets is data contamination and memorization. Research reveals that LLMs have memorized many popular tabular datasets verbatim, leading to inflated performance metrics (Bordt et al., 2024)^[3]. When comparing performance on datasets seen during training versus novel datasets released after training, LLMs perform significantly better on memorized datasets, indicating that memorization leads to overfitting rather than genuine learning capability. ### Sample Efficiency Limitations While LLMs are significantly better than random at solving statistical classification problems, their sample efficiency lags behind traditional statistical learning algorithms, especially as problem dimensionality increases (Bordt et al., 2024)^[3]. This suggests that much of the observed few-shot performance on real-world datasets stems from the LLM's world knowledge rather than true in-context statistical learning ability.

This fundamental constraint prevents LLMs from effectively leveraging larger datasets, though recent work on retrieval-augmented approaches shows promise in addressing this limitation.

question: Compare the various algorithms for compressing trees in terms of computation complexity.

sections.text: Tree compression algorithms are essential for efficient data storage and transmission across various domains, including image processing, video coding, text compression, and network design. These algorithms utilize tree-based data structures to achieve compression while maintaining the ability to reconstruct the original data. This report compares the computational complexity of major tree compression algorithms, analyzing their efficiency in terms of time and space requirements.

Huffman coding is a fundamental tree-based compression algorithm that constructs an optimal prefix-free binary code using a binary tree structure. The algorithm builds a Huffman tree by iteratively combining the two nodes with the lowest frequencies from a priority queue until only one node remains (Kumar et al., 2021). The computational complexity of Huffman coding has been well-established in the literature.The time complexity of Huffman coding is O(n log n), where n is the number of symbols in the alphabet (Baidoo, 2023). This complexity arises from the need to maintain a priority queue during tree construction, with each merge operation requiring O(log n) time. The space complexity is O(n) for storing the tree structure and frequency information. The tree construction process requires considerable computation time for determining the relative position of each symbol on the tree, but the encoding and decoding operations are relatively efficient once the tree is built.

citations.title: Text Compression Algorithms - A Comparative Study
Automated EEG Analysis for Early Diagnosis of Epilepsy: A Comparative Study to Determine Relative Accuracy of Arithmetic and Huffman Coding Algorithms

sections.text: Arithmetic coding represents an alternative approach to tree-based compression that achieves near-optimal compression rates. Unlike Huffman coding, which assigns fixed-length codes to symbols, arithmetic coding encodes entire messages as fractional values within intervals. The computational complexity of arithmetic coding is O(n), where n is the length of the input sequence (Ayona & Al-Janabi, 2022).The linear time complexity makes arithmetic coding theoretically superior to Huffman coding for long sequences. However, the practical implementation requires more complex arithmetic operations, including division and multiplication, which can increase the constant factors. The space complexity is O(1) for the basic algorithm, as it does not require storing an explicit tree structure, though adaptive models may require additional memory.

citations.title: Progressive DCT Image Compression Based On Quad Tree Decomposition for WSN

sections.text: Quadtree-based compression algorithms utilize hierarchical tree structures for spatial data compression, particularly in image and video coding applications. The quadtree structure recursively divides data into four quadrants, creating a tree where each internal node has exactly four children.The computational complexity of quadtree-based compression is typically O(N log N), where N is the number of data points or pixels (Shukla et al., 2005). This complexity includes both the tree construction phase and the compression phase. For rate-distortion optimized quadtree coding schemes, the complexity can be maintained at O(N log N) through efficient pruning and joining strategies. The space complexity is O(N) for storing the tree structure and associated data.Quadtree-segmented Block Truncation Coding (QTS-BTC) represents an efficient variant with low computational complexity, commonly used due to its simplicity (Daga & Fernandez, 2016). The k-d tree variant (KTS-BTC) shows improved performance over traditional quadtree approaches while maintaining similar computational complexity.

citations.title: Rate-distortion optimized tree-structured compression algorithms for piecewise polynomial images
k-d Tree-Segmented Block Truncation Coding for Image Compression

sections.text: Binary tree compression algorithms, including variants used in modern video coding standards, present different complexity characteristics. The Quadtree plus Binary Tree (QTBT) structure used in advanced video coding standards significantly increases computational complexity compared to simpler tree structures.Fast binary tree partition algorithms have been developed to reduce the computational burden. These algorithms can achieve approximately 23% encoding time reduction while maintaining compression efficiency (Lin et al., 2018). The overall complexity depends on the depth of the tree and the decision algorithms used for partitioning.

citations.title: Fast Binary Tree Partition Decision in H.266/FVC Intra Coding

sections.text: Dictionary-based compression algorithms like LZ77, LZ78, and LZW utilize implicit tree structures through their dictionary organizations. These algorithms exhibit different complexity characteristics: - LZ77: The complexity depends on the search window size and matching algorithm efficiency. The search process can be time-consuming, requiring O(n²) time in the worst case, but can be optimized using appropriate data structures. - LZ78: Creates an explicit dictionary with no window size limitations, but the dictionary size can grow indefinitely. The encoding complexity is generally faster than LZ77. - LZW: Based on LZ78 but with dictionary initialization containing all alphabet symbols. The compression delay is related to dictionary size and search method efficiency.The space complexity for dictionary-based algorithms is typically O(d), where d is the dictionary size, which can be bounded or unbounded depending on the specific implementation.

Network design problems with compression introduce additional complexity layers. The compressor placement problem (CPP) is weakly NP-hard, even on instances where basic network design is polynomially solvable (Koster & Tieves, 2015). However, pseudopolynomial algorithms exist for tree instances, and polynomial-time solutions are available for restricted cases.

citations.title: Network Design with Compression: Complexity and Algorithms

sections.text: The computational complexity comparison reveals distinct trade-offs among different tree compression algorithms:1. Huffman Coding: O(n log n) time, O(n) space - well-balanced for most applications2. Arithmetic Coding: O(n) time, O(1) space - theoretically optimal but with higher constant factors3. Quadtree Compression: O(N log N) time, O(N) space - efficient for spatial data4. Binary Tree Compression: Variable complexity depending on optimization strategies5. Dictionary-Based: O(n) to O(n²) time depending on search strategiesThe choice of algorithm depends on the specific application requirements, including data characteristics, real-time constraints, and available computational resources.

Tree compression algorithms exhibit varying computational complexities that must be considered when selecting appropriate methods for specific applications. While Huffman coding provides a good balance of efficiency and simplicity, arithmetic coding offers theoretical optimality at the cost of implementation complexity. Quadtree-based methods excel for spatial data, while dictionary-based approaches provide adaptive compression capabilities. Modern applications often benefit from hybrid approaches that combine multiple techniques to achieve optimal compression performance while managing computational complexity.The ongoing research in fast algorithms and optimization strategies continues to improve the practical performance of these fundamental compression techniques, making them suitable for increasingly demanding applications in data processing and transmission.

question: How have open-source publishing platforms impacted the global distribution of academic publishing?

sections.text: Open-source publishing platforms have fundamentally transformed the global landscape of academic publishing by democratizing access to publishing tools, reducing financial barriers, and enabling broader geographic participation in scholarly communication. This transformation has been particularly significant for institutions in developing countries and has led to the emergence of new publishing models that challenge traditional commercial publishing dominance.

Open-source publishing platforms represent a paradigm shift in academic publishing, providing free, accessible, and customizable solutions for journal management and publication. The most prominent example is Open Journal Systems (OJS), developed by the Public Knowledge Project, which has become "the most common journal management system being discussed frequently in literature" (Publishing with Open Journal Systems (OJS): the engaged university and library support at the University of Stavanger). These platforms offer comprehensive solutions for managing the entire publication workflow, from manuscript submission to final publication. The emergence of these platforms has been driven by the need for more equitable and accessible publishing models. As noted in research on comprehensive approaches to open access, "The Open Access Initiative is gaining momentum due to the worldwide availability of advanced digital tools, online publishing platforms, and systems for tracking academic contributions" (Comprehensive Approach to Open Access Publishing: Platforms and Tools).

sections.text: ### 2.1 Geographic Distribution of Open-Source Publishing The adoption of open-source publishing platforms has shown significant regional variations, with developing countries demonstrating particularly strong uptake. A comprehensive survey of 998 scholarly journals using OJS revealed that these platforms "are distinguished by the number that offer open access to their content, the growth rates in new titles, the participation rates from developing countries, and the extremely low operating budgets" (A Survey of the Scholarly Journals Using Open Journal Systems). Research on global open access publishing patterns indicates that "120 countries are contributing to open access publishing across the globe. From Europe alone 43 countries are actively contributing to OA publishing, alone constituting 35.83% of geographical share, followed by Asia with 34 countries, Africa 17 countries, North America 14 countries, South America 10 counties and Oceania 02 countries" (Global Scenario of Open Access Publishing: A Decadal Analysis of Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) 2003-2012). ### 2.2 Regional Variations in Publishing Models Different regions have adopted varying approaches to open-source publishing. In Latin America, research shows that "74% of the journals of this region included in SCOPUS are gold road ones, and there are practically no green road journals registered" (Open access and Scopus: A new approach to scientific visibility from the standpoint of access). This pattern reflects the region's commitment to diamond open access models, where publishing is free for both authors and readers.

question: Have specialized approaches been developed for providing LLM assistance when people author SQL queries?

sections.text: Yes, specialized approaches have been developed for providing LLM assistance when people author SQL queries. The field has evolved significantly with the emergence of text-to-SQL systems that leverage large language models to transform natural language queries into executable SQL commands. These approaches encompass domain-specific fine-tuning, interactive frameworks, cost-efficient routing systems, and comprehensive user interface solutions designed to bridge the gap between non-technical users and database querying.

Researchers have developed specialized fine-tuning methodologies to enhance LLM performance for SQL generation. Rebei (2023) presents a novel approach that fine-tunes open-source large language models specifically for transforming natural language into SQL queries within specific domains like retail^[1]. This approach involves generating context-specific datasets using GPT-4, then fine-tuning models like Starcoder Plus, Code-Llama, and Mistral using the LoRa technique to optimize for resource constraints^[1]. The fine-tuned models demonstrated superior performance in zero-shot settings compared to baseline GPT-4, with Code-Llama achieving accuracy rates of 81.58% for Snowflake SQL and 82.66% for GoogleSQL^[1]. Similarly, domain-specific applications have been explored extensively. For example, Nugraha et al. (2024) developed specialized approaches for agricultural census data, utilizing CodeLlama-7B to translate human questions into SQL queries for anomaly detection^[2]. Their fine-tuning approach achieved an Average Correct Rate of 69.6% on the SQL-Eval framework, which improved to 77.8% when combined with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting^[2].

A significant advancement in the field has been the development of interactive systems that support multi-turn conversations for SQL generation. Xiong et al. (2024) introduced Interactive-T2S, a framework that generates SQL queries through direct interactions with databases^[3]. This system includes four general tools that facilitate proactive and efficient information retrieval by the LLM, addressing scalability issues when processing wide tables^[3]. The framework demonstrated state-of-the-art results with only two exemplars, underscoring its effectiveness and robustness^[3]. Another notable interactive system is Chat2Data, developed by Zhao et al. (2024), which provides an interactive data analysis system that integrates RAG, vector databases, and LLMs^[4]. This system adopts a three-layer approach: the first layer uses RAG to embed domain knowledge to address hallucination problems, the second layer utilizes vector databases to reduce LLM interactions, and the third layer designs a pipeline agent to decompose complex tasks into multiple subtasks^[4].

Recognizing the computational costs associated with advanced LLM-based text-to-SQL approaches, researchers have developed cost-efficient solutions. Zhu et al. (2025) proposed EllieSQL, a complexity-aware routing framework that assigns queries to suitable SQL generation pipelines based on estimated complexity^[5]. This approach routes simple queries to efficient methods while reserving computationally intensive approaches for complex cases^[5]. The framework introduces the Token Elasticity of Performance (TEP) metric, which captures cost-efficiency by quantifying the responsiveness of performance gains relative to token investment^[5]. EllieSQL reduces token usage by over 40% without compromising performance, achieving more than a 2x boost in TEP over non-routing approaches^[5].

Specialized prompting techniques have been developed to enhance LLM performance in SQL generation. Xu et al. (2024) introduced a Chain-of-Programs (COP) prompting framework that utilizes Pandas code as an intermediate representation aligned with human thinking patterns^[6]. This approach transforms complex SQL queries into a series of simple Pandas queries, with each step validated using a Python interpreter^[6]. The method achieved performance comparable to GPT-4 in zero-shot scenarios when applied to open-source language models^[6]. For low-resource languages, Öztürk (2025) explored a two-stage fine-tuning approach for Turkish text-to-SQL conversion^[7]. The study demonstrated that sequential fine-tuning (first on Turkish instruction data, then on SQL data) outperformed direct SQL fine-tuning, with Phi3 models achieving execution accuracy of up to 99.95%^[7].

To address the gap between non-expert users and complex database querying, specialized user interfaces have been developed. Tian et al. (2024) introduced SQLucid, a novel user interface that integrates visual correspondence, intermediate query results, and editable step-by-step SQL explanations in natural language^[8]. The system empowers users to understand and refine SQL queries easily and precisely, showing significant improvement in task completion accuracy and user confidence compared to existing interfaces^[8].

Several specialized architectures have been developed for text-to-SQL tasks. The research shows various approaches including multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, and semantic enhancement frameworks. These systems typically incorporate components for schema linking, question decomposition, SQL generation, and result refinement to improve accuracy and reliability^[9].

The field of LLM assistance for SQL query authoring has developed numerous specialized approaches that address different aspects of the text-to-SQL challenge. These include domain-specific fine-tuning methodologies, interactive multi-turn systems, cost-efficient routing frameworks, advanced prompting techniques, user-friendly interfaces, and comprehensive architectures. The research demonstrates significant progress in making database querying more accessible to non-technical users while maintaining high accuracy and efficiency. Future developments are likely to focus on further improving cost-efficiency, enhancing user experience, and expanding domain-specific applications.

question: How has the citation graph been used to improve neural language models for scientific papers?

sections.text: The exponential growth of scientific literature has created significant challenges for researchers in finding relevant papers and understanding their relationships. Traditional text-based approaches to document representation and classification often fail to capture the rich structural information present in scientific publishing networks. The citation graph, which represents the relationships between papers through their citation patterns, has emerged as a powerful signal for improving neural language models specifically designed for scientific documents. This report examines how citation graphs have been integrated with neural language models to enhance performance on various scientific document tasks.

### SPECTER: Citation-Informed Document EmbeddingsOne of the most significant developments in this field has been SPECTER (Scientific Paper Embeddings using Citation-informed Transformers), which represents a breakthrough in document-level representation learning for scientific papers (Cohan et al., 2020). SPECTER addresses the limitation of traditional pre-trained language models like BERT, which are designed for token- and sentence-level tasks and do not leverage inter-document relationships that are crucial for scientific document understanding.The key innovation of SPECTER is its use of the citation graph as a training signal during the pre-training phase. Instead of relying solely on masked language modeling objectives, SPECTER trains a Transformer-based model to learn representations where papers that cite each other are positioned closer in the embedding space. This approach allows the model to capture document-level semantic relationships that are not apparent from text content alone.The effectiveness of SPECTER has been demonstrated across multiple downstream tasks, including citation prediction, document classification, and paper recommendation, establishing it as a foundational model for scientific document analysis.### Temporal Evolution of Citation-Based EmbeddingsRecent work has extended the static approach of SPECTER to incorporate temporal dynamics of citation networks. Shen et al. (2024) proposed a Temporal Graph Neural Network (TGN) approach that continuously updates paper embeddings as new citation relationships appear in the literature. This temporal dimension addresses the limitation of static methods that fail to account for the evolving impact and relevance of papers over time.The TGN-based model learns patterns of how scholarly perception of papers evolves, using a learnable memory update module based on Recurrent Neural Networks to predict future citation impact. This approach has shown effectiveness on large-scale datasets, demonstrating superior performance in paper recommendation tasks.

citations.title: SPECTER: Document-level Representation Learning using Citation-informed Transformers

sections.text: ### Citation Graph Collaborative Filtering (CGCF)Guan and Jiang (2022) developed a hybrid approach called Citation Graph Collaborative Filtering (CGCF) that combines pre-trained language models with Graph Neural Networks for scientific paper recommendation. This method addresses two key limitations of existing approaches: the inability to capture higher-order user-paper interaction information and the insufficient exploitation of deep semantic information from text.The CGCF approach follows a three-step process: (1) building a user-paper bipartite graph based on citation relationships, (2) using pre-trained language models to initialize paper embeddings from titles and abstracts, and (3) refining these embeddings through message-passing layers in the graph neural network to capture high-order connectivity information.### BertGCN for Scientific Document ClassificationThe BertGCN architecture has been adapted for scientific document classification tasks, combining the contextual understanding capabilities of BERT with the structural learning abilities of Graph Convolutional Networks. Jang et al. (2023) demonstrated the effectiveness of BertGCN variants for classifying scientific literature, showing that the composition parameter λ, which balances the contributions of BERT and GCN components, plays a crucial role in achieving high classification accuracy.The study revealed that BertGCN achieves consistently good performance when input text is sufficiently long, leveraging BERT's attention mechanism, while the GCN component captures citation-based relationships between documents. This hybrid approach outperforms both pure text-based and pure graph-based methods.### Advanced Fusion StrategiesZhang et al. (2023) proposed a BERT-based Graph Convolutional Neural Network (BERT-GCN) model that enhances scientific paper classification by incorporating multiple training strategies including span masking, learning rate attenuation, and data augmentation. This approach uses GCN to capture structural features from paper titles while BERT handles the deep semantic understanding of textual content.

### Literature Graph RepresentationsIda et al. (2023) developed a novel document classification method that incorporates representations from literature graphs created using both bibliographic and entity information. This approach goes beyond traditional citation-based methods by simultaneously considering multiple types of external information, including citation links, entity descriptions, and medical taxonomies.The method constructs a comprehensive literature graph that captures deep relationships among documents, addressing the limitation of previous approaches that only considered limited relationship types such as word co-occurrence and citation relationships. Experimental results on biomedical document classification datasets demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods.### Weighted Citation Networks with ExplanationZhang et al. (2021) proposed a Weighted Citation Network with Citation Links Explanation (WCN-CLE) algorithm that addresses the interpretability problem in citation recommendation. The approach extracts word fragments through citation network information to provide explanations for citation links, creating a weighted heterogeneous information network with papers and authors as vertices.This method integrates both structural information from the citation graph and semantic information from text content, using network representation learning to obtain vertex feature representations. The approach showed better performance on real-world datasets by effectively combining graph topology with textual semantics.

### Token Embedding Graph Neural NetworksAddressing the computational complexity issues inherent in combining language models with graph neural networks, Cai and Gan (2024) proposed the Token Embedding Graph Neural Network (TEGNN). This approach tackles the severe computational complexity problem that arises when cascading language models with GNNs, particularly as the complexity of GNN grows exponentially with the number of layers.TEGNN introduces a shared token embedding layer that serves as the knowledge link between the language model and GNN components, effectively decoupling the two modules without knowledge loss. Experimental results demonstrated a 70.17% reduction in training time while achieving a 1.04% improvement in classification accuracy.### Multistream ArchitecturesLi et al. (2023) developed a Multistream BERT Graph Convolutional Network (MS-BertGCN) that constructs multiple heterogeneous graphs from different combinations of documents based on within-class similarity. This approach addresses the limitation of using only original documents in corpus construction, potentially losing effective information in the graph topology.

### Hybrid GNN-LLM Approaches for Knowledge GraphsIvanisenko et al. (2024) proposed a hybrid approach combining text-mining techniques with graph neural networks and fine-tuned large language models to extend biomedical knowledge graphs. This method uses citation information and published literature to interpret predicted edges in knowledge graphs, with LLMs providing validation and explanations for predictions.The approach achieved high performance with a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.772 on experimentally confirmed protein interactions, demonstrating the potential of combining citation graph information with modern language models for scientific knowledge discovery.### Citation Context AnalysisKarim et al. (2022) developed methods for citation context analysis using combined feature embedding and deep convolutional neural networks. This work focuses on understanding the qualitative aspects of citations, analyzing the sentiments expressed in citation contexts to provide more nuanced evaluation of research impact beyond simple citation counts.

The integration of citation graphs with neural language models has proven to be a powerful approach for improving performance on scientific document tasks. The key innovations include:1. **Pre-training with Citation Signals**: Models like SPECTER have demonstrated that using citation relationships as training signals during pre-training can significantly improve document-level representations.2. **Hybrid Architectures**: Combining pre-trained language models with graph neural networks allows models to leverage both textual semantic information and structural relationships in citation networks.3. **Temporal Dynamics**: Incorporating temporal aspects of citation networks enables models to capture the evolving nature of scientific impact and relevance.4. **Computational Efficiency**: Novel architectures like TEGNN address the computational challenges of combining language models with graph neural networks, making these approaches more practical for large-scale applications.5. **Knowledge Enhancement**: Using citation graphs as sources of external knowledge helps improve model performance on tasks requiring understanding of inter-document relationships.The field continues to evolve with new approaches addressing scalability, interpretability, and effectiveness across different scientific domains. Future research directions include developing more sophisticated fusion mechanisms, incorporating additional types of scientific relationships beyond citations, and creating more efficient architectures that can handle the ever-growing scale of scientific literature.

question: How do different fairness metrics correlate with each other across various datasets and model architectures?

sections.text: The correlation between different fairness metrics across various datasets and model architectures is a complex and multifaceted issue that has significant implications for machine learning practitioners. Research consistently shows that fairness metrics are often incompatible with each other, exhibit dataset-dependent behavior, and vary significantly across different model architectures. This report synthesizes current research findings to provide a comprehensive understanding of fairness metric correlations and their practical implications.

The theoretical foundation for understanding fairness metric correlations lies in the well-established impossibility theorem of fairness. This theorem demonstrates that common fairness metrics cannot be simultaneously satisfied except under very specific conditions (Bell et al., 2023). The impossibility theorem asserts that trade-offs between different fairness notions are mathematically inevitable when the prevalence of outcomes differs across groups or when perfect prediction accuracy is not achieved (Karthik, 2020).However, recent research has challenged the practical implications of this theorem. Bell et al. (2023) demonstrate that by slightly relaxing the strict mathematical requirements of the impossibility theorem to accommodate practitioners' perspectives, it becomes possible to identify models that satisfy seemingly incompatible fairness constraints. Their empirical analysis across five real-world datasets reveals that achieving fairness along multiple metrics for multiple groups is "much more possible than was previously believed" (Bell et al., 2023).

citations.title: The Possibility of Fairness: Revisiting the Impossibility Theorem in Practice
The Impossibility Theorem of Machine Fairness - A Causal Perspective

sections.text: Research consistently demonstrates that different fairness metrics exhibit limited correlation with each other. Cao et al. (2022) conducted an extensive correlation study between intrinsic and extrinsic fairness metrics across 19 contextualized language models, finding that "intrinsic and extrinsic metrics do not necessarily correlate in their original setting, even when correcting for metric misalignments, noise in evaluation datasets, and confounding factors" (Cao et al., 2022).Similarly, Delobelle et al. (2022) found that "many metrics are not compatible with each other and highly depend on (i) templates, (ii) attribute and target seeds and (iii) the choice of embeddings" when evaluating fairness in pre-trained language models. This incompatibility extends beyond natural language processing to other domains, as evidenced by systematic reviews showing that "different fairness metrics do not present uniform results for a given use case" (Pagano et al., 2023).

sections.text: The correlation between fairness metrics varies significantly across different datasets. Kamalaruban et al. (2024) demonstrated that "certain fairness metrics expose significant bias only after normalization, highlighting the impact of class imbalance" in transaction fraud detection models. This finding suggests that dataset characteristics, particularly class distribution and imbalance, play a crucial role in determining how fairness metrics correlate with each other.The systematic review by Pagano et al. (2023) identified 25 datasets spanning diverse domains including "criminal justice, image enhancement, finance, education, product pricing, and health," noting that dataset characteristics significantly influence fairness metric behavior. This domain-specific variation in metric correlation patterns emphasizes the importance of context-aware fairness evaluation.

Different model architectures exhibit distinct patterns in fairness metric correlations. Zheng et al. (2024) conducted a systematic empirical study examining the relationship between deep neural network fairness and coverage criteria across "five DNN models and nine fairness datasets." Their findings reveal that "the statistical correlation between coverage criteria and DNN fairness is limited" and that "models debiased by different bias mitigation methods have a lower correlation between coverage and fairness compared to the original models" (Zheng et al., 2024).The research demonstrates that architectural choices significantly impact fairness metric behavior. For instance, Iurada et al. (2024) evaluated "14 CD approaches together with 3 state-of-the-art fairness algorithms on 5 datasets of faces and medical images," finding that cross-domain learning approaches can outperform traditional fairness algorithms, suggesting that architectural innovations may help reconcile seemingly incompatible fairness metrics.

citations.title: An Empirical Study on Correlations Between Deep Neural Network Fairness and Neuron Coverage Criteria

sections.text: Comprehensive studies across multiple architectures reveal significant variations in fairness metric correlations. The research by Iurada et al. (2024) introduced a "new Harmonic Fairness (HF) score that can ease unfairness mitigation model comparisons," recognizing the need for unified evaluation frameworks that account for architectural differences in fairness metric behavior.The systematic evaluation challenges are further highlighted by Robertson et al. (2024), who note that "many FairML tools still optimize or constrain for a single fairness objective" despite the known incompatibilities between metrics. Their work introduces a "human-in-the-loop, fairness-aware model selection framework that enables practitioners to effectively navigate complex and nuanced fairness objective landscapes" (Robertson et al., 2024).

citations.title: A Human-in-the-Loop Fairness-Aware Model Selection Framework for Complex Fairness Objective Landscapes

sections.text: In NLP applications, fairness metric correlations exhibit unique patterns influenced by linguistic and contextual factors. Cao et al. (2022) found that the relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic fairness metrics in language models is particularly complex, with correlations varying significantly based on the specific task and evaluation context. The study emphasizes that "fairness or bias evaluation remains challenging for contextualized language models" due to the subjective nature of fairness assessments (Delobelle et al., 2022).

citations.title: Measuring Fairness with Biased Rulers: A Comparative Study on Bias Metrics for Pre-trained Language Models

sections.text: Computer vision applications demonstrate different correlation patterns, particularly in medical imaging contexts. Iurada et al. (2024) introduced landmark detection tasks to fairness evaluation "for the first time in the fairness literature, showing how keypoint localization may be affected by sensitive attribute biases." Their analysis across "5 datasets of faces and medical images spanning several demographic groups" revealed that fairness metric correlations vary significantly based on the specific computer vision task and demographic composition of the dataset.

In recommender systems, fairness metric correlations are influenced by user behavior patterns and item characteristics. Huebner et al. (2024) found that "accuracy and fairness can be achieved simultaneously with the right modeling approach, while diversity can be held constant using these modeling techniques" in news recommendation systems. However, they also noted that "very little empirical research has been done, especially comparing multiple algorithms across different metrics" (Huebner et al., 2024).

citations.title: Evaluating Group Fairness in News Recommendations: A Comparative Study of Algorithms and Metrics

sections.text: The research consistently points to the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks that account for metric incompatibilities. Robertson et al. (2024) advocate for treating "fairness metrics as conflicting objectives in a multi-objective (MO) sense," proposing frameworks that help practitioners "navigate complex and nuanced fairness objective landscapes" rather than optimizing for single metrics.

Given the significant variation in metric correlations across datasets and architectures, practitioners should adopt context-aware approaches to fairness evaluation. The systematic review by Pagano et al. (2023) emphasizes that "more research with varied model architectures is necessary to standardize which ones are more appropriate for a given context."

The research suggests that fairness metric correlations are highly dependent on both dataset characteristics and model architectures. Practitioners should consider:
1. Dataset characteristics: Class imbalance, domain-specific features, and demographic composition significantly influence metric correlations
2. Architectural choices: Different model architectures exhibit distinct patterns in fairness metric behavior
3. Task-specific requirements: The choice of fairness metrics should align with specific application requirements and constraints

The correlation between different fairness metrics across various datasets and model architectures is characterized by complexity, context-dependency, and inherent incompatibilities. While the theoretical impossibility theorem provides important foundational understanding, practical applications reveal that achieving fairness along multiple metrics is more feasible than previously believed, particularly when evaluation approaches account for real-world constraints and practitioner perspectives.Key findings from the research include:
1. Limited inherent correlation: Different fairness metrics exhibit limited correlation with each other, necessitating multi-metric evaluation approaches
2. Dataset dependency: Correlation patterns vary significantly across different datasets, influenced by factors such as class imbalance and domain characteristics
3. Architecture sensitivity: Model architectures significantly impact fairness metric behavior and correlations
4. Context specificity: Domain-specific considerations play crucial roles in determining appropriate fairness evaluation strategiesFuture research should focus on developing standardized evaluation frameworks that account for these complexities while providing practical guidance for practitioners navigating the challenging landscape of fairness metric selection and evaluation.

question: How has literature discussed AI as a design material?

sections.text:
Executive Summary
The concept of artificial intelligence (AI) as a design material has emerged as a significant area of inquiry in human-computer interaction (HCI), user experience (UX) design, and design research. This report synthesizes current literature to explore how scholars and practitioners have conceptualized, theorized, and operationalized AI as a design material. The analysis reveals that AI as a design material represents a paradigm shift from traditional design approaches, introducing unique characteristics that challenge conventional design methodologies and require new frameworks for understanding and practice.

Introduction
The notion of AI as a design material has gained prominence as artificial intelligence technologies become increasingly integrated into everyday products and services. Unlike traditional design materials with fixed properties, AI presents unique challenges and opportunities that require designers to reconceptualize their approaches to creating user experiences. This report examines how literature has discussed AI as a design material across multiple dimensions: theoretical foundations, practical challenges, methodological approaches, and implications for design practice.

Literature Search and Methodology
This review is based on a comprehensive search of academic literature focusing on AI as a design material, human-AI interaction design, and related concepts. The analysis synthesizes findings from peer-reviewed papers, conference proceedings, and theoretical frameworks published between 2018 and 2024.

1. Theoretical Foundations and Conceptual Frameworks

### 1.1 AI as a New Design Material

Literature has established AI as fundamentally different from traditional design materials. Sangüesa and Guersenzvaig (2019) examine AI as a design material with special traits that require new approaches to design practice^1^. The authors question how design should incorporate AI technologies and what ethical implications arise from this integration^1^. This foundational work establishes AI as possessing unique characteristics that distinguish it from conventional materials.

The concept of intelligence as a design material has been further developed by recognizing that AI becomes available as a resource for non-experts like HCI/UX professionals. As articulated in the literature, "intelligence is becoming a new design material" where designers must understand how to work with intelligence as they would with traditional materials like plastic, wood, or metal^2^. This analogy emphasizes the need for designers to understand AI's properties and limitations to create effective user experiences.

### 1.2 Materiality and Agency

Literature has explored the materiality of AI, particularly its dynamic and agentive properties. Caprotti et al. (2024) discuss how AI technologies "have social and material power: they perform work, anticipate and assess risks and opportunities, are aberrant or glitchy, cause accidents, and make new demands on humans"^3^. This understanding of AI's materiality emphasizes its active role in shaping interactions and experiences, moving beyond passive design materials.

The concept of AI as having agency has been further developed in discussions of AI's role in urban contexts, where AI technologies are seen as actors that shape social and material environments^3^. This perspective has implications for how designers understand their role when working with AI as a material.

### 1.3 Frameworks for Understanding AI as Design Material

Literature has proposed various frameworks for understanding AI as a design material. Yang (2021) presents a framework that treats AI systems as "living socio-technical systems that co-evolve with their users"^4^. This framework analogizes the shift to AI design with the transition from desktop computing to ubiquitous computing, suggesting fundamental changes in how designers approach their work^4^.

The concept of Material Lifecycle Thinking (MLT) has been introduced to consider machine learning as a design material throughout its entire lifecycle. This framework recognizes that AI materials have temporal dimensions and evolutionary characteristics that traditional materials lack^5^.

citations.title: AI in HCI Design and User Experience
Design Heuristics for Artificial Intelligence: Inspirational Design Stimuli for Supporting UX Designers in Generating AI-Powered Ideas

sections.text:
2. Practical Challenges and Communication

### 2.1 UX Practitioners' Challenges with AI

Research has identified specific challenges that UX practitioners face when working with AI as a design material. Feng et al. (2023) conducted a comprehensive study with 27 UX practitioners, finding that "UXPs face novel challenges when working with and communicating artificial intelligence (AI) as a design material"^6^. The study revealed that practitioners struggle to clearly communicate AI concepts, though hands-on experience with AI models helped broaden common ground with technical stakeholders^6^.

The research demonstrates that UX practitioners can identify key risks and benefits of AI in their designs and propose concrete next steps for both UX and AI work when given appropriate tools and experiences^6^. This suggests that the challenge lies not in practitioners' inability to work with AI, but in the need for better tools and methodologies to support this work.

### 2.2 Black Box Problem

Literature has addressed the "black box" nature of AI systems as a significant challenge for designers. Kelliher et al. (2018) examine AI as a "formative material to design with, often requiring a nuanced, pragmatic, or indeed skeptical mindset"^7^. The authors discuss how issues of transparency, ethics, bias, and privacy emerge as central concerns when designing with AI^7^.

The black box problem creates challenges for designers who need to understand material properties to work effectively. Traditional design materials have predictable properties, but AI systems may behave in unexpected ways, making it difficult for designers to anticipate user experiences^7^.

### 2.3 Communication and Collaboration

Literature has explored how AI as a design material affects communication and collaboration between designers and technical stakeholders. The concept of "tinkering with AI" has been identified as important for broadening common ground between UX practitioners and engineers^6^. This hands-on approach to working with AI helps designers develop better understanding of AI capabilities and limitations.

Research has also highlighted the importance of multi-stakeholder communication when crafting human-centered AI experiences. The literature suggests that traditional handoff approaches from design to engineering are insufficient when working with AI, requiring more collaborative approaches throughout the design process^6^.

3. Methodological Approaches and Design Processes

### 3.1 Co-Creation and Collaborative Design

Literature has emphasized the need for new methodological approaches when working with AI as a design material. Research has shown that conventional human-centered design approaches, which follow linear or top-down processes, are insufficient for AI design^8^. The dynamic nature of AI material requires design processes that allow for parallel development of AI capabilities and user experience design^8^.

The concept of co-creation has emerged as a key methodological approach. Literature describes how "AI material and its application UX need to be co-created through collaboration between designers and AI engineers"^8^. This approach recognizes that AI's properties cannot be fully specified in advance but must be discovered and shaped through iterative design processes.

### 3.2 Data Probes and Design Tools

Research has identified the crucial role of end-user data as a tool for co-creating AI design material. The concept of "data probes" has been introduced as a method for designers to construct "designerly proxies" and specify material needs for AI^8^. Data probes facilitate divergent thinking, material testing, and design validation in AI design processes^8^.

Literature has explored how data probes enable designers to work with AI material without requiring deep technical knowledge. These tools allow designers to explore AI capabilities and limitations through hands-on experimentation, similar to how designers might test traditional materials^8^.

### 3.3 Participatory Design Approaches

The literature has discussed participatory approaches to AI design, recognizing that stakeholders affected by AI systems should participate in their design. Delgado et al. (2023) present a conceptual framework for evaluating participatory approaches in AI design, derived from synthesis of literature across technology design, political theory, and the social sciences^9^.

This participatory turn in AI design reflects recognition that AI as a design material has social and political implications that require broader stakeholder involvement in design processes^9^. The literature suggests that traditional designer-centric approaches are insufficient for addressing the complex social implications of AI systems.

citations.title: Towards A Process Model for Co-Creating AI Experiences

sections.text:
4. Implications for Design Practice

### 4.1 Changing Role of Designers

Literature has explored how AI as a design material changes the role of designers. Research suggests that with AI as a design material, "the primary role for HCI/UX designers is currently transitioning to augment end users with extended capabilities"^10^. Designers are becoming "creators of the interface between humans and technology by leveraging algorithms"^10^.

This shift requires designers to understand AI not just as a tool but as a capability that can be configured to support specific user experiences. The literature suggests that designers must learn to view AI as "an application service tailored to a specific functionality to support a particular experience"^10^.

### 4.2 Ethical and Social Considerations

Literature has emphasized the ethical implications of AI as a design material. Research has identified several limitations of algorithms that impact their use as design materials, including that "algorithms are not neutral or objective" and "have a point of view with potentially biased outputs"^10^.

The literature suggests that designers working with AI material must develop critical awareness of these limitations and their implications for user experiences. This includes understanding how AI systems can perpetuate biases and create unfair outcomes for different user groups^7^.

### 4.3 New Design Competencies

Literature has identified new competencies that designers need when working with AI as a design material. These include understanding AI capabilities and limitations, ability to work with data and algorithms, and skills in collaborative design processes with technical stakeholders^6^.

Research has also highlighted the importance of developing "AI literacy" among designers, including understanding of machine learning concepts, data requirements, and algorithmic decision-making processes^6^. This literacy is essential for effective communication and collaboration in AI design projects.

5. Applications and Case Studies

### 5.1 Domain-Specific Applications

Literature has explored applications of AI as a design material across various domains. In architectural design, research has examined how AI can serve as a design partner rather than a tool, emphasizing the need to integrate multi-modal AI systems with existing parametric design tools^11^. This work demonstrates how AI as a design material requires domain-specific adaptation and integration with existing design practices.

In materials science, literature has explored how AI enables new paradigms for material design and manufacturing. Research describes a transformation from "designing the materials" to "designing with materials," where AI becomes integral to the design process itself^12^. This shift illustrates how AI as a design material can fundamentally change design paradigms within specific domains.

### 5.2 Educational Applications

Literature has examined the application of AI as a design material in educational contexts. Research has explored how AI can support learning while maintaining human agency and skill development. The concept of "human-machine teaming" has been introduced as an approach that goes beyond "human-in-the-loop" approaches to create "synergistic interactions in which machines help people think critically and gain wisdom"^13^.

This educational application of AI as a design material demonstrates how the concept extends beyond traditional HCI contexts to encompass broader considerations of human development and learning^13^.

### 5.3 Urban and Smart City Applications

Literature has explored AI as a design material in urban contexts, examining how AI technologies shape urban experiences and governance. Research has recognized that AI systems in urban contexts "do not merely layer onto existing urban infrastructures" but actively shape "forms of management and practices of everyday life"^3^.

This urban application of AI as a design material illustrates how the concept has implications for large-scale systems and policy design, not just individual user interfaces^3^.

sections.text:
6. Future Directions and Research Opportunities

### 6.1 Emerging Frameworks and Models

Literature has identified several emerging frameworks for understanding and working with AI as a design material. The concept of "User Experience 3.0 (UX 3.0)" has been proposed as a paradigm framework for human-centered AI systems, recognizing that traditional UX approaches require significant adaptation for AI contexts^14^.

Research has also explored the development of standardized approaches to human-computer interaction design for AI products, suggesting the need for systematic frameworks to guide practice^15^. This work indicates ongoing efforts to establish more structured approaches to AI design.

### 6.2 Tool Development and Support Systems

Literature has identified the need for better tools to support designers working with AI as a design material. Research has called for "recommendations for design and AI tools to enhance multi-stakeholder communication and collaboration when crafting human-centered AI experiences"^6^.

The literature suggests that future tool development should focus on making AI more accessible to designers while maintaining the ability to work with AI's unique properties and constraints^6^. This includes developing better visualization tools, prototyping environments, and collaboration platforms.

### 6.3 Research Gaps and Opportunities

Literature has identified several research gaps in understanding AI as a design material. These include the need for better understanding of how designers conceptualize AI material properties, development of evaluation methods for AI design processes, and investigation of long-term implications of AI integration in design practice^6^.

Research has also highlighted the need for more diverse perspectives in AI design research, including greater attention to participatory approaches and consideration of social justice implications^9^.

sections.text:
Conclusion
The literature reveals that AI as a design material represents a fundamental shift in design practice, theory, and methodology. Unlike traditional design materials with fixed properties, AI presents unique challenges including dynamic behavior, agency, ethical implications, and requirements for collaborative design processes. The literature has established theoretical foundations for understanding AI as a design material while identifying practical challenges that designers face in working with these technologies.

Key contributions of the literature include: recognition of AI's unique material properties including agency and dynamism; development of frameworks for understanding AI as a socio-technical material; identification of communication and collaboration challenges in AI design; proposal of new methodological approaches including co-creation and participatory design; and exploration of ethical and social implications of AI as a design material.

The literature suggests that successful integration of AI as a design material requires new competencies, tools, and collaborative approaches. Future research should focus on developing better support systems for designers, establishing standardized frameworks for AI design practice, and addressing ethical and social justice implications of AI integration in design.

This comprehensive review demonstrates that AI as a design material is not merely a technological advancement but a paradigm shift that requires fundamental reconsideration of design theory, practice, and education. The literature provides a foundation for this reconsideration while identifying numerous opportunities for future research and development.

question: What are the best practices to protect a software against vulnerabilities from third party libraries?

sections.text: Modern software development heavily relies on third-party libraries and dependencies, with studies showing that 97% of applications use open-source software and 78% of code comes from third-party sources (Zahan, 2023). However, this widespread adoption has created significant security risks, as evidenced by a 700% increase in software supply chain attacks (Zahan, 2023). This report examines the current state of research on best practices for protecting software against vulnerabilities from third-party libraries, providing evidence-based recommendations for practitioners.

citations.title: Software Supply Chain Risk Assessment Framework

sections.text: Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tools are essential for identifying and managing vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies. These tools "scan the dependency networks, and cross-reference them with known vulnerabilities catalogued in databases such as the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) and the GitHub Advisory Database" (Fretter et al., 2023). Research shows that SCA tools primarily differ in three key dimensions: vulnerability database sources, dependency scanning techniques, and additional analysis capabilities for inferring dependency usage (Naseer et al., 2021). However, practitioners must be aware of the limitations of SCA tools. A comparative study found that "the count of reported vulnerable dependencies ranges from 17 to 332 for Maven and from 32 to 239 for npm projects across the studied tools" (Naseer et al., 2021). This variation highlights the importance of not relying on a single tool, as "practitioners should not rely on any single tool at the present, as that can result in missing known vulnerabilities" (Naseer et al., 2021). Accurate identification of third-party libraries is crucial for effective vulnerability management. Advanced fingerprinting techniques like OSSFP have demonstrated significant improvements in detection accuracy, achieving "90.84% of recall and 90.34% of precision" while being "22 times faster than the other tool" (Wu et al., 2023). These tools work by "removing common and trivial functions and keeping only the core functions to build the fingerprint index for each TPL project" (Wu et al., 2023).

sections.text: The integration of automated vulnerability scanning into CI/CD pipelines represents a critical best practice for early vulnerability detection. This "Shift-Left Security" approach ensures that "development teams can identify vulnerabilities related to container images early in the pipeline" (Alqahtani et al., 2024). The methodology enables organizations to "identify and correct problems with container images as early as possible in the development life cycle" (Alqahtani et al., 2024). Vulnerability scanning tools can be seamlessly integrated into CI/CD pipelines through platforms like "Jenkins, GitLab CI, or Azure DevOps" allowing "developers to receive immediate feedback on security vulnerabilities and weaknesses introduced by code changes" (Sharma & Sharma, 2024). This integration enables "automatic scanning for vulnerabilities during the building process" ensuring that "vulnerabilities are discovered and then solved within the system during the production stage" (Alqahtani et al., 2024). Effective vulnerability management requires scanning at multiple stages of the development pipeline. This includes: - Static Analysis: Tools that "inspect the container image painlessly to identify the Rice vulnerabilities using real signatures or criteria" (Alqahtani et al., 2024) - Dynamic Analysis: Systems that "trace vulnerabilities that can only emerge as from the process of running the system in real time" (Alqahtani et al., 2024) - Dependency Scanning: Tools that "analyse third-party dependencies, libraries, and components for known vulnerabilities and security issues" (Sharma & Sharma, 2024)

sections.text: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) has emerged as a critical component for supply chain security. An SBOM is "a formal, machine-readable inventory of software components and dependencies, information about those components, and their relationships" (Hussein et al., 2024). The importance of SBOMs has been emphasized by government mandates, with "the Biden administration signed the Executive Order on Improving the Nation's Cybersecurity in May 2021" requiring SBOMs for federal software procurement (Hussein et al., 2024). The SBOM lifecycle involves two critical phases: generation and consumption. Research indicates that "SBOMs can facilitate vulnerability management" by providing transparency into software composition (Antonopoulou et al., 2024). Current SBOM formats include "Software Identification (SWID) tagging, Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX), and CycloneDx" (Antonopoulou et al., 2024). SBOMs enable vulnerability scanners to "check the presence of known vulnerabilities without retrieving the dependency list" (Antonopoulou et al., 2024). Modern vulnerability scanners such as "ShiftLeftScan, Grype, KubeClarity, Bomber use the SBOM as source for their analysis of dependencies" (Antonopoulou et al., 2024).

sections.text: Effective dependency management requires comprehensive risk assessment of third-party providers. This involves "evaluating third-party providers' security protocols, performance history, and adherence to industry standards" as part of "a comprehensive risk assessment process" (Emeka, 2024). Organizations must balance the benefits of leveraging external components against the risks of "over-dependence on third-party components" which can create vulnerabilities if external entities "experience breaches or fail to maintain adequate security measures" (Emeka, 2024). Timely patching represents a critical defense mechanism. Research emphasizes that "vulnerable versions should be identified, vulnerability patches should be back-ported to these versions, and affected dependants should be identified and updated" (Xie et al., 2024). To minimize risks during updates, organizations can employ "multi-version execution techniques to roll back any failing updates" (Xie et al., 2024). Organizations should implement debloating techniques to reduce attack surface. Developers can "use debloating techniques to trim redundant dependencies from a software system" (Xie et al., 2024). This approach minimizes "the reliance on (vulnerability-inducing) third-party components" (Xie et al., 2024).

sections.text: Effective governance requires establishing processes that address "license compliance, component approval, and supply chain management" (Harutyunyan & Riehle, 2023). Organizations need comprehensive policies that cover "license management, dependency management, and vulnerability localization and repair" as "key steps in ensuring the security of software systems" (Zeng et al., 2024). Organizations must implement "continuous monitoring of vulnerability data from open source package ecosystems" (Naseer et al., 2021). This includes establishing "frameworks and metrics to identify false positives for dependency vulnerabilities" (Naseer et al., 2021). The governance framework should ensure "adherence to security standards, industry regulations, and organizational policies" (Alqahtani et al., 2024).

This represents advancement beyond traditional "code-level similarity comparison" methods (Xu et al., 2024). Future approaches must address "ecosystem-wide intervention strategies to maximize the overall health of the ecosystem in the presence of known vulnerabilities or emerging security threats" (Xie et al., 2024). This includes managing "new types of dependencies in emerging systems" including "pre-trained models, and cloud services, beyond third-party libraries" (Xie et al., 2024).

sections.text: Protecting software against vulnerabilities from third-party libraries requires a multi-faceted approach combining automated scanning tools, comprehensive governance frameworks, and proactive dependency management. The research clearly indicates that no single tool or approach is sufficient; organizations must implement layered security strategies that include SCA tools, SBOM implementation, CI/CD integration, and continuous monitoring. As the software supply chain continues to evolve, organizations must stay informed about emerging threats and adapt their security practices accordingly. The evidence suggests that successful implementation of these best practices requires organizational commitment, appropriate tooling investment, and cultural shift toward security-first development practices. Organizations that fail to implement comprehensive third-party library security measures face significant risks, as demonstrated by the exponential increase in supply chain attacks targeting these dependencies.

question: What are some biologically-inspired robot path planning algorithms?

sections.text: This report provides a comprehensive overview of biologically-inspired robot path planning algorithms, which have emerged as effective solutions for autonomous navigation in complex environments. These algorithms draw inspiration from natural phenomena and biological behaviors to solve the challenging problem of finding optimal, collision-free paths for mobile robots. The algorithms covered include swarm intelligence approaches such as ant colony optimization, particle swarm optimization, and artificial bee colony, as well as evolutionary algorithms like genetic algorithms and neural network-based approaches.

Robot path planning is a fundamental challenge in autonomous robotics, requiring the generation of collision-free trajectories from a starting point to a target destination while optimizing various criteria such as path length, smoothness, and safety. Traditional path planning methods often struggle with complex environments, dynamic obstacles, and multi-objective optimization. Biologically-inspired algorithms offer solutions by mimicking natural processes that have evolved to solve optimization problems effectively (1). The field has evolved from static to dynamic environments, from two-dimensional to high-dimensional spaces, and from single-robot to multi-robot systems. Metaheuristic algorithms have become the most effective approach for solving complex optimization problems in mobile robot path planning due to their algorithmic intelligence and adaptability (2).

sections.text:
### 2.1 Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) Ant Colony Optimization is one of the most widely applied biologically-inspired algorithms for robot path planning. The algorithm mimics the foraging behavior of ants, which deposit pheromones on paths to communicate optimal routes to other ants. Recent developments include the Parallel Ant Colony Optimization (PACO) algorithm, which addresses traditional ACO problems of local optimum, susceptibility to deadlocks, and low search efficiency. The PACO algorithm constructs a rank-based pheromone updating method to balance exploration space and convergence speed, reducing average total time by 50.71%, 46.83%, and 46.03% on different grid map scales while maintaining solution accuracy (3). The Island-type ACO (INACO) algorithm represents another significant improvement, establishing intermediate islands between starting and ending positions to reduce deadlock ants. This approach achieved average iterative times of 2.7 in 20

20 grid environments and 4.7 in 30

30 grid environments, with significantly fewer lost ants (4). Fractional-order enhanced ACO has been developed specifically for car-like mobile robots (CLMRs) with suspension systems. This approach adopts a global multifactorial heuristic function with dynamic angle constraints, adaptive pheromone adjustment, and fractional-order state-transfer models to handle both narrow and large-scale scenes effectively (5). ### 2.2 Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) Particle Swarm Optimization algorithms simulate the social behavior of bird flocks or fish schools. Enhanced PSO (ePSO) algorithms have been combined with vertical cell decomposition methods for robot path planning and mapping. The approach uses middle points within decomposed cells, regulated by biologically-inspired optimization to generate optimal robot trajectories while approximating complex geometry more accurately (6). ### 2.3 Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) The Artificial Bee Colony algorithm mimics the foraging behavior of honey bees. The Node Movement Artificial Bee Colony (NMABC) algorithm addresses traditional ABC problems of high path complexity with increased nodes. It incorporates improved initial path generation methods and neighborhood search techniques for iterative path optimization (7). Multi-objective ABC algorithms have been developed to optimize both path length and path safety simultaneously. The Improved Multi-Objective ABC (IMO-ABC) incorporates path-shortening and path-crossing operators, variable neighborhood local search strategy, and global search strategy to enhance both exploitation and exploration capabilities (8). ### 2.4 Bacterial Foraging Optimization (BFO) Bacterial Foraging Optimization algorithms simulate the foraging behavior of E. coli bacteria. The Robust Bacterial Foraging (RBF) algorithm addresses the traditional BFO problem of getting stuck in local minima by generating virtual obstacles in problematic areas, causing robots to retract and regenerate safe paths. This approach is extendable to multiple robots through information sharing about virtual obstacles (9). BFO has been successfully applied to minimize path length and number of turns while avoiding collisions, demonstrating effectiveness in complex environments with various obstacle distributions (10).

sections.text: ### 3.1 Genetic Algorithms (GA) Genetic Algorithms simulate the process of natural selection and evolution. The Hybrid Adaptive Genetic Algorithm (HAGA) integrates an optimized two-optimization operator with enhanced Adaptive Genetic Algorithm for efficient path planning in diverse tasks and complex road conditions. HAGA divides solutions into TOP and ordinary layers, with the TOP layer optimized using adaptive operators and the ordinary layer using S-type and hyperbolic tangent functions (11). Recent improvements include directional guidance for population initialization and novel crossover operators. The Improved Genetic Algorithm (IGA) employs non-common point crossover operators, range mutation operators, and simplification operators to achieve better path planning results (12). ### 3.2 Metaheuristic Nature-Inspired Algorithms Various nature-inspired algorithms have been developed for path planning, including: - **Firefly Algorithm (FA)**: Simulates the flashing behavior of fireflies for optimization - **Cuckoo Search Algorithm (CS)**: Mimics the brood parasitic behavior of cuckoo birds - **Dragonfly Algorithm (DA)**: Based on the swarming behavior of dragonflies - **Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA)**: Inspired by the hunting behavior of humpback whales - **Sparrow Search Algorithm (SSA)**: Simulates the foraging and anti-predator behaviors of sparrows These algorithms focus on different aspects of optimization and have shown effectiveness in various environmental conditions (2).

sections.text: ### 4.1 Biologically Inspired Neural Networks (BINN) Biologically Inspired Neural Networks have been extensively applied in path planning, particularly for Complete Coverage Path Planning (CCPP) tasks. The improved BINN algorithm distinguishes connectivity between different environmental areas and uses path backtracking algorithms to autonomously plan collision-free paths while reducing path repetition ratios (13). The combination of BINN with Q-learning addresses problems of local optimal paths and high path coverage ratios. This hybrid approach introduces global environment information through reinforcement learning methods, optimizing path planning strategies near obstacles and achieving 100% coverage with lower path repetition ratios (14). Neural networks have also been combined with pedestrian location prediction using Kalman filter algorithms for active obstacle avoidance strategies, enabling collision-free trajectory planning in dynamic environments (15).

The approach uses improved RRT to create differentiated pheromone distributions, introduces dynamic strategies for evaporation coefficients, and employs reward-punishment mechanisms for pheromone updates (16). ### 5.2 Genetic Algorithm-Dynamic Window Approach The fusion of improved Genetic Algorithm with Dynamic Window Approach enhances robots' ability to avoid dynamic obstacles while solving shorter and smoother paths. This combination improves warehouse operation efficiency and reduces logistics costs (17). ### 5.3 Graph-Based Methods with Biologically Inspired Algorithms The synergy between graph-based methods and biologically inspired algorithms enhances robot path planning efficiency. Middle point cell decomposition combined with enhanced PSO leverages vertical cell decomposition as spatial partitioning technique, with middle points regulated by biologically inspired optimization (6).

question: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as kyber/dilithium compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?

sections.text: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms, particularly CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium, have emerged as the leading candidates for replacing RSA and ECDSA in the quantum era. This report analyzes their performance characteristics, energy consumption, and the potential impact of future hardware optimizations on their deployment.

Recent benchmarking studies reveal that post-quantum algorithms demonstrate competitive performance compared to classical cryptographic methods. CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium achieve efficient execution times, outperforming classical cryptographic schemes such as RSA and ECDSA at equivalent security levels (Performance Analysis and Industry Deployment of Post-Quantum Cryptography Algorithms). Key findings from constrained device testing show that CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium are the most efficient PQAs in key encapsulation and signature algorithms respectively (Constrained Device Performance Benchmarking with the Implementation of Post-Quantum Cryptography). In IoT environments, specifically on ARM processors, Kyber and Dilithium create keys faster than RSA but perform on par with ECC, with Dilithium showing at least 6% speedup in signature operations compared to ECC and RSA (QR TPM in Programmable Low-Power Devices). The computational load distribution varies significantly between PQC and classical algorithms. The Dilithium/Kyber stack distributes computational load more equally among server and client, while maintaining faster execution times compared to Falcon alternatives (Falcon/Kyber and Dilithium/Kyber Network Stack on Nvidia's Data Processing Unit Platform). However, lattice-based algorithms like Kyber require considerable computational resources despite offering a strong balance between security and efficiency (Performance Evaluation of Post-Quantum Cryptography: A Comprehensive Framework for Experimental Analysis).

sections.text: Energy efficiency analysis reveals that specialized hardware implementations significantly reduce power consumption for PQC algorithms. A highly-efficient lattice-based cryptography processor demonstrates that optimized designs can run at 200 MHz with only 2.01 mW for Kyber KEM 512 and 2.13 mW for Dilithium 2, achieving superior Performance x Power x Area (PPAP) metrics compared to state-of-the-art solutions (A Highly-efficient Lattice-based Post-Quantum Cryptography Processor for IoT Applications). Hardware accelerators show substantial energy efficiency improvements. For ASIC implementations, energy consumption reduction factors reach up to 9.5 for NewHope, 7.7 for Kyber, and 2.1 for Saber compared to pure software implementations (RISQ-V: Tightly Coupled RISC-V Accelerators for Post-Quantum Cryptography). The power consumption of hardware implementations varies significantly based on platform: FPGA implementations range from 0.37W to 1.20W, while ASIC implementations consume between 2.94W and 7.61W, with the higher ASIC consumption offset by significantly higher operating frequencies (Whipping the Multivariate-based MAYO Signature Scheme using Hardware Platforms).

sections.text: The Number Theoretic Transform represents one of the most computationally intensive components of Kyber and Dilithium algorithms. Hardware acceleration of NTT operations through specialized pipeline architectures and optimized butterfly operations significantly improves performance (Hardware Design and Optimization of Polynomial Multiplication for Post-Quantum Cryptography Algorithm Based on NTT). Advanced NTT implementations utilize recursive approaches and two-stage butterfly operations to reduce hardware complexity while maintaining high throughput (Hardware Design and Optimization of Polynomial Multiplication for Post-Quantum Cryptography Algorithm Based on NTT). Modern hardware optimizations leverage Single-Instruction-Multiple-Data (SIMD) architectures to accelerate polynomial operations. Customized SIMD implementations support efficient parallel execution of polynomial operations in 256-bit mode and acceleration of cryptographic hash functions in 320-bit mode (A Highly-efficient Lattice-based Post-Quantum Cryptography Processor for IoT Applications).
