question: What are the most important open challenges in Federated Learning?

sections.text: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a transformative machine learning paradigm that enables collaborative model training across distributed devices while preserving data privacy. However, despite its rapid growth and adoption, FL faces numerous significant challenges that limit its practical deployment and effectiveness. This report analyzes the most critical open challenges in federated learning based on recent research findings and identifies key areas requiring further investigation.

One of the most fundamental challenges in federated learning is the presence of non-independently and identically distributed (non-IID) data across participating clients. This heterogeneity significantly impacts model convergence and performance (Li et al., 2019)¹. The challenge manifests in several ways: - Distribution skew: Different clients may have vastly different data distributions, leading to biased local models - Convergence degradation: Non-IID data slows down convergence rates and can lead to suboptimal global models - Model drift: Local models may diverge significantly from the global optimum due to heterogeneous local data Research has shown that heterogeneity of data slows down convergence and requires careful consideration of learning rate schedules to prevent models from being stuck in suboptimal solutions (Li et al., 2019)¹.

System heterogeneity presents additional challenges beyond data distribution differences. Clients in federated learning networks often have varying computational capabilities, memory constraints, and network connectivity (Chen et al., 2024)². This heterogeneity creates: - Straggler effects: Slower devices can become bottlenecks in the training process - Resource constraints: Limited computational power and memory affect local training quality - Network variability: Inconsistent connectivity impacts communication efficiency and participation rates

While federated learning aims to preserve privacy by keeping data local, sharing model updates can still lead to privacy breaches. Several attack vectors have been identified: - Gradient inversion attacks: Malicious actors can reconstruct training data from shared gradients - Model inversion attacks: Attackers can extract sensitive information about training data from model parameters - Membership inference attacks: Adversaries can determine whether specific data points were used in training Chen et al. (2024)³ emphasize that despite FL's privacy-preserving design, the vulnerability of communication links and potential for cyber threats remain significant concerns.

Federated learning systems are vulnerable to various adversarial attacks that can compromise model integrity: - Data poisoning attacks: Malicious clients can inject corrupted data to degrade model performance - Model poisoning attacks: Adversaries can submit malicious model updates to compromise the global model - Byzantine attacks: Faulty or malicious participants can disrupt the training process Zhang et al. (2022)⁴ provide a comprehensive analysis of security threats from both malicious aggregators and participants, highlighting the need for robust defense mechanisms.

Communication costs represent a major bottleneck in federated learning deployments, particularly for resource-constrained devices: - Bandwidth limitations: Frequent model updates consume significant network resources - Latency issues: High communication latency can slow down training rounds - Energy consumption: Communication overhead affects battery life in mobile devices Research indicates that communication overhead can be reduced by up to 60% through efficient aggregation techniques and neighbor selection strategies (Chen et al., 2023)⁵.

As federated learning systems grow in size, scalability becomes increasingly challenging: - Server bottlenecks: Centralized aggregation servers can become performance bottlenecks - Client selection: Efficiently selecting participating clients from large populations - Model aggregation: Computational complexity of aggregating numerous model updates Malik (2024)⁶ identifies scalability hurdles stemming from communication overhead, resource constraints, and diverse client populations as major impediments to FL adoption.

Federated learning systems can perpetuate or amplify existing biases present in local datasets: - Minority group discrimination: Global models may discriminate against underrepresented groups - Performance disparities: Models may perform significantly better for some clients than others - Representation bias: Clients with larger datasets may dominate the learning process Wang et al. (2023)⁷ investigate how personalization in federated learning can impact fairness, particularly in healthcare applications where biased outcomes could exacerbate health disparities.

The tension between personalization and fairness presents a fundamental challenge: - Individual optimization: Personalized models may improve individual performance but reduce overall fairness - Global equity: Ensuring fair treatment across all participants while maintaining model quality - Dynamic fairness: Maintaining fairness as client populations and data distributions change over time Zhu et al. (2024)⁸ demonstrate that statistical heterogeneity creates tension among accuracy, fairness, and robustness, requiring careful balancing of these competing objectives.

The theoretical understanding of federated learning convergence remains incomplete, particularly under realistic conditions: - Non-convex optimization: Most practical FL applications involve non-convex problems with limited theoretical guarantees - Asynchronous updates: Real-world FL systems often involve asynchronous communication, complicating convergence analysis - Partial participation: Not all clients participate in every round, affecting convergence properties

Developing efficient federated learning algorithms requires addressing multiple competing objectives: - Communication-computation trade-offs: Balancing local computation with communication frequency - Aggregation strategies: Designing robust aggregation methods that handle heterogeneous updates - Adaptive methods: Developing algorithms that can adapt to changing network conditions and client populations Legler et al. (2024)⁹ emphasize the need for effective client selection strategies and solutions for ensuring system scalability and stability as new clients join the network.

The lack of standardized protocols and frameworks creates barriers to widespread adoption: - Protocol compatibility: Different FL implementations may not be interoperable - Evaluation metrics: Inconsistent evaluation criteria make it difficult to compare approaches - Deployment complexity: Complex setup and maintenance requirements limit practical adoption

Translating theoretical FL algorithms to practical deployments faces numerous challenges: - Device management: Handling dynamic client populations and device failures - Quality assurance: Ensuring model quality without direct access to training data - Regulatory compliance: Meeting data protection regulations across different jurisdictions Abbas et al. (2024)¹⁰ highlight the importance of addressing data heterogeneity, scalability, and system interoperability issues for successful FL deployment in healthcare systems.

Medical federated learning faces unique challenges due to regulatory requirements and data sensitivity: - Regulatory compliance: Meeting strict healthcare data protection regulations - Clinical validation: Ensuring model reliability for medical decision-making - Institutional barriers: Overcoming legal and institutional obstacles to data collaboration Yoo et al. (2022)¹¹ identify specific open problems in medical federated learning, including handling sensitive patient data and ensuring model interpretability for clinical use.

Federated learning in IoT environments presents additional challenges: - Resource constraints: Extremely limited computational and memory resources - Network instability: Unreliable connectivity and intermittent participation - Energy efficiency: Battery-powered devices require energy-efficient algorithms

Several emerging technologies show promise for addressing current FL challenges: - Blockchain integration: Using blockchain for secure and transparent model aggregation - Differential privacy: Advanced privacy-preserving techniques for stronger security guarantees - Homomorphic encryption: Enabling computation on encrypted model updates

Future research should focus on: - Adaptive algorithms: Developing FL algorithms that can automatically adapt to changing conditions - Multi-objective optimization: Balancing multiple competing objectives simultaneously - Theoretical guarantees: Providing stronger convergence guarantees under realistic conditions The comprehensive survey by Kairouz et al. (2019)¹² presents an extensive collection of open problems and challenges that continue to guide federated learning research.

Federated learning faces numerous interconnected challenges that must be addressed for widespread practical adoption. The most critical open challenges include: 1. Data and system heterogeneity: Developing robust algorithms that can handle diverse data distributions and system capabilities 2. Privacy and security: Strengthening privacy guarantees while defending against adversarial attacks 3. Communication efficiency: Reducing communication overhead while maintaining model quality 4. Fairness and bias: Ensuring equitable treatment across all participants 5. Theoretical foundations: Developing stronger theoretical understanding and guarantees 6. Practical deployment: Addressing real-world implementation challenges and standardization needs Addressing these challenges requires interdisciplinary collaboration between machine learning researchers, systems engineers, privacy experts, and domain specialists. The rapid growth of federated learning research demonstrates the community's commitment to solving these problems, but significant work remains to realize FL's full potential in practical applications. The future of federated learning depends on successfully navigating these challenges while maintaining the core principles of privacy preservation and collaborative learning. As the field continues to evolve, addressing these open challenges will be crucial for enabling the secure, efficient, and fair deployment of federated learning systems across diverse applications and domains.

question: What are good practices for detecting AI-generated texts in situations where false positives are extremely expensive?

sections.text: Based on the research I've gathered, I can now provide a comprehensive report on best practices for detecting AI-generated texts in situations where false positives are extremely expensive. Let me compile the findings into a structured report.

Detecting AI-generated text in situations where false positives carry extremely high costs requires a fundamentally different approach than standard AI detection systems. This report examines evidence-based strategies for minimizing false positive rates while maintaining acceptable detection performance, drawing from recent research in AI detection, ensemble methods, and high-stakes classification systems.

Current AI detection tools exhibit significant inconsistencies when applied to human-written content, producing false positives that can have devastating consequences in high-stakes environments (Elkhatat et al., 2023). Research demonstrates that existing detection tools show "inconsistencies, producing false positives and uncertain classifications" when evaluating authentic human content, with some tools misclassifying up to 16% of human-written text as AI-generated (Bellini et al., 2024).
The robustness of AI detection systems is particularly concerning given their susceptibility to adversarial attacks. Studies show that paraphrasing attacks can reduce detection accuracy from 70.3% to 4.6% while maintaining only a 1% false positive rate (Krishna et al., 2023). This vulnerability underscores the need for more robust approaches when false positives are costly.

Detecting AI-generated text in high-stakes environments requires a paradigm shift from accuracy-focused to reliability-focused approaches. The evidence strongly supports implementing conservative threshold settings, ensemble methods with corrective filtering, proactive watermarking, and human-in-the-loop verification systems. question: what are the advantages and disadvantages of visiotactile, piezoelectric, trieboelectric tactile sensors for robots?

sections.text: Visiotactile sensors offer several significant advantages for robotic applications. They provide high-resolution tactile information through optical sensing mechanisms, enabling detailed surface geometry and force estimation (Ren et al., 2024). These sensors can capture multiple sensing modalities simultaneously, including contact localization, normal force estimation, slip detection, and object geometry estimation, making them highly versatile for robotic manipulation tasks (Huang et al., 2023). Camera-based tactile sensors can provide high-density surface geometry and force information for robots during interaction with target objects, offering superior spatial resolution compared to traditional tactile sensors (Ren et al., 2024). The visual output from these sensors is compatible with existing machine learning techniques initially developed for computer vision, facilitating seamless integration into robotic learning frameworks (Qi et al., 2023).However, visiotactile sensors face significant limitations in robotic applications. The reduced object visibility that occurs when robots reach for objects or when grippers encompass objects during grasping creates challenges for continuous tracking (Huang et al., 2023). When mounted directly to robot wrists for closer perspective, these sensors generally increase the size and bulkiness of the end effector, leading to additional constraints on movement and reduced motion capabilities (Huang et al., 2023). Most existing visiotactile methods cannot achieve accurate reconstruction with high efficiency, which impedes their applications in robots due to computational overhead requirements (Ren et al., 2024). Additionally, the complexity of integrating cameras and lighting systems within fingertip-sized sensors presents significant engineering challenges, particularly for anthropomorphic hands where space constraints are critical (Qi et al., 2023).

sections.text: Piezoelectric tactile sensors demonstrate several compelling advantages for robotic applications. These sensors are inherently self-powered, converting external mechanical pressure into electrical energy without requiring external power sources, which makes them particularly important for energy-efficient robotic systems (Tang et al., 2024). They exhibit high sensitivity and fast response times, enabling accurate detection of dynamically changing tactile signals (Carluccio et al., 2023). Piezoelectric sensors can respond to a wide range of dynamic mechanical stimuli and convert them into measurable electrical signals, making possible accurate detection of object shapes, textures, and real-time touch sensing (Tang et al., 2024). PVDF-based piezoelectric sensors offer significant advantages in flexibility, stretchability, chemical stability, and electromechanical conversion compared to conventional rigid piezoelectric materials (Qi et al., 2023).Despite their advantages, piezoelectric tactile sensors have notable limitations for robotic applications. Inorganic piezoelectric materials such as PZT lack flexibility, hindering their application on complex curved surfaces typical of robotic hands and grippers (Carluccio et al., 2023). The sensors are primarily responsive to dynamic forces and may have limited capability for static force measurement, which can be problematic for certain robotic manipulation tasks (Huang et al., 2024). Piezoelectric sensors can be susceptible to environmental interference and noise, and their output signals may require complex signal processing and conditioning circuits (Dong & Huo, 2023). The fabrication process for high-performance piezoelectric tactile sensors can be complex and may involve specialized materials and manufacturing techniques (Tang et al., 2024).

sections.text: Triboelectric tactile sensors offer unique advantages for robotic applications, particularly in terms of energy efficiency and fabrication simplicity. These sensors are inherently self-powered, converting external mechanical energy into electricity through triboelectric effects, which can greatly reduce power consumption of the entire sensing system (Gao et al., 2024). They demonstrate excellent sensitivity and can detect various mechanical stimuli including pressure, sliding, and proximity without requiring external power sources (Zhao et al., 2024). Triboelectric sensors have advantages of easy fabrication, high efficiency, and a wider choice of materials compared to other sensor technologies (Sun et al., 2018). The fabrication methods for triboelectric sensors are relatively simple and cost-effective, making them suitable for large-scale production and integration into robotic systems (Gao et al., 2024). These sensors can achieve multi-modal sensing capabilities, including normal force detection, shear force sensing, and even three-dimensional tactile perception (Zhao et al., 2024).Triboelectric tactile sensors also present several challenges for robotic applications. The triboelectric effect can be sensitive to environmental conditions such as humidity and temperature, which may affect sensor performance and reliability in varying operating conditions (Gao et al., 2024). The sensors may experience signal degradation over time due to wear of the triboelectric surfaces, particularly in high-frequency contact applications common in robotic manipulation (Sun et al., 2018). Triboelectric sensors can be susceptible to electromagnetic interference and may require careful shielding and signal conditioning to maintain accuracy (Dong & Huo, 2023). The output signals from triboelectric sensors are typically AC in nature, which may require additional signal processing circuitry for integration with robotic control systems (Zhao et al., 2024). Additionally, achieving consistent and repeatable triboelectric properties across large sensor arrays can be challenging for manufacturing (Gao et al., 2024).

Crosstalk between sensing points, space requirements for wiring, and the physical size of sensing hardware represent major bottlenecks for increasing spatial resolution in robotic tactile sensing (Dong & Huo, 2023). The complexity of large-scale sensor arrays introduces additional challenges including noise from environmental interference and difficulties in efficient fabrication and user-friendly assembly (Huang et al., 2024). Recent advances in tactile sensing technologies suggest promising directions for robotic applications. The development of hybrid approaches combining multiple sensing mechanisms, such as piezoelectric and triboelectric devices, may offer enhanced performance characteristics (Sun et al., 2018). Self-powered tactile sensors, particularly those based on piezoelectric and triboelectric principles, are expected to play increasingly important roles in energy-efficient robotic systems (Tang et al., 2024). question: What datasets and methods are used to pre-train models on table specific tasks?

sections.text: Table pre-training has emerged as a crucial research area aimed at developing models that can understand and reason over tabular data. Recent progress in large language models has motivated researchers to explore similar pre-training approaches for structured tabular data, addressing the unique challenges posed by the two-dimensional nature of tables and their heterogeneous content.

The most commonly used datasets for table pre-training come from web-crawled table collections. **WikiTables** represents one of the most prominent datasets, containing over 1.6 million tables extracted from Wikipedia^[CT-BERT: Learning Better Tabular Representations Through Cross-Table Pre-training]. This dataset provides high-quality tables with clear semantics and has been widely adopted due to its structured nature and contextual information including captions, page titles, and section titles.WebTables constitutes another major dataset, with the latest corpus containing 233 million tables extracted from HTML pages from Common Crawl^[TabLib: A Dataset of 627M Tables with Context]. The **WDC WebTable Corpus** provides an additional 125 million tables, offering substantial scale for pre-training large models^[ENTRANT: A Large Financial Dataset for Table Understanding].### Specialized Domain Datasets**ENTRANT** represents a significant contribution to financial domain table understanding, comprising millions of tables transformed to reflect cell attributes, positional and hierarchical information^[ENTRANT: A Large Financial Dataset for Table Understanding]. This dataset demonstrates the importance of domain-specific table collections for specialized applications.**GitTables** provides a different perspective by extracting tables from CSV files hosted on GitHub, containing approximately 1 million tables^[TabLib: A Dataset of 627M Tables with Context]. This dataset offers structural diversity compared to HTML-centric web tables.### Comprehensive Multi-Source CollectionsRecent work has focused on combining multiple data sources to create more comprehensive pre-training corpora. **CT-BERT** utilizes nearly 2,000 high-quality tabular datasets, each guaranteed to possess clear semantics and clean labels^[CT-BERT: Learning Better Tabular Representations Through Cross-Table Pre-training]. TUTA combines web tables from Wikipedia with the WDC WebTable corpus and web-crawled spreadsheets to compile a dataset of 57.9 million tables^[TUTA: Tree-based Transformers for Generally Structured Table Pre-training]. This approach ensures both volume and diversity by including different table structures and document types.

The dominant approach in table pre-training employs transformer-based architectures, with most methods adapting BERT-style models for tabular data. **TaBERT** represents a foundational work that pre-trains on a substantial corpus of 26 million tables and their corresponding English contexts, effectively acquiring contextual representations for both utterance tokens and structured database schemas^[TREB: a BERT attempt for imputing tabular data imputation].**TAPEX** introduces a novel approach by learning a neural SQL executor over synthetic data, addressing data scarcity through automatically synthesized executable SQL queries and their execution outputs^[TAPEX: Table Pre-training via Learning a Neural SQL Executor]. This method achieved state-of-the-art results on WikiSQL (89.5% accuracy), WikiTableQuestions (57.5% accuracy), SQA (74.5% accuracy), and TabFact (84.2% accuracy).### Specialized Pre-training ObjectivesModern table pre-training methods employ various specialized objectives tailored to tabular data characteristics. **TaBERT** uses two main objectives: masked column prediction (MCP) to learn general column information and cell value recovery (CVR) to capture representative cell values related to utterances^[TaBERT: Pretraining for Joint Understanding of Textual and Tabular Data].**PASTA** proposes sentence-table cloze pre-training specifically for fact verification tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of task-specific pre-training objectives^[PASTA: Table-Operations Aware Fact Verification via Sentence-Table Cloze Pre-training].### Structural Encoding ApproachesEffective table pre-training requires careful consideration of structural information. Methods primarily focus on two areas: architectural enhancements and training refinements. Architectural innovations include incorporating table structure into models through encoding structural information at input layers or embedding such information within internal model mechanisms^[A Hierarchical Multi-Task Learning Framework for Semantic Annotation in Tabular Data].**PORTAL** employs modified transformer encoders with column name embeddings instead of traditional positional encodings, allowing the model to recognize structural attributes where importance is dictated by column names rather than sequential order^[PORTAL: Scalable Tabular Foundation Models via Content-Specific Tokenization].### Generative Approaches**TapTap** represents the first attempt to leverage generative table pre-training for tabular prediction, pre-training on large corpora of real-world tabular data to generate high-quality synthetic tables^[Generative Table Pre-training Empowers Models for Tabular Prediction]. This approach supports various applications including privacy protection, low-resource scenarios, missing value imputation, and imbalanced classification.### Multi-Modal Pre-trainingRecent work has explored combining tabular and textual information. **OTTeR** conducts retrieval-centric mixed-modality synthetic pre-training to enhance representation learning through modality-enhanced representation and mixed-modality negative sampling strategies^[Mixed-modality Representation Learning and Pre-training for Joint Table-and-Text Retrieval in OpenQA].

Table pre-training methods are typically evaluated on several benchmark tasks including:Question Answering: WikiTableQuestions, SQA (Sequential Question Answering)Fact Verification: TabFact datasetSemantic Parsing: WikiSQL datasetTable Classification: Various cell type and table type classification tasksThe **OpenRT** framework provides a standardized evaluation environment for comparing different table pre-training models across multiple tasks, implementing six different models on question answering, fact checking, and text generation datasets^[OpenRT: An Open-source Framework for Reasoning Over Tabular Data].

Despite significant progress, table pre-training faces several challenges. The scarcity of large-scale, high-quality tabular data compared to text corpora remains a fundamental limitation. Additionally, the heterogeneous nature of tables across different domains and the need for cross-table generalization present ongoing research challenges.Recent work on **TabSketchFM** introduces sketch-based approaches to enhance data discovery effectiveness, demonstrating significant improvements in unionable, joinable, and subset table identification tasks^[TabSketchFM: Sketch-based Tabular Representation Learning for Data Discovery over Data Lakes].

question: What interfaces have researchers developed for helping people optimize LLMs for a task, and what are the biggest remaining user problems?

sections.text: The field of Large Language Model (LLM) optimization has rapidly evolved, with researchers developing various interfaces to help users customize and improve LLM performance for specific tasks. This report examines the current state of interfaces developed for LLM optimization and identifies the primary user challenges that remain unresolved.

Recent research has introduced several interface approaches focused on prompt engineering and evaluation. CoPrompter represents a significant advancement in this area, providing a framework that identifies misalignment between LLM responses and prompt instructions [CoPrompter: User-Centric Evaluation of LLM Instruction Alignment for Improved Prompt Engineering]. The system generates evaluation criteria questions derived directly from prompt requirements and transforms these into user-editable checklists. This approach addresses the challenge of "heavy human involvement and tedious trial-and-error" that characterizes traditional prompt engineering processes.Several interfaces have been developed to democratize LLM fine-tuning and personalization. Watson et al. propose an end-to-end personal fine-tuning framework that incorporates user-friendly tools for identification, annotation, and simulation across diverse contexts [Towards an End-to-End Personal Fine-Tuning Framework for AI Value Alignment]. Their framework aims to create a token-based system that allows users to easily impart their values and preferences to AI systems, thereby reducing the complexity of value elicitation and personalization.The PEFT-U framework specifically addresses parameter-efficient fine-tuning for user personalization, introducing benchmarks for evaluating personalized NLP models [PEFT-U: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for User Personalization]. This approach recognizes that current foundation models treat users as a collective rather than distinct individuals, highlighting the need for more personalized approaches.For text-to-image generation, researchers have proposed interface design considerations for prompt engineering using stable diffusion models [Designing interfaces for text-to-image prompt engineering using stable diffusion models: a human-AI interaction approach]. This work addresses the challenge that "artists still face challenges when attempting to create images that reflect their specific themes and formats" due to the complexity of prompt engineering.The optimization domain has seen the development of specialized interfaces like OptiMUS, which combines LLMs with optimization solvers [OptiMUS: Optimization Modeling Using MIP Solvers and large language models]. This system addresses the challenge of describing optimization problems to LLMs and automatically generating solver code, though it faces limitations in handling large-scale problems and ensuring reliable outputs.

sections.text: Despite interface improvements, significant complexity barriers remain. The research indicates that users still struggle with "tedious trial-and-error" processes when dealing with complex prompt instructions [CoPrompter: User-Centric Evaluation of LLM Instruction Alignment for Improved Prompt Engineering]. The challenge of making LLM optimization accessible to non-technical users persists across multiple domains.Trust emerges as a critical user concern, particularly in professional settings. Research on workplace LLM chatbots reveals that "trust challenges arise from a perceived lack of credibility and transparency as a result of hallucinations, as well as concerns about data privacy" [Enhancing Trust in LLM Chatbots for Workplace Support through User Experience Design and Prompt Engineering]. Users require improved conversational experiences with "more human-likeness, better contextual understanding abilities, and higher flexibility in input and output formats."A fundamental challenge lies in the computational requirements for LLM optimization. Current approaches face "substantial memory and computational demands" when attempting to fine-tune on resource-constrained devices [Enabling Efficient On-Device Fine-Tuning of LLMs Using Only Inference Engines]. This limitation prevents widespread adoption of personalized LLM optimization among individual users.LLM optimization interfaces struggle with variable representations in problem descriptions. Research identifies that "an optimization problem can be described in many ways," and "while humans can easily adapt to these variations, LLMs may struggle depending on their training data and methods" [OptiMUS: Optimization Modeling Using MIP Solvers and large language models]. This highlights the need for more robust interfaces that can handle diverse problem formulations.LLMs face fundamental limitations in handling large-scale optimization problems due to "limited context size" and performance degradation with longer inputs [OptiMUS: Optimization Modeling Using MIP Solvers and large language models]. This constraint severely limits the applicability of current interfaces to real-world problems involving substantial amounts of data.Current research reveals a tension between personalization and generalization in LLM optimization. While personalization approaches like RAG-based and PEFT-based methods show improvements over non-personalized models, they face challenges with "cold-start users" who have limited personal data [Comparing Retrieval-Augmentation and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Privacy-Preserving Personalization of Large Language Models].

question: What are some principles for designing just-in-time interventions in a programming scenario?

sections.text: Just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs) represent a transformative approach to personalized support in programming education. These interventions provide real-time, contextually relevant assistance to learners based on their current state and needs (Teusner et al., 2021). The growing demand for effective programming education has driven researchers to explore how timing, personalization, and adaptive feedback can enhance learning outcomes in programming contexts.

citations.title: Just-in-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs) in Mobile Health

sections.text: The fundamental principle of just-in-time interventions is providing support at the optimal moment when learners are most receptive to assistance. Research demonstrates that timing plays a crucial role in determining whether support provision will be beneficial, with the right time being defined by events or conditions rather than clock time (Nahum-Shani et al., 2018). In programming education, this translates to monitoring student behavior patterns and intervening when students show signs of struggle or prolonged inactivity.Teusner et al. (2018) found that automated interventions triggered by extended working time on programming exercises could increase help-seeking behavior by up to 66%. Their research showed that students who received considerably more than average working time to solve an exercise benefited from encouragement to ask for help, demonstrating the importance of timing-based triggers.Effective just-in-time interventions in programming rely on continuous monitoring of student behavior to identify when support is needed. This involves tracking metrics such as:- Time spent on exercises- Frequency of code execution attempts- Error patterns and debugging behavior- Help-seeking patternsTeusner's research analyzing over five million executions from student submissions revealed that behavioral data could be used to deduce exercise difficulties and identify students' patterns in approaching programming problems (Teusner, 2021). This data-driven approach enables interventions to be triggered based on objective indicators of student struggle rather than arbitrary time intervals.Just-in-time interventions must be tailored to individual learners' needs, skill levels, and learning contexts. Research shows that personalized interventions are more effective than one-size-fits-all approaches (Kwak et al., 2023). In programming education, this means:- Adapting intervention content based on students' programming experience levels- Providing different types of support for different types of problems- Considering individual learning preferences and backgroundsMaranga et al. (2024) demonstrated that adaptive assessment systems using machine learning algorithms could dynamically adjust programming problem difficulty based on individual student performance, showing significant improvements in student engagement and learning outcomes.Effective just-in-time interventions in programming should offer various types of support to address different learning needs:Peer Feedback Facilitation: Teusner's research showed that receiving peer feedback on programming problems improved overall course scores by up to 17%, while merely formulating questions about problems improved scores by 14% (Teusner, 2021).Automated Feedback Systems: Zhong and Zhan (2024) developed an intelligent tutoring system that provides real-time guidance through informative tutoring feedback, demonstrating effectiveness in promoting computational thinking and reducing cognitive load.Tailored Exercises: Providing bonus exercises specifically designed to address individual weaknesses can help students overcome specific conceptual barriers (Teusner et al., 2018).Just-in-time interventions must balance being helpful with avoiding disruption to the learning process. The goal is to reduce counterproductive struggles without eliminating instructionally beneficial trial-and-error learning (Teusner et al., 2018). Research indicates that:- Interventions should encourage help-seeking rather than provide immediate solutions- Students should maintain agency in deciding whether to engage with interventions- The timing of interventions should respect students' problem-solving processesFor just-in-time interventions to be practical in programming education, they must be scalable to large numbers of students. This requires:- Automated detection of intervention triggers- Systematic approaches to content generation and delivery- Efficient feedback mechanisms that don't require constant instructor involvementTeusner's field experiments with over 5,000 active students demonstrated that automated just-in-time interventions could be successfully deployed at scale, with Request for Comment interventions increasing help-seeking behavior by up to 158% (Teusner, 2021).Just-in-time interventions should incorporate feedback loops that allow for continuous refinement based on student responses and outcomes. This includes:- Monitoring intervention effectiveness- Adjusting trigger conditions based on student feedback- Refining content based on observed student needsModern just-in-time interventions should be seamlessly integrated with existing educational technology infrastructure. This includes compatibility with learning management systems, programming environments, and assessment platforms to provide a cohesive learning experience.

question: What strategies are used to improve robustness and safety of quadrotor UAVs in extreme weather conditions?

sections.text: Quadrotor Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) face significant challenges when operating in extreme weather conditions, including high winds, precipitation, fog, and temperature variations. These environmental factors can severely impact flight stability, navigation accuracy, and overall mission success. This report examines the current state-of-the-art strategies for enhancing quadrotor robustness and safety in such challenging conditions, covering control algorithms, sensor fusion techniques, fault-tolerant systems, and environmental adaptation methods.

### 1.1 Sliding Mode Control (SMC) Approaches Sliding Mode Control has emerged as a robust control strategy for quadrotors operating in extreme weather conditions. Research demonstrates that SMC provides superior disturbance rejection capabilities compared to traditional PID controllers (Ullah et al., 2024). The technique is particularly effective in handling the nonlinear dynamics and external perturbations typical of severe weather scenarios. Xu et al. (2020) developed a backstepping sliding-mode control scheme combined with cascade active disturbance rejection control for quadrotor UAVs, showing enhanced robustness to external disturbances and model uncertainties. Their approach decomposes the attitude dynamic system into serial-connected subsystems, enabling more precise control in challenging conditions. ### 1.2 Model Predictive Control (MPC) with Gaussian Process Compensation Traditional PID control systems are "less robust and easily affected by external factors such as wind disturbance" (Xiong, 2024). Model Predictive Control addresses this limitation by utilizing the UAV's dynamic model and target constraints to enable adaptive control in changing environments. Xiong (2024) enhanced MPC with Gaussian Process Regression to learn historic data and predict errors, resulting in higher trajectory tracking accuracy and improved robustness compared to conventional control methods. ### 1.3 Adaptive and Hybrid Control Strategies Yuan (2024) proposed an adaptive PID control strategy optimized using genetic algorithms and simulated annealing for stable trajectory tracking in strong wind conditions. The experimental results demonstrated significant enhancement in flight stability and accuracy compared to traditional PID algorithms. Sadi et al. (2023) developed a hybrid PID-Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) control approach for quadrotors operating in wind-disturbed environments such as mangroves. This bio-inspired optimization technique showed improved UAV robustness and adaptability under varying wind conditions.

sections.text: ### 2.1 Actuator Fault Tolerance Fault-tolerant control systems are essential for maintaining UAV safety when hardware components fail during extreme weather operations. Aymene et al. (2024) presented an adaptive fault-tolerant approach for quadrotor attitude control that addresses both sensor and actuator faults using backstepping technique and fuzzy logic estimation. The system maintains "practical fixed-time stability of the closed-loop system even when faults appear." Jebelli et al. (2023) developed a method for position and altitude tracking control that continues to function correctly "even if one or two rotors of the quadrotor stop working." Their approach combines Lyapunov stability theory with neural network adaptive schemes, demonstrating remarkable stability and performance robustness despite complete rotor failure. ### 2.2 Sensor Fault Detection and Compensation Shi et al. (2019) designed an actuator fault tolerant controller based on adaptive RBF neural network and sliding mode control. Their system approximates external disturbances of unknown upper bound using RBF neural networks and realizes online estimation of actuator faults through adaptive strategies.

### 3.1 GNSS/IMU Integration Reliable navigation in extreme weather requires robust sensor fusion techniques. Analysis of GNSS/IMU sensor fusion shows that combining Global Navigation Satellite System data with Inertial Measurement Unit information significantly improves aircraft localization accuracy. The Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) approach provides 3D position accuracy improvements of up to 23.47% compared to Extended Kalman Filter methods. ### 3.2 Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) for GPS-Denied Environments In extreme weather conditions where GPS signals may be compromised, Visual-Inertial Odometry becomes crucial. Research on integrating GRU with Kalman filters demonstrates enhanced VIO performance in complex environments where traditional navigation systems fail. ### 3.3 Multi-Sensor Fusion Strategies UAV systems typically incorporate multiple sensors including GPS modules, IMU sensors, and ultrasound sensors for comprehensive environmental awareness. The different output data rates from various sensors require sophisticated synchronization strategies to maintain navigation accuracy during adverse weather conditions.

### 4.1 Climate-Resilient UAV Design Research on climate-resilient UAVs focuses on enhancing energy-efficient communication in harsh environments including rain, fog, and snow. Saif et al. (2023) demonstrated that climate-resilient UAVs can achieve "significant enhancements in energy efficiency, reduced interference, increased data transmission rates, and optimal channel gain under various weather conditions." ### 4.2 All-Weather Sensing Technologies Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) technology provides unique advantages for UAV operations in extreme weather conditions. Unlike optical sensors that are severely affected by "cloud, ice, snow, rain, and haze conditions," SAR can achieve "all-day, all-weather rapid imaging under various weather conditions such as day, night, cloud, snow, rain." ### 4.3 Weather Pattern Recognition and Route Planning AI-driven weather pattern recognition systems are being developed for safe route planning in autonomous aerial vehicles. These systems incorporate weather data into navigation frameworks, considering factors such as wind fields in three-dimensional space and precipitation probability along potential routes.

### 5.1 Trajectory Generation in Extreme Wind Conditions For UAVs operating in extreme environments where wind disturbances may exceed the vehicle's closed-loop stability bounds, specialized trajectory generation methods are essential. Research has developed controllers with dual modes of operation: normal mode for standard conditions and drift mode for extreme weather scenarios. In drift mode, "a drift frame that moves with the prevailing wind is established in which the vehicle maintains control authority to generate and track trajectories." This approach allows UAVs to maintain operational capability even when environmental conditions exceed normal flight parameters. ### 5.2 Environmental Condition Adaptation UAV systems must be capable of real-time adaptation to changing environmental conditions. This includes on-board updates to navigation parameters based on current weather conditions and the ability to transition between protected and windy environments while maintaining safety margins.

### 6.1 Denoising and Image Enhancement Advanced signal processing techniques are crucial for maintaining sensor effectiveness in extreme weather. Research on denoising deep neural networks shows significant improvements in object detection performance under adverse weather conditions. Weather-specific preprocessing can improve mean Average Precision scores from 4% to 70% in extreme fog scenarios. ### 6.2 Radar and Lidar Integration Multi-sensor approaches combining radar and lidar technologies provide redundancy and improved reliability in extreme weather conditions. These systems can continue operating when optical sensors fail due to precipitation or low visibility conditions.

The enhancement of quadrotor UAV robustness and safety in extreme weather conditions requires a multi-faceted approach combining advanced control algorithms, fault-tolerant systems, enhanced sensor fusion, and weather-adaptive technologies. Key strategies include: 1. **Advanced Control Systems**: Implementation of sliding mode control, model predictive control with Gaussian process compensation, and adaptive hybrid control strategies that can handle nonlinear dynamics and external perturbations. 2. **Fault-Tolerant Design**: Development of systems that can continue operating despite sensor or actuator failures, using adaptive algorithms and neural network-based compensation. 3. **Robust Navigation**: Integration of GNSS/IMU sensor fusion, visual-inertial odometry, and multi-sensor approaches to maintain navigation accuracy in GPS-denied or compromised environments. 4. **Weather-Adaptive Technologies**: Implementation of climate-resilient designs, all-weather sensing capabilities, and AI-driven weather pattern recognition for intelligent route planning. 5. **Specialized Flight Modes**: Development of drift mode operations and environmental adaptation capabilities for extreme wind conditions. The research demonstrates that while traditional PID control systems are insufficient for extreme weather operations, modern approaches incorporating machine learning, adaptive control theory, and multi-sensor fusion can significantly improve UAV robustness and safety. Future developments should focus on real-time environmental adaptation, improved weather prediction integration, and enhanced fault tolerance capabilities. These strategies collectively enable quadrotor UAVs to operate safely and effectively in challenging weather conditions that would otherwise ground conventional systems, expanding their operational envelope and improving mission success rates in critical applications such as search and rescue, environmental monitoring, and emergency response.

question: what are some datasets used for evaluating variable type inference for decompiled binaries?

sections.text: The TYDA dataset is one of the most comprehensive and recent datasets for binary variable type recovery evaluation (Li et al., 2025). TYDA contains 163,643 binary programs compiled from C packages sourced from Gentoo and Debian repositories, covering four architectures (x86_64, x86, ARM, and AARCH64) and four compiler optimization levels (O0, O1, O2, and O3) (Li et al., 2025). The dataset was specifically designed to address the high function duplication rate problem found in previous datasets, with peer-reviewed quality standards. From the x86_64 architecture binaries compiled with O0 optimization alone, researchers extracted 21 million functions and 105 million variables using pyelftools to parse DWARF information (Li et al., 2025).

citations.title: Beyond the Edge of Function: Unraveling the Patterns of Type Recovery in Binary Code

sections.text: The DIRT (Dataset for Idiomatic ReTyping) dataset was created for the DIRTY framework by Chen et al. (2021). This dataset was constructed by randomly sampling C and C++ projects from GitHub using GHCC, which compiles each project with debugging symbols (Chen et al., 2021). The dataset creation process involves compiling binaries with debug information, decompiling them using the Hex-Rays decompiler to obtain ground truth variable names and types, then stripping the debugging symbols and decompiling again to simulate real-world stripped binaries. DIRTY demonstrated the ability to recover original variable names 66.4% of the time and original types 75.8% of the time using this dataset (Chen et al., 2021).

The DIRE dataset is used for decompiled variable name recovery evaluation and contains 3,195,962 decompiled x86-64 functions with their corresponding abstract syntax trees (Yadavally et al., 2023). The dataset was created by scraping open-source C codes from GitHub, compiling them with debug information, and decompiling using Hex-Rays decompiler (Yadavally et al., 2023). The dataset includes proper annotations of decompiled variable names and their corresponding original gold-standard names, with a train-dev-test split of 80:10:10 (Yadavally et al., 2023).

Cao and Leach (2023) created a dataset specifically for evaluating variable type recovery using the open-source Ghidra decompiler. This dataset was developed to address the limitation that the original DIRTY model was evaluated only on Hex-Rays decompiler output, which has expensive licensing restrictions (Cao and Leach, 2023). The researchers demonstrated that DIRTY's architecture could achieve comparable performance on Ghidra-decompiled data, with overall accuracy of 73.5% for variable retyping compared to 73.9% for Hex-Rays (Cao and Leach, 2023).

The TypeFSL dataset contains 3,003,117 functions and was designed to address the challenge of imbalanced type distributions in binary type recovery (Song et al., 2024). This dataset enables few-shot learning evaluation, with TypeFSL achieving 77.9% and 84.6% accuracy in 20-way 5-shot and 10-shot classification tasks respectively across different architectures and optimization levels (Song et al., 2024).

The VarCorpus dataset is used for evaluating variable renaming performance and includes multiple decompiler outputs (IDA and Ghidra) across different optimization levels (Green et al., 2024). STRIDE, a lightweight technique for variable type and name prediction, was evaluated on this dataset and achieved higher accuracy than VarBERT on 11 out of 16 dataset splits with an average improvement of 1.55% (Green et al., 2024).

DeMinify evaluated variable type inference on minified code datasets including a Python dataset with 180,000 methods and a JavaScript dataset with 322,000 files (Li et al., 2023). These datasets focus on source code rather than binary code but provide insights into variable type recovery from obfuscated code representations (Li et al., 2023).

question: How does in-context learning for LLMs differ from traditional machine learning model training?

sections.text: The landscape of machine learning has evolved significantly with the advent of large language models (LLMs), introducing novel paradigms that challenge traditional training methodologies. While conventional machine learning relies on iterative parameter updates through gradient-based optimization, in-context learning (ICL) represents a fundamentally different approach that enables models to adapt to new tasks without any parameter modifications (Dong et al., 2023)¹. This report examines the key differences between these two paradigms across multiple dimensions including learning mechanisms, computational requirements, data utilization, and performance characteristics.

In-context learning represents a paradigm shift from traditional machine learning approaches. As defined in the literature, "In-context learning is a paradigm that allows language models to learn tasks given only a few examples in the form of demonstration" (Dong et al., 2023)². The key characteristic of ICL is that it "does not require parameter updates and is directly performed on pretrained LLMs" (Dong et al., 2023)³. The mechanism operates through a scoring function where the model evaluates candidate answers based on a demonstration set containing task instructions and example input-output pairs. The likelihood of predictions is computed over the entire input sequence, allowing the model to adapt its behavior based purely on the contextual information provided in the prompt (Dong et al., 2023)⁴. Traditional machine learning fundamentally relies on iterative parameter updates through gradient-based optimization. The core mechanism involves "stochastic gradient descent algorithm to solve the defects of traditional algorithm" where "model parameters are updated according to the first-order gradients of the empirical risks with respect to the parameters being optimized, while backpropagation is implemented for calculating the gradients of parameters" (Patil & Gudivada, 2024)⁵. This approach requires explicit training phases where "gradient descent algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, are commonly employed to update iteratively the parameters θ in the direction of the steepest descent. The backpropagation algorithm efficiently computes the gradients and propagates them through the network, enabling parameter updates" (Huang et al., 2023)⁶.

In-context learning presents unique computational trade-offs compared to traditional training. While ICL eliminates the need for parameter updates, it introduces different computational challenges. As noted in recent research, "processing prompts with several demonstrations every time the model parses logs can contribute to further computational costs. In-context learning prompted with few-shot demonstrations requires the model to process both the target instance and all the demonstrations during each inference, leading to an increased inference time" (Li et al., 2024)⁷. The computational efficiency of ICL depends heavily on context window limitations. "The context size of the model's inputs limits the number of demonstrations that can be used. For example, performing in-context learning with four prompts on Flan-T5-Base exceeds its context size of 512 tokens" (Li et al., 2024)⁸. Traditional machine learning concentrates computational costs during the training phase. "The training of machine learning models presents new challenges" as models require extensive computational resources for "stochastic gradient descent algorithm to solve the defects of traditional algorithm" (Xiao et al., 2024)⁹. However, once trained, traditional models typically have lower inference costs compared to ICL approaches. The training process involves "distributed training framework and distributed training system" which "reduce the communication load effectively and improve the overall performance of the system" (Xiao et al., 2024)¹⁰. This front-loaded computational approach contrasts sharply with ICL's inference-time processing requirements.

In-context learning operates with minimal data requirements, typically utilizing only a few demonstration examples. The approach enables "LLMs to adapt flexibly to new tasks by incorporating data within the input sequence context, rather than through weight updates as in fine-tuning" (Pawelczyk et al., 2023)¹¹. This paradigm allows for "rapid prototyping and facilitates the integration of additional knowledge by simply changing the prompt" (Huang et al., 2024)¹². The data utilization in ICL is fundamentally different as it relies on "demonstration examples are part of the prompt" rather than traditional training datasets (Dong et al., 2023)¹³. This approach enables zero-shot and few-shot learning capabilities where models can "perform new tasks without any additional parameter training or updates. Instead, training examples are provided to the LLM via prompts" (Huang et al., 2024)¹⁴. Traditional machine learning approaches typically require substantial amounts of training data to achieve optimal performance. The learning process involves "learning language representation in self-supervised ways" using "large and diverse dataset" (Patil & Gudivada, 2024)¹⁵. Traditional methods depend on "dividing the training data into smaller subsets, called mini-batches, and computing the gradients and parameter updates based on these mini-batches" (Huang et al., 2023)¹⁶. The data requirements scale with model complexity and task difficulty, often necessitating extensive preprocessing and augmentation techniques to achieve satisfactory performance across diverse applications.

In-context learning demonstrates remarkable adaptability to new tasks and domains. Research shows that "prompt engineering substantially improved and focused the chatbot's output" and enables models to adapt to "new tasks without additional training of the base model" (Russe et al., 2024)¹⁷. This flexibility allows for real-time task switching and domain adaptation without model retraining. The adaptability of ICL extends to various learning scenarios including "zero-shot learning, few-shot learning, and embedding-based retrieval mechanisms" which have become "indispensable in delivering tailored outputs" (Russe et al., 2024)¹⁸. This dynamic adaptation capability represents a significant departure from traditional static model architectures. Traditional machine learning models typically require dedicated training for each specific task or domain. The learning process involves "task-specific to task-independent to task-and-language-independent architectures" evolution, but each model iteration requires separate training phases (Patil & Gudivada, 2024)¹⁹. This approach, while potentially achieving higher task-specific performance, lacks the dynamic adaptability of ICL. Traditional models face challenges with "catastrophic forgetting" when adapting to new tasks, often requiring careful architecture design and training strategies to maintain performance across multiple domains.

In-context learning offers several advantages including "efficiency, there is no parameter update process. No catastrophic forgetting, as LM parameters remain fixed. Applicable in zero-shot settings" (Liu et al., 2023)²⁰. However, ICL also faces significant limitations: "Because prompts are the only method that provide the task specification, heavy engineering is necessary to achieve high accuracy. In particular in the in-context learning setting, providing many answered prompts can be slow at test time, and thus cannot easily use large training datasets" (Liu et al., 2023)²¹. The performance of ICL is highly sensitive to prompt design and demonstration selection, with research showing that "selecting effective demonstrations is also crucial for improving the performance of in-context learning, as it is sensitive to the format and order of the prompts" (Li et al., 2024)²². Traditional machine learning approaches offer more predictable optimization paths through established gradient-based methods. The "gradient descent algorithm is a widely used iterative algorithm for finding local minima in multivariate functions" with well-understood convergence properties (Dhingra, 2024)²³. However, these methods face challenges with "final iterations often either overshoot the minima or make minimal progress, making it challenging to determine an optimal stopping point" (Dhingra, 2024)²⁴. Traditional approaches benefit from decades of optimization research, including adaptive learning rate methods and regularization techniques that provide robust training frameworks for diverse applications.

In-context learning and traditional machine learning represent fundamentally different paradigms for model adaptation and task performance. While traditional machine learning relies on explicit parameter updates through gradient-based optimization, in-context learning achieves task adaptation through contextual demonstration without parameter modification. Each approach presents distinct advantages: ICL offers rapid task switching and eliminates catastrophic forgetting, while traditional methods provide more predictable optimization and potentially superior task-specific performance. The choice between these paradigms depends on specific application requirements, computational constraints, and the need for dynamic adaptability versus specialized performance optimization. The evolution from traditional machine learning to in-context learning reflects a broader shift in artificial intelligence toward more flexible, generalizable systems that can adapt to new tasks with minimal additional training. As both paradigms continue to evolve, understanding their complementary strengths and limitations becomes crucial for developing effective AI systems across diverse applications.

question: what datasets are commonly used to evaluate SLAM methods

sections.text: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms require rigorous evaluation to assess their performance, robustness, and applicability to real-world scenarios. The evaluation of SLAM methods depends heavily on the availability of high-quality benchmark datasets that provide diverse scenarios, accurate ground truth data, and standardized evaluation metrics (Handa et al., 2014). This report examines the most commonly used datasets for SLAM evaluation, organized by sensor modality and application domain.

The TUM RGB-D dataset is one of the most widely used benchmark datasets for RGB-D SLAM evaluation (Kuyu & Vatansever, 2025). The dataset consists of 39 sequences recorded in indoor environments using a Microsoft Kinect sensor, providing synchronized RGB and depth images at 30 Hz along with ground truth trajectory data obtained from a high-accuracy motion capture system (Soliman et al., 2023). The dataset includes sequences with varying characteristics such as different texture conditions, presence of dynamic objects, and different scales of environments, making it suitable for comprehensive SLAM evaluation (Kornilova et al., 2022). The dataset is particularly valuable because it provides standardized evaluation metrics including Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE), which have become the standard metrics for SLAM evaluation (Kuyu & Vatansever, 2025). The TUM RGB-D dataset has been extensively used to evaluate various SLAM algorithms including ORB-SLAM, LSD-SLAM, and other state-of-the-art systems. The Imperial College London and National University of Ireland Maynooth (ICL-NUIM) dataset focuses specifically on RGB-D SLAM evaluation and provides synthetic data for comprehensive benchmarking (Handa et al., 2014). The dataset consists of handheld RGB-D camera sequences within synthetically generated environments, offering perfect ground truth poses and surface models that enable quantitative evaluation of both trajectory estimation and surface reconstruction accuracy (Handa et al., 2014). The synthetic nature of the data allows for precise control of environmental conditions and provides noise-free ground truth that would be difficult to obtain in real-world scenarios.

The KITTI dataset is one of the most popular benchmark datasets for outdoor visual SLAM evaluation (Kuyu & Vatansever, 2025). The dataset contains 22 stereo image sequences covering a total distance of 39.2 km, captured from a moving vehicle equipped with color and grayscale stereo cameras, along with 3D laser scanner data and GPS/INS ground truth (Soliman et al., 2023). The KITTI dataset is particularly valuable for evaluating SLAM algorithms in autonomous driving scenarios, though it is somewhat limited in motion patterns as the vehicle predominantly moves forward without significant vertical motion. The EuRoC MAV dataset has become one of the most widely used datasets for evaluating visual-inertial SLAM algorithms (Soliman et al., 2023). The dataset consists of 11 sequences captured from stereo cameras and IMU sensors mounted on a micro aerial vehicle (MAV) in indoor environments with varying motion and illumination conditions (Kornilova et al., 2022). The dataset provides sequences of different difficulty levels (easy, medium, and difficult) and includes highly accurate ground truth obtained from laser trackers and motion capture systems. The dataset is particularly challenging due to rapid translations and rotations typical of aerial vehicle motion, making it an excellent benchmark for testing SLAM robustness. The TUM MonoVO dataset is specifically designed for evaluating monocular visual SLAM and odometry algorithms (Soliman et al., 2023). The dataset contains photometrically calibrated indoor and outdoor sequences captured using handheld monocular cameras, providing ground truth for long-range tracking accuracy evaluation. This dataset complements other benchmarks by focusing on the specific challenges of monocular SLAM systems.
