sections.text: TartanAir is a large-scale synthetic dataset that has gained significant popularity for SLAM evaluation, particularly for pushing the limits of visual SLAM algorithms (Teed & Deng, 2021). The dataset provides photo-realistic simulation environments with various lighting conditions, weather effects, dynamic objects, and challenging camera motions. TartanAir was used as the benchmark for the ECCV 2020 SLAM competition and offers diverse outdoor and indoor scenes that are extremely challenging for SLAM algorithms. The synthetic nature allows for perfect ground truth while providing realistic visual conditions. The OpenLORIS-Scene dataset is designed to evaluate the real-world practicality of lifelong SLAM algorithms for service robots (Shi et al., 2019). The dataset captures scene changes caused by day-night shifts and human activities, providing a unique benchmark for evaluating SLAM robustness in dynamic environments. The dataset includes sequences collected by wheeled robots in indoor environments with significant environmental changes such as varying lighting conditions and dynamic objects. ScanNet is a comprehensive dataset containing RGB-D sequences from indoor environments, providing rich information including camera motion, surface reconstruction, and semantic annotations (Soliman et al., 2023). The dataset encompasses over 1,500 indoor RGB-D sequences and supports multiple vision tasks beyond SLAM, making it a versatile benchmark for various computer vision applications.

citations.title: IBISCape: A Simulated Benchmark for multi-modal SLAM Systems Evaluation in Large-scale Dynamic Environments

sections.text: The evaluation of SLAM algorithms typically relies on two primary metrics: Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE) (Kuyu & Vatansever, 2025). ATE measures the global consistency of the estimated trajectory by comparing the absolute differences between estimated and ground truth poses, while RPE measures the local accuracy by evaluating the drift over time between successive poses. These metrics provide complementary insights into SLAM performance, with ATE being particularly suited for evaluating complete SLAM systems and RPE being more appropriate for assessing visual odometry drift. Recent developments have introduced specialized benchmarks for specific SLAM components. The EVOLIN benchmark focuses on line detection and association in SLAM systems, providing comprehensive evaluation of line-based features (Ivanov et al., 2023). Similarly, the EVOPS benchmark evaluates plane segmentation from RGB-D and LiDAR data, offering specialized metrics for geometric feature evaluation (Kornilova et al., 2022).

The landscape of SLAM evaluation datasets is diverse and comprehensive, covering various sensor modalities, environmental conditions, and application domains. The most commonly used datasets include TUM RGB-D for RGB-D SLAM, KITTI for outdoor visual SLAM, EuRoC MAV for visual-inertial systems, and increasingly TartanAir for challenging synthetic scenarios. These datasets, combined with standardized evaluation metrics like ATE and RPE, provide a robust framework for comparative evaluation of SLAM algorithms. The continued development of specialized benchmarks and synthetic datasets reflects the evolving needs of the SLAM community and the push toward more robust, real-world applicable algorithms.

question: Can you recommend a suitable theoretical lens for qualitative research concerning robotics process automation (RPA) implementations?

sections.text: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) implementation represents a significant organizational transformation that affects multiple dimensions of business operations. When conducting qualitative research on RPA implementations, selecting appropriate theoretical lenses is crucial for understanding the complex interplay between technology, organization, and social factors. This report examines several theoretical frameworks that can provide valuable insights for researchers investigating RPA implementation phenomena.

The TOE framework is particularly well-suited for examining RPA implementation as it addresses three critical dimensions that influence technology adoption decisions (Kedziora et al., 2021). The technological dimension examines factors such as RPA capabilities, compatibility with existing systems, and technical complexity. The organizational dimension considers aspects like top management support, organizational structure, and resource availability. The environmental dimension encompasses external factors including competitive pressure, regulatory requirements, and market conditions. This framework is especially valuable for qualitative research because it provides a structured approach to understanding the multifaceted nature of RPA implementation decisions. Research demonstrates that organizations implementing RPA are influenced by operational benefits, employee impact considerations, and risk factors that align with the TOE framework's comprehensive perspective (Kedziora et al., 2021).

citations.title: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) Implementation Drivers: Evidence of Selected Nordic Companies

sections.text: Socio-technical systems theory offers a particularly relevant lens for RPA implementation research, as it recognizes that social systems and technology are interrelated and must be considered simultaneously in managing organizations. This theory emphasizes how the interaction between tasks, people, structure, and technology impacts efficiency, productivity, and quality of work. The socio-technical systems framework has been developed as a six-dimensional structure comprising: 1) People 2) Infrastructure 3) Technology 4) Culture 5) Process/procedures 6) Goals. It offers an organization-centric view of how these various components interact in a complex system. This framework is particularly valuable for RPA research because it acknowledges that digital transformation will not remove the need for human interactions, but rather change the way humans interact with computers. The socio-technical systems framework is therefore an effective tool to analyze technological innovations, not as single elements, but as part of a structure of interrelated components. This includes consideration of institutional, organizational and social innovations that should accompany technological innovations, in order to optimize the benefits, regulate the growth, and mitigate potential side effects.

Institutional theory provides valuable insights for understanding RPA implementation by explaining how organizations are motivated to align their structures and behaviors with the values, norms, and expectations espoused by institutions in their environments. This theory is particularly useful for RPA research because it helps explain why organizations adopt automation technologies not just for efficiency gains, but also to maintain legitimacy within their institutional environment. Institutional theory grasps the irrational sides of organizations and acknowledges that organizations, along with explicit formalized structures, have implicit informal cultures guiding organizational behavior. This theory highlights how cultural and social processes in a working collective develop patterns of the most preferred ways to think and act, which achieve a rule-like status. The theory identifies three types of institutional traits: (a) cultural-cognitive, (b) normative and (c) regulative. Implementation is likely to be influenced by coercive, normative, and mimetic pressures from institutions within an organization's environment. For RPA research, this suggests that implementation strategies should seek congruence with the values, norms, and expectations of relevant institutions in the implementing organization's environment.

Recent research suggests that combining multiple theoretical frameworks can provide a more comprehensive understanding of technology implementation. Studies have successfully integrated the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) model, and Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework to provide a more holistic understanding of technology adoption processes. This multi-theoretical approach addresses the complexity of RPA implementation by incorporating different perspectives: perceived usefulness and job relevance (from TAM), innovation attributes and communication channels (from DOI), and technological, organizational, and environmental contexts (from TOE). Such integration offers a novel contribution by providing a more complete understanding of RPA adoption factors. The integration of these theories also introduces important concepts such as time as a critical innovation artifact, highlighting its significance in the adoption process. This approach can help researchers understand how different theoretical lenses complement each other in explaining RPA implementation phenomena.

The Critical Success Factors framework, specifically adapted for RPA implementation, provides a structured approach to understanding the key elements that determine implementation success. This framework categorizes factors into three main areas: RPA in the organization, development of RPA, and operation of RPA. The CSF framework is particularly valuable for qualitative research because it provides a comprehensive structure for investigating implementation success factors. Research using this framework has identified key success factors including strategic support, management commitment, organizational culture, training, communication, policy compliance, expertise, change management, documentation, resource management, compliance, monitoring, and evaluation (Ariyantho & Sutjipto, 2024). This framework enables researchers to systematically examine the multifaceted nature of RPA implementation success and provides a basis for understanding the challenges and risks faced by organizations undertaking digital transformation initiatives.

citations.title: Transforming Financial Management: An RPA Implementation Case Study at PT Telkom Indonesia

sections.text: For qualitative research on RPA implementations, researchers should consider adopting a multi-theoretical approach that combines insights from several frameworks. The TOE framework provides a comprehensive structure for understanding implementation drivers, while socio-technical systems theory offers crucial insights into the human-technology interaction aspects of RPA. Institutional theory helps explain organizational motivations beyond pure efficiency gains, and the CSF framework provides practical guidance for identifying success factors. This theoretical pluralism allows researchers to capture the complexity of RPA implementation phenomena from multiple perspectives, leading to more nuanced and comprehensive research findings. The choice of specific theoretical lenses should be guided by the research questions, context, and objectives of the study.

question: What are metrics to mesures the quality of human robot communication?

sections.text: Human-robot interaction (HRI) has become increasingly important as robots are deployed in various domains including healthcare, education, and industry. The quality of human-robot communication is crucial for successful interaction outcomes, yet evaluating this quality remains challenging. Research has revealed that communication quality should be assessed not only through objective measures such as task completion time or accuracy, but also through subjective human experiences (Mizuchi et al., 2023). This report examines the various metrics used to measure the quality of human-robot communication, categorizing them into objective and subjective measures.

citations.title: Designing Evaluation Metrics for Quality of Human-Robot Interaction in Guiding Human Behavior

sections.text: Objective metrics provide quantifiable measures of communication effectiveness through direct measurement of interaction outcomes. Success rate is one of the most commonly used objective metrics, measuring the percentage of successfully completed tasks or communication exchanges (Ramirez-Amaro et al., 2021). Task completion time represents another fundamental objective measure, tracking the duration required to complete specific communication-based tasks.Interaction force measurements capture the physical aspects of human-robot communication, particularly relevant in collaborative scenarios where robots must physically interact with humans (Ramirez-Amaro et al., 2021). Joint effort measurements assess the mechanical efficiency of robotic systems during communication tasks, providing insights into the robot's physical performance during interaction.Timing-based metrics are essential for evaluating communication quality, including response time, turn-taking efficiency, and communication latency. These metrics are particularly important for assessing the naturalness and fluency of human-robot dialogues. Research has shown that proper timing in communication significantly impacts user perception of interaction quality (Ramirez-Amaro et al., 2021).Recent research has introduced metrics such as Robot Attention Demand (RAD), which measures the cognitive resources required by humans to effectively communicate with robots (Amine et al., 2023). This metric showed a 41% reduction when using advanced communication interfaces, indicating improved communication efficiency. Fan-out time, measuring how long humans can effectively manage multiple robot communications simultaneously, also serves as an important objective metric.

citations.title: Trends of Human-Robot Collaboration in Industry Contexts: Handover, Learning, and Metrics
Human-Robot Interaction using VAHR: Virtual Assistant, Human, and Robots in the Loop

sections.text: Trust represents one of the most critical subjective metrics for evaluating human-robot communication quality. Research has identified trust as a multi-dimensional construct encompassing three key categories: robot characteristics (performance-based and attribute-based factors), human characteristics (ability-based and personality-based factors), and environmental characteristics (team collaboration and tasking factors) (Diquilibrium et al., 2023).A psychometric scale has been developed specifically for measuring trust in human-robot collaboration, consisting of three components: "Safe co-operation" (4 items), "Robot and gripper reliability" (4 items), and "Robot's motion and pick-up speed" (2 items) (Ferraguti et al., 2023). This scale uses a five-point Likert scale ranging from "Strongly Disagree" to "Strongly Agree."Engagement measures the level of user involvement and attention during human-robot communication. This includes metrics such as eye contact duration, body language analysis, and spontaneous movement patterns (Casso et al., 2024). Research has shown that spontaneous body sway can be modulated by social robots, providing a behavioral measure of engagement that doesn't rely on conscious user reporting.Affinity metrics assess the emotional connection and comfort level between humans and robots. These measures often evaluate the robot's impression on users and the smoothness of interaction dynamics (Obi & Funakoshi, 2024).User satisfaction encompasses multiple dimensions including perceived usefulness, ease of use, and overall experience quality. Comfort metrics evaluate both psychological and physical comfort during human-robot communication. Research has shown that comfort can be measured through physiological indicators such as heart rate variability and through behavioral observations of user gestures and posture (Casso et al., 2024).Subjective assessment of communication quality includes metrics for evaluating the appropriateness of explanations, instruction clarity, and the robot's ability to adapt to human behavior patterns. Factor analysis has revealed four key evaluation dimensions that humans prioritize: appropriateness of attribute explanation, instruction conciseness, behavioral adaptability, and guidance effectiveness (Mizuchi et al., 2023).

Role of Reference Frames for a Safe Human–Robot Interaction

Exploring Engagement in Human-Robot Interaction through the Quantification of Human Spontaneous Movement
Respiration-enhanced Human-Robot Communication

sections.text: A comprehensive framework for evaluating proficiency-based human-robot communication has been developed, encompassing four cyclical stages: Robot Self-Assessment of proficiency (RSA), Robot Communication of Proficiency to human (RCP), Human Understanding of Proficiency (HUP), and Robot Perception of Human intentions, values, and assessments (RPH) (Norton et al., 2022).This framework provides metrics for each stage, considering temporal aspects (a priori, in situ, and post hoc evaluations) and the interconnections between different stages of the communication process. The framework draws from related fields including explainability, transparency, and introspection to create a comprehensive evaluation approach.Recent research has explored the integration of multiple communication modalities, including respiratory patterns, to enhance human-robot communication quality (Obi & Funakoshi, 2024). Metrics for multi-modal communication assess the coordination between different communication channels and their combined effectiveness in conveying information and intent.

citations.title: Respiration-enhanced Human-Robot Communication
Metrics for Robot Proficiency Self-assessment and Communication of Proficiency in Human-robot Teams

sections.text: Eye-tracking metrics provide objective measures of attention and trust in human-robot communication. Gaze entropy and gaze transition entropy serve as indicators of communication quality, particularly in dynamic interaction scenarios (Zhang et al., 2022). These metrics offer continuous, non-intrusive monitoring of user attention patterns during communication tasks.Physiological metrics include heart rate variability, galvanic skin response, and other autonomic nervous system indicators that reflect user stress, engagement, and comfort levels during human-robot communication. These metrics provide objective measures of subjective experiences without requiring explicit user reporting.Behavioral metrics assess user movement patterns, gesture frequency, and spatial positioning relative to the robot. These measures provide insights into user comfort, engagement, and communication effectiveness through observable behaviors rather than self-reported experiences.

citations.title: Capturing Dynamic Trust Metrics during Shared Space Human Robot Collaboration: An eye-tracking approach

sections.text: Current research emphasizes the need for holistic evaluation approaches that combine objective and subjective metrics (Menolotto et al., 2024). The integration of self-reporting questionnaires with human-centric data collected through wearable sensing technologies represents a promising direction for comprehensive communication quality assessment.The field lacks standardized metrics and benchmarks that can be applied across different human-robot communication systems. This absence of common evaluation frameworks hinders the development of unified assessment methodologies and makes it difficult to compare results across different studies and applications.Future research must address the temporal aspects of communication quality metrics, considering how quality measures change over time as humans adapt to robot communication patterns and develop familiarity with the system.

citations.title: Assessing Trust in Collaborative Robotics with Different Human-Robot Interfaces

sections.text: The measurement of human-robot communication quality requires a multi-faceted approach incorporating both objective and subjective metrics. Objective measures provide quantifiable assessments of performance, efficiency, and technical effectiveness, while subjective metrics capture the human experience including trust, engagement, satisfaction, and comfort. The most comprehensive evaluation frameworks integrate multiple metric types and consider temporal aspects of communication quality development. Future research should focus on developing standardized evaluation protocols and exploring novel physiological and behavioral indicators that can provide more nuanced assessments of communication quality in human-robot interactions.

question: In auditory speech perception using iEEG, I will use Temporal Response Function (TRF) to determine correlations between stimulus characteristics (variations in the acoustic signal envelope, for example) and characteristics of recorded neuronal activity. I would like to fully understand the different stages of data processing carried out, as well as the reasoning and hypotheses behind them.

sections.text: Temporal Response Functions (TRFs) are linear regression models that characterize the relationship between continuous stimulus features and neural responses in auditory speech perception research (1). The TRF approach represents a significant advancement over traditional event-related potential (ERP) methods, as it allows for the analysis of neural responses to naturalistic, continuous speech stimuli rather than artificial, repetitive stimuli (2). In iEEG studies, TRFs enable researchers to examine how acoustic features of speech are encoded in neural activity at different cortical locations with high temporal and spatial resolution (3). The fundamental equation for a TRF is: r(t) =   ∑τ  s(t-τ) × h(τ) + ε(t) where r(t) is the neural response at time t, s(t) is the stimulus feature, h(τ) is the temporal response function at lag τ, and ε(t) is the residual error (4).

sections.text: The preprocessing of iEEG data for TRF analysis involves several critical steps designed to remove artifacts and prepare the data for analysis. The raw iEEG signals are typically bandpass filtered with cutoff frequencies ranging from 0.1 Hz to 40 Hz, depending on the specific research focus (5). A notch filter at 50 Hz (or 60 Hz in North America) is applied to remove power line interference (6). The continuous EEG data undergoes artifact rejection procedures to remove contaminated segments. This typically involves both automatic and manual artifact rejection processes, with amplitude thresholds commonly set at ±100 μV to exclude epochs with excessive noise (7). Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is frequently employed to identify and remove artifacts related to eye movements, muscle activity, and other non-neural sources (8). Unlike traditional ERP analysis, TRF analysis preserves the continuous nature of both stimulus and neural data. However, the data is often segmented into manageable blocks for computational efficiency (9). Baseline correction is applied using pre-stimulus intervals, typically ranging from 100-200 ms before stimulus onset (10).

sections.text: The most commonly used stimulus feature in auditory TRF analysis is the acoustic envelope, which represents the instantaneous power of the speech signal (11). The envelope is extracted using multiple methods, with the gammatone filterbank approach being preferred over traditional Hilbert transform methods due to its superior performance in neural tracking (12). The gammatone filterbank-based envelope extraction involves: 1. Decomposing the speech signal into frequency bands using gammatone filters (typically 20-5000 Hz with 256 filter channels) 2. Computing the absolute value of the analytic signal for each frequency band 3. Applying power-law compression (typically raising to the power of 0.3) to mimic auditory system processing 4. Summing across frequency bands to obtain the broadband envelope (13) Beyond the envelope, researchers extract various acoustic features including: - Acoustic onsets: derived from the first derivative of the envelope using auditory edge detection algorithms (14) - Spectral features: representing different frequency components of the speech signal (15) - Phonetic features: capturing sublexical information such as phoneme onsets (16) All predictor variables are typically downsampled to match the neural data sampling rate (usually 100-1000 Hz) and z-scored for standardization (17).

sections.text: TRF estimation is typically performed using regularized linear regression, with ridge regression being the most common approach (18). The ridge regression formulation includes a penalty term to prevent overfitting:   β  = (X'X +   λ I)^(-1)X'y where   λ  is the regularization parameter that controls the degree of shrinkage applied to the regression coefficients (19). The regularization parameter   λ  is optimized using cross-validation procedures, typically employing 10-fold cross-validation to ensure robust parameter selection (20). The process involves: 1. Splitting the data into training and validation sets 2. Performing a grid search over   λ  values (typically from 10^-8 to 10^8) 3. Selecting the   λ  that maximizes the correlation between predicted and actual neural responses 4. Training the final model using the optimal   λ  on the entire dataset (21) TRFs are estimated across a range of time lags, typically from -150 to 450 ms, to capture both anticipatory and response components of neural processing (22). The choice of time window depends on the specific research question and the expected latency of neural responses to acoustic features (23).

sections.text: The TRF approach is based on the assumption that the auditory system can be approximated as a linear time-invariant system for the purpose of modeling neural responses to speech (24). This hypothesis suggests that the neural response to complex stimuli can be predicted by the linear convolution of simpler stimulus features with the system's impulse response (i.e., the TRF) (25). TRF analysis in auditory cortex is guided by the hierarchical processing model, which proposes that different acoustic features are processed at different levels of the auditory system (26). Early responses (30-80 ms) are thought to reflect basic acoustic processing, while later responses (90-130 ms and beyond) represent more complex linguistic processing (27). In attention-based TRF studies, the underlying hypothesis is that selective attention modulates cortical envelope tracking, with attended speech showing stronger neural entrainment compared to unattended speech (28). This differential tracking is thought to reflect the brain's ability to selectively enhance relevant acoustic information while suppressing irrelevant background noise (29).

Studies suggest that at least 5-10 minutes of continuous data are needed for robust TRF estimation, with shorter segments being prone to onset artifacts and reduced statistical power (34). The linear assumption underlying TRF analysis may not capture all aspects of neural processing, particularly nonlinear interactions between different stimulus features or neural adaptation effects (35). Advanced methods incorporating nonlinear components are being developed to address these limitations. TRF analysis can be applied to different frequency bands of the neural signal, with different bands capturing different aspects of neural processing. Low-frequency bands (1-9 Hz) typically show strong envelope tracking, while high-frequency bands (70-120 Hz) may reflect local neural activity (36).

question: Describe what is known about overfitting in in-context learning.

sections.text: In-context learning (ICL) has emerged as a remarkable capability of large language models (LLMs) and transformers, enabling them to perform tasks without additional parameter updates by utilizing demonstrations provided in the input context. This paradigm has fundamentally changed how we approach machine learning tasks, offering a form of few-shot learning that doesn't require traditional training procedures. However, as with any learning paradigm, the phenomenon of overfitting presents unique challenges and considerations in the context of ICL.

Recent research has identified a phenomenon called "benign overfitting" in the context of in-context learning. Frei and Vardi (2024) demonstrated that trained transformers can exhibit benign overfitting in-context, where the model memorizes all of its in-context examples (including those with noisy labels) yet still generalizes near-optimally for clean test examples¹. This phenomenon occurs when in-context examples are corrupted by label flipping noise, suggesting that transformers possess a remarkable ability to maintain generalization performance despite fitting to noisy demonstrations.### 2.2 Theoretical FoundationsThe understanding of benign overfitting in transformers has been extended through theoretical analysis. Zhang et al. (2025) developed a generalization theory for two-layer transformers with labeled flip noise, presenting error bounds for both benign and harmful overfitting under varying signal-to-noise ratios². The research categorizes training dynamics into three distinct stages, each with corresponding error bounds, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding when overfitting becomes benign versus harmful.### 2.3 Conditions for Benign OverfittingThe occurrence of benign overfitting in ICL depends on several factors:- The number of pre-training tasks- The quantity of in-context examples- The signal-to-noise ratio of the demonstrations- The implicit regularization properties of the learning algorithmFrei and Vardi (2024) characterize how many pre-training tasks and in-context examples are needed for trained transformers to generalize well at test-time, providing theoretical bounds on when benign overfitting emerges¹.

A significant challenge in ICL is the presence of noisy labels in demonstrations. Cheng et al. (2024) explored the robustness of transformers' in-context learning capabilities in the presence of noisy samples, showing that while transformers exhibit notable resilience against diverse types of noise in demonstration labels, they remain vulnerable to certain forms of corruption³.### 3.2 Impact on PerformanceResearch has shown that noisy labels in demonstrations can severely degrade ICL performance and reduce the stability of predictive results. This is particularly problematic in real-world scenarios where demonstrations are retrieved from potentially corrupted datasets⁴. The issue becomes more pronounced when scaling up the usage of demonstrations to larger numbers, as the likelihood of including noisy samples increases.### 3.3 Mitigation StrategiesSeveral approaches have been proposed to address noisy demonstrations:- **Training with noise**: Introducing noise during training as a form of data augmentation can improve robustness during inference³- **Demonstration selection**: Using influence functions and other methods to select high-quality demonstrations- **Robust training procedures**: Developing training methods that are inherently more robust to noise

sections.text: Nguyen and Reddy (2024) provided mechanistic insights into the transition from memorization to generalization during in-context learning⁵. Their work shows that the sub-circuits responsible for memorization and generalization can be viewed as largely independent, with the relative rates at which these sub-circuits learn explaining the transition rather than capacity constraints.### 4.2 Task Diversity ThresholdThe research reveals a memorization scaling law that determines the task diversity threshold at which networks generalize. This threshold is crucial for understanding when ICL will exhibit beneficial generalization versus problematic memorization⁵.### 4.3 Differential Learning KineticsThe transition from memorization to generalization is governed by differential learning kinetics, where different components of the network learn at different rates. This understanding helps explain various ICL-related phenomena, including the long-tailed distribution of when ICL is acquired and the bimodal behavior of solutions near the task diversity threshold⁵.

Research on neural processes has shown that models using attention mechanisms are more severely affected by noise, leading to "in-context overfitting"⁶. This suggests that while attention mechanisms enhance the capacity for in-context learning, they also increase susceptibility to over-adapting to noisy contexts.### 5.2 Model Architecture EffectsThe architecture of the transformer significantly influences its susceptibility to overfitting. Linear transformers, for example, have been shown to be non-robust and can be manipulated to output arbitrary predictions by perturbing a single example in the in-context training set⁷.### 5.3 Demonstration Quality and SelectionThe quality and selection of demonstrations play crucial roles in determining whether ICL will overfit. Poor demonstration selection can lead to biased learning and reinforcement of incorrect patterns, while careful selection can enhance generalization performance.

This unreliability stems from the model's sensitivity to prompt templates, demonstration permutations, and the specific examples chosen for the context⁸.### 6.2 Calibration MethodsTo address reliability issues, researchers have proposed calibration methods such as Linear Probe Calibration (LinC), which calibrates model output probabilities to achieve more reliable predictions while requiring minimal additional samples⁸.### 6.3 Adversarial RobustnessThe adversarial robustness of ICL remains a significant concern. Anwar et al. (2024) demonstrated that transformers can be vulnerable to hijacking attacks, where adversaries manipulate prompts to force specific outputs⁷. However, adversarial training can enhance robustness against such attacks.

question: What are leading approaches for evaluating complex scientific question answering systems in NLP?

sections.text: ## Introduction The evaluation of complex scientific question answering (QA) systems in Natural Language Processing (NLP) presents unique challenges that distinguish it from general domain QA evaluation. Scientific QA systems must handle technical terminology, domain-specific reasoning, and complex multi-step inferences while maintaining factual accuracy (Farea et al., 2022). This report examines the leading approaches for evaluating these systems, organized into key evaluation methodologies and their applications.

citations.title: Evaluation of Question Answering Systems: Complexity of Judging a Natural Language

sections.text: ## 1. Evaluation Taxonomies and Framework Classifications ### 1.1 Dual-Branch Evaluation Taxonomy The evaluation of QA systems can be systematically organized into two main branches as proposed by Farea et al. (2022): **Human-Centric Evaluation Scores (HCES)** and **Automatic Evaluation Scores (AES)**. This taxonomy recognizes that "translating human judgment into measurable metrics continues to be an open issue" and that "many of the available evaluation scores are not task-agnostic" (Farea et al., 2022). ### 1.2 Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Characteristics For multilingual knowledge graph question answering, researchers have identified three pivotal characteristics that serve as reference points for method selection: **resource efficiency**, **multilinguality**, and **portability** (Perevalov et al., 2024). These characteristics provide a framework for evaluating system performance across diverse deployment scenarios.

sections.text: ## 2. Automatic Evaluation Metrics ### 2.1 Traditional Lexical Metrics Traditional automatic metrics include **BLEU**, **ROUGE**, **METEOR**, **Exact Match**, and **F1 score**. However, these metrics "often struggle to capture the nuanced and diverse responses" in scientific QA contexts (Phatthiyaphaibun et al., 2024). The limitations are particularly pronounced for scientific domains where technical accuracy and conceptual understanding are paramount. ### 2.2 Embedding-Based Metrics Modern embedding-based metrics such as **BERTScore**, **BARTScore**, and **BLEURT** show improved correlation with human judgments. Research demonstrates that "embedding-based automatic NLG evaluation methods, such as BERTScore and BLEURT, have a higher correlation with human ratings, compared to word-overlap metrics, such as BLEU and ROUGE" (Clinciu et al., 2021). ### 2.3 LLM-Based Evaluation Approaches Recent advances have introduced **Large Language Model (LLM)-based metrics** that offer "more fine-grained evaluations" (Phatthiyaphaibun et al., 2024). These approaches leverage the reasoning capabilities of LLMs to assess answer quality across multiple dimensions, though challenges such as score clustering remain.

sections.text: ## 3. Human-Centric Evaluation Approaches ### 3.1 Expert-Based Evaluation Human evaluation by domain experts remains the gold standard for scientific QA evaluation. Expert assessment is particularly crucial for complex scientific questions where "there are multiple correct answers, or multiple ways to express a correct answer for a single input" (Schubert et al., 2024). ### 3.2 Crowdsourcing Approaches Crowdsourcing has emerged as a "fast, scalable, and cost-effective alternative to expert evaluations" (Iskender et al., 2020). However, implementing crowdsourcing for scientific QA requires careful consideration of worker expertise and appropriate task design to handle technical content. ### 3.3 Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation Human-in-the-loop evaluation frameworks provide continuous feedback during system development. The **GENIE6 human-in-the-loop leaderboard framework** has been proposed to "score answers in tasks where the answers can be long and drawn from extensive documents" (Bayes et al., 2024).

Domain-Specific Evaluation Approaches ### 4.1 Scientific Domain Benchmarks Several benchmarks have been developed specifically for scientific QA evaluation: - **SciQ**: A dataset of science exam questions designed to evaluate NLP models' understanding and reasoning within scientific domains (Welbl et al., 2017) - **ARC Challenge (ARC-C)**: Contains science exam questions requiring higher-order reasoning (Clark et al., 2018) - **SciQAG**: A framework for automatically generating science question-answer pairs with fine-grained evaluation (Wan et al., 2024) ### 4.2 Specialized Domain Evaluation Domain-specific evaluation approaches have been developed for various scientific fields: - **Biomedical QA**: Specialized frameworks like the **Pika framework** for protein question answering that includes "a curated, debiased dataset tailored for PQA and a biochemically relevant benchmarking strategy" (Carrami & Sharifzadeh, 2024) - **Climate Science**: The **ClimaQA framework** provides automated evaluation specifically for climate question answering models (Manivannan et al., 2024)

Multi-Aspect Evaluation Frameworks ### 5.1 CHIE Framework The **CHIE framework** introduces a multi-aspect evaluation approach incorporating four dimensions: **Correctness**, **Helpfulness**, **Irrelevance**, and **Extraneousness**. This framework "uses binary categorical values rather than continuous rating scales" and "aligns well with human judgments" (Phatthiyaphaibun et al., 2024). ### 5.2 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Evaluation For RAG-based scientific QA systems, specialized evaluation approaches consider both retrieval and generation components. Research shows that "conventional metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 score may not fully capture LLMs' capabilities" in these systems (Alinejad et al., 2024).

The evaluation of "RAG Pipeline in Multimodal LLM-based Question Answering Systems" presents new challenges for comprehensive assessment (Barochiya et al., 2024). ### 6.2 Cross-Lingual Scientific QA Evaluation Multilingual evaluation presents additional complexity, as demonstrated by the **Uhura benchmark** which reveals that "all models perform better in English than in African languages" and that "LMs struggle with answering scientific questions and are more prone to generating false claims in low-resource African languages" (Bayes et al., 2024). ### 6.3 Long-Form Answer Evaluation The evaluation of long-form scientific answers remains particularly challenging. Current approaches include developing "reference-free evaluation metrics for tasks where reference-based metrics are inadequate or impractical" and implementing "unified evaluation benchmark for long-form answers" (Bayes et al., 2024).

sections.text: ## Conclusion The evaluation of complex scientific question answering systems requires a multifaceted approach that combines automatic metrics, human evaluation, and domain-specific considerations. While traditional metrics provide baseline assessments, the field is moving toward more sophisticated evaluation frameworks that can capture the nuanced requirements of scientific reasoning and domain expertise. The development of specialized benchmarks, multi-aspect evaluation frameworks, and human-in-the-loop approaches represents the current state-of-the-art in scientific QA evaluation. Future research directions include improving cross-lingual evaluation capabilities, developing better metrics for long-form scientific answers, and creating more robust evaluation frameworks that can handle the increasing complexity of multimodal scientific QA systems. The integration of LLM-based evaluation approaches with traditional metrics shows promise for creating more comprehensive and accurate assessment methods for scientific QA systems.

question: What are the key differences between participatory design and co-design?

sections.text: Participatory design and co-design are two closely related collaborative design approaches that have emerged from distinct historical and theoretical foundations, though they are often used interchangeably in contemporary literature (Hodson, Svanda, & Dadashi, 2023). Both approaches aim to involve stakeholders in the design process, but they differ significantly in their philosophical underpinnings, methodological approaches, and the extent of user involvement. Participatory design has its roots in the Scandinavian design tradition of the 1960s and 1970s, emerging from democratic ideals and worker participation movements (Gall et al., 2021). Co-design, on the other hand, has evolved more recently as a distinct approach that emphasizes "collective creativity" and collaborative idea generation (Nguyen et al., 2023).

sections.text: ### Participatory Design Participatory design is fundamentally grounded in democratic principles and social justice ideologies. It operates from the premise that "people whose activity and experiences will ultimately be affected most directly by a design outcome ought to have a substantive say in what that outcome is" (Hasanin, 2013). This approach has an explicit ideological commitment to involving end-users in the design process, not merely to create better-suited products, but to democratize the design process itself. The approach is deeply embedded in the Scandinavian design tradition and operates on the principle that design should be driven by "a consistent socio-technical approach that appreciates the context in which the technology will be used and the processes and practices within that context" (Hasanin, 2013). Participatory design seeks to empower users and challenge traditional power structures in design. ### Co-Design Co-design, while also collaborative, is primarily focused on "collective creativity" and collaborative problem-solving (Nguyen et al., 2023). It is defined as "active collaboration between stakeholders in the design of solutions to a pre-specified problem" (Willmott, Hurley, & Rundle-Thiele, 2022). Co-design emphasizes the creative process and facilitates multi-professional negotiation by transcending traditional boundaries between designers and users. The approach is less explicitly ideological than participatory design, focusing more on practical collaboration and creativity rather than democratic participation as an end in itself.

sections.text: ### Participatory Design Participatory design follows a process described as "investigating, understanding, reflecting upon, establishing, developing and supporting mutual learning between multiple participants in collective 'reflection-in-action'" (Hasanin, 2013). The methodology emphasizes three main areas: "the politics of design, the nature of participation and methods, tools and techniques" (Hasanin, 2013). The process is characterized by: - Extended engagement throughout the entire design lifecycle - Emphasis on mutual learning between designers and users - Focus on understanding users' realities and contexts - Integration of users' articulated needs with appropriate technological solutions ### Co-Design Co-design employs a more structured methodology often organized into distinct phases. A typical co-design process includes four stages: "(1) Exploration (2) Co-Design (3) Validation (4) Development" (Nguyen et al., 2023). The process is characterized by: - Shorter duration and more intensive collaboration periods - Focus on collective creativity and idea generation - Structured workshops and collaborative sessions - Emphasis on rapid prototyping and iterative development

sections.text: ### Participatory Design Participatory design offers more extensive user involvement and influence in the design process. It aims to blur the roles between designers and users, with "the roles of the designer and researcher blur and the user becomes a critical component of the process" (Hasanin, 2013). The approach emphasizes bi-directional learning and gives users significant agency in shaping both the process and outcomes. Participatory design "aims for inclusivity" and true collaboration that "rests on mutual understanding, acknowledging the dynamic nature of community collaboration and the holistic impact of shaping relationships" (Rodil et al., 2024). It emphasizes long-term engagement and relationship-building. ### Co-Design Co-design involves active collaboration but typically with more structured roles and boundaries. While users are involved as active participants, the process is often more designer-facilitated. The approach "gives users more influence than traditional design methods but potentially less than participatory design" (Nguyen et al., 2023). Co-design focuses on bringing together different stakeholders to collaborate on specific design challenges, with "the line between designer and user (or community member) begins to blur and the creation process becomes a shared activity" (Nguyen et al., 2023).

sections.text: ### Participatory Design Participatory design typically requires more extensive resources and longer-term commitment. It involves sustained engagement with communities and stakeholders, often requiring "extended design spaces for participants beyond the confines and temporality constraints of academic calendars or research funding awards" (Nicholson et al., 2022). The approach demands significant investment in relationship-building and community engagement, which can be resource-intensive but leads to deeper understanding and more sustainable outcomes. ### Co-Design Co-design is generally more resource-efficient in terms of time and financial investment. As noted in comparative studies, "with a shorter duration and less intensive user involvement, co-design offers a more resource efficient means of solution generation" (Willmott, Hurley, & Rundle-Thiele, 2022). However, this efficiency comes with trade-offs in terms of the depth of engagement and the breadth of solutions generated.

sections.text: ### Participatory Design Participatory design tends to generate more diverse and contextually appropriate solutions due to its emphasis on deep understanding of user contexts and needs. The approach "expands the solution space by allowing for human-centred problem framing and in so doing gives rise to greater diversity in solutions generated" (Willmott, Hurley, & Rundle-Thiele, 2022). The focus on long-term engagement and relationship-building often leads to more sustainable and widely adopted solutions. ### Co-Design Co-design typically produces more focused solutions that address specific, pre-defined problems. While the solutions may be more immediately implementable, they may have less diversity due to the more structured and time-limited nature of the process. The approach is particularly effective for addressing well-defined challenges where stakeholders can collaborate intensively over shorter periods.

Co-design, while also collaborative, is more focused on collective creativity, structured collaboration, and resource-efficient solution generation. question: Does active learning work well when fine-tuning large language models?

sections.text: The effectiveness of active learning (AL) for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) is a nuanced topic with both promising successes and significant challenges. Recent research reveals a mixed landscape where traditional active learning approaches face fundamental difficulties when applied to LLMs, particularly when combined with parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. However, novel approaches specifically designed for LLMs show considerable promise, suggesting that with appropriate adaptations, active learning can indeed be effective for LLM fine-tuning.

Recent research has identified a critical issue termed the "uncertainty gap" when applying active learning to LLMs with parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. Zhang et al. (2024) found that "simply fine-tuning an LLM with LoRA under an uncertainty-based active learning framework yields consistently inferior performances compared to passive learning" [1]. This phenomenon occurs because "the uncertainty calculated for selecting data during active learning comes from the full parameters, while only partial parameters remain tuned during PEFT" [1]. The uncertainty gap represents a fundamental mismatch between how uncertainty is calculated (using full model parameters) and how the model is actually trained (using only a subset of parameters in methods like LoRA). This discrepancy undermines the core assumption of active learning that uncertainty measures accurately reflect the model's training needs. Another significant challenge is poor model calibration in LLMs. Research by Xiong et al. (2023) demonstrates that "LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns of expressing confidence" [2]. This overconfidence issue is particularly problematic for active learning, which relies on accurate uncertainty estimates to select the most informative samples. Kapoor et al. (2024) emphasize that "prompting on its own is insufficient to achieve good calibration" [3], highlighting the need for specialized approaches to obtain reliable uncertainty estimates from LLMs. The calibration problem is compounded by the fact that LLMs often produce confidence scores that don't accurately reflect their actual knowledge or uncertainty. The computational demands of applying active learning to LLMs present additional challenges. Traditional active learning methods often require multiple forward passes, ensemble methods, or gradient calculations, all of which become prohibitively expensive when working with models containing billions of parameters. This scalability issue has limited the widespread adoption of active learning for LLMs in practice.

sections.text: Despite the challenges, several research efforts have developed specialized active learning approaches that show significant promise for LLMs. The STAR framework by Zhang et al. (2024) addresses the uncertainty gap problem by introducing "a dynamic uncertainty measurement that combines the uncertainty of the base model and the uncertainty of the full model during the iteration of active learning" [1]. This approach specifically tackles the mismatch between uncertainty calculation and parameter updates in parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Muldrew et al. (2024) developed an innovative approach for active preference learning in LLMs, showing that "our approach improves both the rate of learning and final performance of fine-tuning on pairwise preference data" [4]. Their method uses "the predictive entropy of the language model and a measure of certainty of the implicit preference model optimized by DPO" [4] to create more effective acquisition functions. Several studies have demonstrated substantial improvements in data efficiency when active learning is properly adapted for LLMs. The DELIFT framework by Agarwal et al. (2024) shows that "DELIFT can reduce the fine-tuning data size by up to 70% without compromising performance" [5]. This represents a significant advancement in making LLM fine-tuning more practical and cost-effective. Similarly, research on parameter-efficient methods combined with active learning has shown that "with an epinet, we can augment LMs to output the kind of uncertainty estimates that are useful to prioritize label acquisition. On GLUE tasks, this allows us to train a BERT model using 2x fewer labels" [6]. Recent work has focused on developing better uncertainty estimation methods specifically for LLMs. Kapoor et al. (2024) demonstrate that "fine-tuning on a small dataset of correct and incorrect answers can create an uncertainty estimate with good generalization and small computational overhead" [3]. Their approach shows that "a thousand graded examples are sufficient to outperform baseline methods" [3].

question: With respect to signal processing which operator is more sensitive to noise detection, first order or second order and why?

sections.text: In signal processing, second-order operators are fundamentally more sensitive to noise than first-order operators. This increased sensitivity stems from the mathematical properties of differentiation, where taking higher-order derivatives amplifies high-frequency components, including noise. While both operators are useful for different applications, their noise sensitivity characteristics require careful consideration in practical implementations.

### 1.1 Mathematical Basis The fundamental difference between first-order and second-order operators lies in their mathematical properties and response to signal characteristics. First-order differential operators, such as the gradient operator, are primarily used for detecting edges by computing the rate of change of pixel intensities¹. In contrast, second-order operators, such as the Laplacian operator, compute the rate of change of the first-order derivative and are designed to detect zero-crossings in the second derivative¹. ### 1.2 Noise Amplification Mechanism Second-order derivative operators inherently amplify noise more than first-order operators due to their fundamental mathematical properties. As noted in the literature, "the second-order derivative has a stronger response to fine details and is more sensitive to noise"². This increased sensitivity occurs because differentiation in the frequency domain corresponds to multiplication by frequency components, and higher-order derivatives involve higher powers of frequency, thereby amplifying high-frequency noise components more significantly.

First-order operators like the Sobel and Prewitt operators are designed to detect edges by computing gradients, and while they do amplify noise, the amplification is less severe than second-order methods. ### 2.2 Second-Order Operators Second-order operators, particularly the Laplacian operator, are significantly more sensitive to noise. question: How do external events influence software projects? Explain with a few recent examples.

sections.text:
External events have increasingly become critical factors that shape software project outcomes, methodologies, and strategic directions. This report examines how various external forces
—ranging from global pandemics to geopolitical conflicts, technological disruptions, and climate events—influence software development projects through multiple pathways including workforce adaptation, technological acceleration, supply chain impacts, and strategic pivots.

The COVID-19 pandemic represents one of the most significant external events affecting software projects in recent history. Research indicates that the pandemic fundamentally transformed software development practices and accelerated digital transformation initiatives across organizations (Ho et al., 2024).

### 1.1 Remote Work Transformation

The pandemic forced an unprecedented shift to remote work, fundamentally altering software development processes. Studies show that 89% of institutions managed to continue services seamlessly through remote work arrangements, though challenges emerged in integrating various communication tools (Aytekin et al., 2025). The transition to remote work was characterized by both opportunities and challenges:

- Accelerated Digital Adoption: Organizations rapidly adopted digital tools and platforms to maintain productivity (Ho et al., 2024)
- Workforce Adaptation: Software development teams had to quickly adapt to distributed collaboration models (Sereda, 2022)
- Infrastructure Challenges: The shift revealed gaps in technical infrastructure and cybersecurity preparedness (Alotibi & Abdulwahid, 2023)

### 1.2 Impact on Software Development Productivity

Research examining software development during the pandemic reveals mixed outcomes. A comprehensive study of 100 GitHub projects and 279 software development professionals found that while COVID-19 did not significantly impact software project metrics such as commits and pull requests, it severely affected developers' wellbeing, causing high stress levels and sleep disorders (Bao et al., 2020).

The pandemic's impact varied significantly across different aspects of software development:
- Individual vs. Collaborative Work: The sudden transition to work-from-home led engineers to focus more on individual tasks, temporarily reversing the social trend in software engineering (Neumann et al., 2021)
- Communication Patterns: Teams experienced changes in communication dynamics, with some reporting improved transparency while others struggled with informal communication loss (Miller et al., 2021)

question: Which frequency characteristics of seismic P-wave can be used to distinguish it from other waves?

sections.text: Seismic waves generated by earthquakes and other seismic sources propagate through the Earth's interior and exhibit distinct frequency characteristics that can be used for wave type discrimination. P-waves (primary waves) are the fastest-traveling seismic waves and possess unique frequency domain properties that differentiate them from S-waves (secondary waves), surface waves, and other seismic phenomena. Understanding these frequency characteristics is crucial for accurate seismic monitoring, earthquake detection, and discrimination between natural seismic events and anthropogenic sources.

P-waves exhibit distinct corner frequency characteristics that serve as a primary discriminant from other wave types. Research has shown that P-wave corner frequencies typically range from 1.0 to 23 Hz, with significant variation depending on the seismic source type (Saadalla et al., 2023). For shallow earthquakes, P-wave source spectra demonstrate higher corner frequencies (8.8–23 Hz) compared to other seismic sources such as quarry blasts (1.0–2.6 Hz) within the same magnitude range (Saadalla et al., 2023). The ratio of P-wave to S-wave corner frequencies (fc(P)/fc(S)) provides a robust discriminant parameter. Studies have demonstrated that this ratio ranges from 1.04 to 1.51 (average 1.28) for earthquakes, while explosions display a range between 1.52 and 2.84 (average 1.97) (Ataeva et al., 2017). The fc(P)/fc(S) discrimination threshold value for segregating quarry explosions from earthquakes has been estimated to be around 1.51-1.52 (Ataeva et al., 2017).

sections.text: P-waves demonstrate distinctive high-frequency spectral characteristics that differentiate them from other wave types. The high-frequency P/S spectral amplitude ratio resulting from differences in corner frequencies acts as an effective discriminator between different seismic sources (Ataeva et al., 2017). Regional spectral amplitude ratios effectively discriminate between different seismic events, typically at higher frequencies above about 3 to 4 Hz (Fisk, 2006; Xie & Patton, 1999). P-wave spectra exhibit characteristic spectral slopes that can be parameterized using the omega-square source model. The spectral slope parameter, along with corner frequency and constant level, uniquely determines P-wave spectral characteristics (Tjøstheim, 1975). Research indicates that P-wave spectra can be approximated by two straight lines in a double logarithmic scale, characterized by three parameters: constant level Ω, spectral corner frequency fc, and high-frequency spectral slope s (Tjøstheim, 1975). P-wave attenuation characteristics show distinct frequency dependence that can be used for wave discrimination. Studies have shown that P-wave quality factor follows a power law relationship Q = Q₀ × fⁿ, with frequency-dependent attenuation characterized by Qα = (11.22 ± 2.2) × f^(1.09 ± 0.07) (Moustafa et al., 2023). This frequency dependence differs from other wave types, providing an additional discriminant parameter.

sections.text: P-wave discrimination is most effective within specific frequency bands. Research has identified that P-wave spectral characteristics are optimally preserved and analyzed within the 0.5-4 Hz frequency band (Tjøstheim, 1975). This frequency range provides sufficient resolution for extracting discriminant features while minimizing the effects of noise and attenuation. P-wave frequency characteristics are influenced by site-specific geological conditions. Studies have shown that P-wave spectral ratios at rock sites exhibit large amplification in frequency ranges of 3-10 Hz, with peaks at high frequencies around 10 Hz (Applicability of On-Site P-Wave Earthquake Early Warning, 2011). In contrast, sedimentary basin sites show broader frequency amplification ranges of 0.3-10 Hz (Applicability of On-Site P-Wave Earthquake Early Warning, 2011). P-wave frequency characteristics are affected by propagation path effects, with high-frequency components experiencing greater attenuation. The frequency-dependent quality factor for P-waves shows n values ranging between 0.85 and 1.19, indicating strong frequency dependence in attenuation characteristics (Moustafa et al., 2023).

sections.text: P-waves can be distinguished from surface waves through their frequency characteristics and propagation velocities. Surface waves, particularly Rayleigh waves, exhibit distinct dispersion characteristics with frequency-dependent phase velocities (Lin et al., 2022). P-waves maintain relatively constant velocities across frequency ranges, unlike the dispersive nature of surface waves. P-waves can be differentiated from anthropogenic noise sources through frequency domain analysis. Train-induced vibrations, a common noise source, display dominant high-frequency components with large high-frequency to low-frequency ratios compared to seismic P-waves (Recent Research on and Prospects regarding Disaster Prevention Technology, 2023). This frequency characteristic allows for effective discrimination between seismic P-waves and noise sources. Advanced discrimination techniques utilize multiple P-wave frequency characteristics simultaneously. Machine learning approaches have successfully used combinations of P-wave spectral features, including corner frequency, spectral ratios, and frequency-dependent parameters, achieving discrimination accuracies of up to 100% for certain applications (Elkhouly & Ali, 2024).

sections.text: The frequency characteristics of seismic P-waves provide multiple discriminant parameters for distinguishing them from other wave types. Key distinguishing features include corner frequencies typically ranging from 1.0 to 23 Hz for earthquakes, characteristic P-wave to S-wave corner frequency ratios, distinct high-frequency spectral content, and frequency-dependent attenuation properties. These characteristics, when analyzed within optimal frequency bands (0.5-4 Hz for spectral analysis, 3-10 Hz for high-frequency discrimination), enable effective discrimination between P-waves and other seismic phenomena. The combination of multiple frequency-domain parameters enhances discrimination accuracy and provides robust tools for seismic monitoring and analysis applications.

question: What are some tasks where fine tuning smaller models is beneficial over using LLMs?

sections.text: While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive general capabilities, there are several scenarios where fine-tuning smaller models provides distinct advantages over using LLMs directly. These advantages primarily stem from computational efficiency, privacy constraints, resource limitations, and domain-specific performance requirements.

Fine-tuning smaller models is particularly advantageous in real-world industrial environments where computational resources are limited. Research has shown that compact models like FLAN-T5 (780M parameters) can perform on par or even better than much larger zero-shot LLMs (from 7B to above 70B parameters) for specific tasks like meeting summarization [1]. This makes fine-tuned smaller models a suitable cost-efficient solution for real-world industrial deployment where the substantial computing resources required for LLMs are prohibitive [1]. In edge computing environments, where computational resources are inherently limited, fine-tuned smaller models offer significant advantages. The deployment of large-scale language models on edge devices faces challenges including high computational demands, energy consumption, and potential data privacy risks [2]. Small Language Models (SLMs) like the Shakti series (100M-500M parameters) have been specifically designed to address these constraints, enabling on-device intelligence for smartphones, smart appliances, and IoT systems [2]. When carefully engineered and fine-tuned, these compact models can meet and often exceed expectations in real-world edge-AI scenarios [2].

sections.text: Fine-tuning smaller models excels in medical and healthcare domains where specialized knowledge is crucial. Research demonstrates that domain-specific fine-tuning can rapidly adapt base models to specialized domains like medicine, producing models comparable to GPT-3.5-turbo while using significantly fewer computational resources [3]. This approach is particularly valuable in medical applications where domain-specific knowledge is essential and general LLMs may lack the required specialized expertise [3]. In legal applications, fine-tuned smaller models have shown remarkable performance advantages. Studies show that small neural networks trained with augmented data achieve outcomes comparable to those of other large language models, with the best-performing deep learning model trained on augmented data outperforming few-shot GPT-3 by 18% in F1-score for legal overruling tasks [4]. This demonstrates that smaller models can be highly effective for specialized legal tasks when properly trained with domain-specific data [4]. The Task-Fine-Tune methodology has proven effective across diverse domains including finance, healthcare, law, psychology, consumer services, and human resources. Fine-tuned models using this approach not only achieve superior performance on specific tasks but also significantly outperform models with higher general capabilities in their respective domains [5]. This suggests that for individuals and small organizations, models precisely tailored to specific business contexts are more beneficial than those with broadly superior general capabilities [5].

sections.text: When dealing with sensitive data, fine-tuning smaller models offers significant privacy advantages. In privacy-sensitive domains, directly using external LLMs on private data is strictly prohibited by stringent data security and privacy regulations [6]. Fine-tuned smaller models can be deployed locally, ensuring that sensitive data never leaves the organization's infrastructure, while still providing effective performance for domain-specific tasks [6]. Smaller models deployed on personal devices (PCs, smartphones) provide enhanced privacy protection compared to cloud-based LLMs. The CoGenesis framework demonstrates that collaborative approaches using smaller models on local devices can address privacy concerns while maintaining competitive performance [7]. This approach allows organizations to maintain control over their data while still benefiting from AI capabilities [7].

sections.text: For specialized reasoning tasks like causal graph validation, fine-tuned smaller models consistently outperform prompt-based LLMs. Research shows that fine-tuned models achieve up to a 20.5-point improvement in F1 score compared to prompt-based approaches, even when using smaller-parameter language models [8]. This demonstrates that for specific analytical tasks requiring precise reasoning, fine-tuned smaller models can be more effective than general-purpose LLMs [8]. In game-theoretic decision-making tasks requiring theory of mind capabilities, fine-tuned smaller models can bridge the performance gap with larger models effectively. Studies show that fine-tuned smaller models achieve 46% improvement in alignment with larger model behavior, with remarkable performance extending to out-of-sample scenarios [9]. This suggests that for strategic reasoning tasks, fine-tuned smaller models can provide cost-effective alternatives to larger models [9].

sections.text: Advanced fine-tuning techniques like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and its variants enable efficient adaptation of smaller models while maintaining performance. The Chain of LoRA (COLA) framework demonstrates that iterative optimization can bridge the gap between LoRA and full parameter fine-tuning without additional computational costs [10]. These techniques make fine-tuning smaller models particularly attractive for organizations with limited computational resources [10]. Fine-tuning techniques for smaller models offer significant advantages in memory efficiency and computational costs. Methods like DP-ZO for private fine-tuning possess significant advantages over traditional approaches in memory efficiency while maintaining privacy guarantees [11]. This makes smaller model fine-tuning particularly suitable for scenarios where both computational efficiency and privacy are important [11].

While LLMs excel in general-purpose applications, smaller fine-tuned models provide more cost-effective, privacy-preserving, and often superior performance for specific use cases. The choice between fine-tuning smaller models and using LLMs should be guided by the specific requirements of computational resources, privacy constraints, domain expertise needs, and deployment environment.

question: What are some common UI designs for sense-making, information organization, and AI writing tools?

sections.text: ### Visual Sensemaking InterfacesVisual sensemaking interfaces are designed to support users in constructing understanding from complex information. The process involves "organizing data to structure the unknown, helping individuals gain a deeper and more nuanced comprehension by extrapolating information from the data" (Steering LLM Summarization with Visual Workspaces for Sensemaking). Modern sensemaking tools employ several key design patterns:Spatial Organization Strategies: Research shows that "spatial organization is a popular knowledge externalization strategy, but can happen at different scales" (How Sensemaking Tools Influence Display Space Usage). Users organize either abstract nodes representing facts or concepts, or resort to organizing windows when conceptual organization tools aren't available.Interactive Spatial Representations: Visual workspaces such as Space to Think and Jigsaw serve as "intermediate representations to facilitate human sensemaking and analytics" (Steering LLM Summarization with Visual Workspaces for Sensemaking). These tools provide schematization mechanisms that help users structure their understanding.Graph-Based Visualization: The bidirectionally linked concept-graph (BLC) approach allows users to "externalize their knowledge through a graph" while "combining features of CLIP (attaching lists of document references to nodes and edges) and ScratchPad (referencing specific websites or passages within)" (How Sensemaking Tools Influence Display Space Usage).

sections.text: ### Collage-Based Design ApproachA revolutionary approach to AI writing tool design employs the concept of "Collage" with "four facets: 1) fragmenting text in writing interfaces, 2) juxtaposing voices (content vs command), 3) integrating material from multiple sources (e.g. text suggestions), and 4) shifting from manual writing to editorial and compositional decision-making, such as selecting and arranging snippets" (Collage is the New Writing: Exploring the Fragmentation of Text and User Interfaces in AI Tools).### Suggestion Interface DesignAI writing tools utilize two primary approaches for text suggestions: "inline and list of suggestions" with distinct user experience implications. Studies show that "people using the inline interface provided longer reviews on average, while participants using the list of suggestions experienced more ease of use" (Enhancing Peer Review with AI-Powered Suggestion Generation Assistance: Investigating the Design Dynamics).### Collaborative Writing InterfacesModern AI writing assistants are designed as "intelligent and interactive writing assistants" that are "capable of autonomous decision-making and/or text generation" while being "interactive if they reflect human input and/or output and facilitate an iterative process to produce a written artifact" (A Design Space for Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants).Three Categories of AI Writing Tools:1. Fluent multipurpose generation: Tools that "generate completions or suggestions that are inserted directly into the user's text" designed to be "relevant, grammatically correct and potentially included into the final output without modification" (Ai.llude: Investigating Rewriting AI-Generated Text to Support Creative Expression).2. Task-specific targeted suggestions: Tools that focus "on supporting one particular type of writing task, providing targeted suggestions rather than general text completion" (Ai.llude: Investigating Rewriting AI-Generated Text to Support Creative Expression).3. Resources for interpretation: Tools that "provide resources for interpretation as their text generation goal" (Ai.llude: Investigating Rewriting AI-Generated Text to Support Creative Expression).### Writer-Centric Design ConsiderationsResearch emphasizes that "writers prioritize personal values of authentic self-expression and love of process when deciding if and how to employ AI writing aids" (Preserving Writer Values in AI Writing Assistance Tools). This has led to design approaches that preserve writer agency and creative control.Professional vs. Hobbyist Needs: Studies reveal that "hobbyists emphasize personal expression and ownership, while professionals prioritize productivity" (From Pen to Prompt: How Creative Writers Integrate AI into their Writing Practice), necessitating different UI approaches for different user groups.
