question: What are existing methods to elicit user intents when an automation encounters ambiguity, especially in failure cases?

sections.text: This report examines existing methods for eliciting user intents when automated systems encounter ambiguity, particularly during failure scenarios. Through analysis of recent research in human-AI interaction, dialogue systems, and interactive machine learning, we identify key approaches including clarification dialogue strategies, mixed-initiative interaction frameworks, active learning with uncertainty quantification, and interactive user feedback mechanisms. The findings reveal that effective intent elicitation requires combining multiple techniques to handle the complex interplay between system uncertainty, user trust, and interaction design.

Modern automated systems frequently encounter ambiguous situations where user intent is unclear, particularly during failure scenarios. These ambiguities can arise from incomplete information, conflicting signals, or situations outside the system's training distribution. The ability to effectively elicit user intents in such scenarios is crucial for maintaining system reliability and user trust.

Research has shown that task-oriented dialogue systems can effectively handle ambiguous user commands through systematic clarification strategies. Alfieri et al. (2022) developed a solution for contact center virtual assistants that identifies when a user command is ambiguous and generates clarification questions containing the top-N most likely intents ^[Intent Disambiguation for Task-oriented Dialogue Systems]. This approach significantly outperformed popularity-based models in terms of disambiguation accuracy.Den Hengst et al. (2024) introduced the Conformal Intent Classification and Clarification (CICC) framework, which transforms uncertainty scores from intent classifiers into clarification questions guaranteed to contain the true intent at a predefined confidence level ^[Conformal Intent Classification and Clarification for Fast and Accurate Intent Recognition]. This method generates small, focused clarification questions that improve both speed and accuracy of intent resolution.Lautraite et al. (2021) proposed a multi-stage clarification mechanism for question-answering systems that handles ambiguous queries through iterative refinement ^[Multi-stage Clarification in Conversational AI: The case of Question-Answering Dialogue Systems]. Their approach prevents the common problem of providing either irrelevant direct answers or generic fallback messages when intent is unclear.Muroň et al. (2023) developed an interactive toponym disambiguation method specifically for dialogue systems, using dialogue clarification techniques to ask users for additional information ^[User-Driven Toponym Disambiguation Using Dialogue]. They introduced novel questioning strategies and the Equi-population partitioning method for selecting suitable features to formulate disambiguation questions.

Mixed-initiative systems represent a key approach to handling ambiguity by allowing both human and AI agents to take initiative in the interaction. Nguyen et al. (2018) demonstrated this approach in fact-checking systems, where human knowledge combines with automated information retrieval ^[Believe it or not: Designing a Human-AI Partnership for Mixed-Initiative Fact-Checking]. Their research revealed that while users generally trust AI predictions, transparency becomes crucial when the model makes errors.Niraula et al. (2024) conducted extensive research on human-AI interaction in medical decision-making, showing that collaborative decision-making involves complex relationships between expert knowledge, patient state, and AI recommendations ^[Intricacies of Human-AI Interaction in Dynamic Decision-Making for Precision Oncology: A Case Study in Response-Adaptive Radiotherapy]. Their findings indicate that effective systems must account for varying levels of user trust and expertise.Abbas et al. (2024) developed AI-enhanced decision support systems for control room operations that adapt intervention strategies based on both system state and human performance ^[Analyzing Operator States and the Impact of AI-Enhanced Decision Support in Control Rooms: A Human-in-the-Loop Specialized Reinforcement Learning Framework for Intervention Strategies]. Their approach achieved 95.8% accuracy in predicting operator performance and capacity to handle system upsets.

Interactive machine learning provides mechanisms for users to provide feedback when systems encounter failures. Honeycutt et al. (2020) found that while soliciting user feedback can improve system performance, it paradoxically reduces user trust and perceptions of system accuracy ^[Soliciting Human-in-the-Loop User Feedback for Interactive Machine Learning Reduces User Trust and Impressions of Model Accuracy]. This highlights the need for careful design of feedback mechanisms.Guo et al. (2022) developed explanation-driven interactive machine learning (XIML) systems that combine explanations with user feedback mechanisms ^[Building Trust in Interactive Machine Learning via User Contributed Interpretable Rules]. Their research showed that interactivity improves user satisfaction, though the role of visual explanations was less prominent than expected.Kawabe and Sugano (2024) proposed multimodal large language model assistants that help non-expert users articulate their requirements when building machine learning models ^[A Multimodal LLM-based Assistant for User-Centric Interactive Machine Learning]. The system monitors user interactions and translates vague needs into concrete formulations, preventing failures due to inadequate training data specification.Teso et al. (2022) provided a comprehensive overview of how explanations can be used beyond transparency to elicit user control in interactive machine learning systems ^[Leveraging explanations in interactive machine learning: An overview]. They identified approaches for learning new models from scratch and editing existing ones through explanation-based interaction.

Active learning systems use uncertainty estimates to determine when to query users for additional information. Thomas et al. (2024) studied how active learning query policies and uncertainty visualizations influence user trust in automated systems ^[Assessing User Trust in Active Learning Systems: Insights from Query Policy and Uncertainty Visualization]. They found that query policies significantly influence user perceptions of system capabilities.Fuchsgruber et al. (2024) developed ground-truth Bayesian uncertainty estimates for active learning that prove effective in guiding uncertainty sampling toward optimal queries ^[Uncertainty for Active Learning on Graphs]. Their approach consistently outperformed other uncertainty estimators by developing principled uncertainty estimation methods.Liu et al. (2024) demonstrated intent elicitation in computer vision tasks through iPose, an interactive tool for 3D human pose reconstruction ^[iPose: Interactive Human Pose Reconstruction from Video]. When automatic reconstruction fails due to ambiguities, the system allows users to manipulate pose projections through 2D operations, with updates propagated temporally to reduce workload.

Yang (2021) developed a framework for understanding AI system design complexity that identifies four levels of systems based on capability uncertainty and output complexity ^[Profiling Artificial Intelligence as a Material for User Experience Design]. This framework helps designers understand when different intent elicitation methods are most appropriate.Keerthichandra et al. (2024) developed intent classification systems for intelligent tutoring that recognize diverse student behaviors including requests for clarification ^[Large Language Model-Based Student Intent Classification for Intelligent Tutoring Systems]. Their approach achieved high accuracy in recognizing when students need additional support or clarification.

Research consistently shows tension between providing user control and maintaining trust. While users desire the ability to correct perceived system flaws, the act of providing feedback can reduce confidence in system capabilities. This suggests that intent elicitation mechanisms must be carefully designed to maintain appropriate levels of trust.The effectiveness of intent elicitation methods varies significantly across domains, user expertise levels, and task types. Systems must adapt their approaches based on the specific context of use and characteristics of the user population.Many intent elicitation approaches require significant cognitive effort from users. Balancing the need for clear intent specification with manageable cognitive load remains an ongoing challenge.

Future systems should dynamically adapt their intent elicitation strategies based on user behavior, system performance, and context. This includes adjusting the level of detail in clarification questions and the frequency of user queries.Combining multiple interaction modalities (voice, gesture, text, visual) can provide richer channels for intent elicitation, potentially reducing ambiguity and improving user experience.Rather than waiting for failures to occur, systems should proactively model potential ambiguities and prepare clarification strategies in advance.

Effective intent elicitation in automated systems requires a multi-faceted approach combining clarification dialogue strategies, mixed-initiative interaction frameworks, active learning techniques, and careful attention to user experience design. The research shows that while these methods can significantly improve system performance in ambiguous situations, they must be implemented thoughtfully to maintain user trust and minimize cognitive burden. Future work should focus on developing adaptive, context-sensitive approaches that can dynamically adjust their intent elicitation strategies based on user needs and system capabilities.

question: Are there papers that use different formats of Q&A with the user to clarify intent and compose more complicated prompts to LLM?

sections.text: Yes, there are several papers that explore different formats of Q&A interactions with users to clarify intent and compose more sophisticated prompts for Large Language Models (LLMs). This research spans multiple domains including conversational AI, code generation, search systems, and interactive prompt engineering. The approaches range from template-based clarification questions to sophisticated multi-turn dialogue systems that progressively refine user intent.

Recent research has demonstrated significant interest in developing systems that engage users in multi-turn conversations to clarify intent and improve prompt quality. Liu et al. Ramezan et al. (2025) proposed the Multi-turn Multi-modal Clarifying Questions (MMCQ) task, which combines text and visual modalities to refine user queries over multiple conversation turns². Their approach uses prompt engineering to create two agents that interact - one acting as the conversational agent and another as the user - to demonstrate effective information gathering through structured dialogue.

question: How is artificial intelligence being utilized to enhance the diagnosis and treatment of sleep apnea?

sections.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing sleep apnea diagnosis and treatment by offering more accessible, accurate, and efficient alternatives to traditional polysomnography (PSG). The rapid development of AI technologies has led to significant improvements in pre-detection, monitoring, and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), addressing the limitations of conventional approaches that are costly, time-consuming, and require specialized facilities¹².

Traditional Diagnostic Limitations The gold standard for sleep apnea diagnosis is overnight polysomnography (PSG) conducted in specialized sleep laboratories. However, this method requires significant workforce resources, is expensive, and has limited availability due to restricted bed capacity³. These examinations are particularly challenging because experienced personnel must analyze extensive data, creating bottlenecks in the diagnostic process⁴. Machine Learning Approaches to Diagnosis Recent systematic reviews have demonstrated that machine learning (ML) models show excellent performance in diagnosing sleep apnea using easily obtainable features from various physiological signals⁵. A comprehensive review of 132 studies revealed that ML models successfully diagnose sleep apnea using: - Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals - Pulse oximetry data - Sound signals - Heart rate variability patterns These AI-based approaches facilitate the clinical work of sleep medicine specialists by providing rapid diagnosis capabilities that can prevent the development of various complications, including severe morning headaches and daytime drowsiness². Wearable Technology and Remote Monitoring AI-powered wearable devices represent a significant advancement in sleep apnea detection. Recent research demonstrates that smartwatch-based machine learning models can achieve impressive accuracy rates for sleep apnea detection, with some studies reporting 85% accuracy⁶. These devices leverage multiple sensors to monitor: - Heart rate and heart rate variability - Blood pressure - Physical activity patterns - Sleep patterns in real-time Wireless wearable sensor systems have proven particularly effective for hospitalized patients, with studies showing 88% sensitivity in detecting moderate-severe sleep apnea using photoplethysmography (PPG) and finger temperature features⁷. Deep Learning and Signal Processing Advanced deep learning approaches have shown remarkable success in sleep apnea detection. Studies utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for automatic feature extraction from respiratory data have demonstrated significant improvements over traditional methods⁸. Single-channel ECG analysis using deep learning has achieved 79.45% accuracy in OSA severity classification, significantly outperforming traditional SVM classifiers with RR Intervals and ECG derived respiration (EDR) signal feature extraction⁹. Deep learning analysis of polysomnography features has revealed that oxygen saturation (SpO2) provides the highest classification accuracy (98%) for distinguishing normal sleep from apnea events, followed by nasal air flow (85%), ECG (77%), and heart rate (63%)¹⁰.

sections.text: CPAP Therapy Optimization Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy remains the primary treatment for OSA, but poor adherence is a significant challenge. AI is being employed to address this issue through multiple approaches: Adherence Prediction: Machine learning models can predict CPAP treatment adherence using clinical features such as 24-hour diastolic blood pressure, daytime systolic pressure, arousal index, uric acid levels, and triglycerides. Artificial neural networks have achieved an AUC of 0.84 in predicting therapy adherence¹¹. Predictive Pressure Adjustment: Advanced ML algorithms can detect sleep apnea events 30-90 seconds in advance using ECG data during CPAP titration. Support vector machines have demonstrated 98.2% accuracy in forecasting sleep apnea events 60 seconds before they occur, enabling proactive pressure adjustments¹². Treatment Monitoring: AI-powered systems can continuously monitor CPAP therapy effectiveness using electrophysiological models to analyze respiratory patterns, blood oxygen saturation, and ECG-respiratory rate correlations¹³. Surgical Treatment Prediction Machine learning models have shown promising results in predicting outcomes following surgical treatment for sleep apnea⁵. These AI-guided approaches help clinicians make informed decisions about surgical interventions and optimize treatment strategies based on individual patient characteristics. Personalized Treatment Approaches AI enables the identification of OSA subgroups with heterogeneous treatment effects. Machine learning analysis of clinical trials has revealed that different patient subgroups may respond differently to CPAP therapy, allowing for more personalized treatment approaches¹⁴.

Multi-Modal Sensor Integration AI systems are increasingly integrating multiple sensor modalities to improve diagnostic accuracy. The combination of oximetry, airflow analysis, heart rate variability, and other physiological parameters provides comprehensive sleep analysis capabilities¹⁵.

Validation across diverse populations and the development of real-time alerting systems for preventing complications such as sudden cardiac death are areas of active research⁹.

From wearable devices that enable home-based monitoring to sophisticated algorithms that optimize CPAP therapy, AI technologies are addressing the fundamental challenges of sleep apnea management. question: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) receivers can provide a reference clock signal known as Pulse-per-Second (PPS or 1-PPS). Is the PPS physically generated through a digitally-controlled oscillator (or line driver) whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the estimated clock bias (retrieved by means of PVT algorithms)?

sections.text: The research question asks whether GNSS receivers generate the Pulse-per-Second (PPS) signal through a digitally-controlled oscillator (DCO) or line driver whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the estimated clock bias from Position, Velocity, and Time (PVT) algorithms. Based on the available literature, the answer is **yes, but with important nuances about the specific implementation approach**.

GNSS receivers do indeed generate PPS signals through a process that involves local oscillator steering based on clock bias estimates derived from PVT algorithms. However, the implementation typically involves disciplined oscillators rather than simple periodic re-initialization¹. The receiver can steer the local oscillator or an external GNSS-disciplined oscillator (DO) to output the physical 1-PPS signal whose wavefronts are aligned to the GNSS reference time scale with a given uncertainty¹. The receiver clock bias is common to all the received signals and is estimated through the PVT algorithm as a further unknown of the multilateration problem¹. The generation process of the 1-PPS strictly depends on the position, velocity, and time (PVT) solution, thus making use of the PN code and its phase offset, the message preamble, and the navigation data¹.

citations.title: Nanosecond-Level Resilient GNSS-Based Time Synchronization in Telecommunication Networks Through WR-PTP HA

sections.text: The clock bias estimation is indeed a fundamental part of the PVT solution. The receiver clock bias must be estimated at every epoch due to the poor long-term frequency stability of the internal quartz oscillator within the receivers². With three coordinates and a receiver clock bias, there are four unknowns to be estimated at each epoch². The satellite clock bias is compensated through a first-or second-order polynomial model based on the clock bias correction parameters carried by the navigation message, i.e., clock offset, clock drift, and clock drift rate¹. The uncertainty of the PPS signal is lower-bounded by the uncertainty of the receiver's clock bias estimation¹.

The physical implementation of PPS generation varies among different receiver architectures, but commonly involves disciplined oscillators rather than simple DCOs with periodic re-initialization. Clock Steering Approaches Clock steering is a routine operation to constrain the receiver clock bias since the large bias affects the signal tracking and orbit computation³. The clock steering means that the pseudorange and carrier phase measurements of all satellites are adjusted to control the receiver clock bias³. The subsystem that generates the 1-PPS wavefronts is able to steer it almost continuously¹. Hardware Implementation Modern GNSS receivers often use all-digital phase-locked loops (ADPLLs) where the high frequency signal is generated in a digitally controlled oscillator (DCO) and the signal frequency is determined by a series of bits⁴. Some implementations use Temperature Compensated Voltage Controlled Crystal Oscillators (TCVCXO) for synchronization⁵. Different receiver manufacturers implement varying approaches to PPS generation. For example, some receivers maintain PPS output aligned to the reference clock after steering to GNSS time, while others continuously steer to GNSS time⁶.

citations.title: Nanosecond-Level Resilient GNSS-Based Time Synchronization in Telecommunication Networks Through WR-PTP HA

sections.text: The literature suggests that modern GNSS receivers typically employ continuous disciplining rather than periodic re-initialization. The 1-PPS signal generation system can steer the output almost continuously¹, and any action that can alter the propagation delays may immediately affect the disciplination of the output 1-PPS¹. This continuous approach is more sophisticated than simple periodic re-initialization, as it provides better stability and accuracy. The disciplined oscillator approach allows for smooth adjustments rather than abrupt corrections that could introduce timing discontinuities.

citations.title: Nanosecond-Level Resilient GNSS-Based Time Synchronization in Telecommunication Networks Through WR-PTP HA

sections.text: The research confirms that GNSS receivers do generate PPS signals through mechanisms that involve digitally-controlled oscillators (or disciplined oscillators) whose timing is continuously adjusted based on clock bias estimates from PVT algorithms. However, the implementation is typically more sophisticated than simple periodic re-initialization, involving continuous disciplining to maintain optimal synchronization with GNSS time scales. The specific implementation details vary among different receiver architectures and manufacturers, but the fundamental principle of using PVT-derived clock bias estimates to steer the local oscillator for PPS generation is consistent across the literature.

question: During pre-training, why is the transformer embedding layer initialized randomly, rather than with pre-trained embeddings from existing models?

sections.text: The practice of initializing transformer embedding layers with random values rather than pre-trained embeddings during pre-training has become standard in the field of deep learning. This choice appears counter-intuitive given the well-established benefits of pre-trained representations and transfer learning. However, recent research has revealed several compelling reasons why random initialization is preferred for transformer pre-training.

The primary reason for using random initialization stems from the sensitivity of deep neural networks to parameter distribution and their effect on gradient flow. Transformers, like other deep networks, are highly sensitive to the variance of their parameters for proper gradient flow ^1^. Studies have established that neural networks require parameters to be initialized within a specific variance range to enable effective gradient flow and faster convergence during training ^1^. Random initialization schemes such as Xavier (Glorot) initialization are specifically designed to maintain this optimal parameter distribution. Xavier initialization restricts model parameter values, including token embeddings, to be zero-centered and within a narrow variance range that promotes stable gradient flow ^1^. This initialization method keeps the scale of gradients roughly the same across all layers, which is crucial for effective training ^2^. In contrast, pre-trained embeddings are not necessarily subject to these distributional constraints. Research has shown that pre-trained embeddings from models like GloVe, T5, and mT5 have significantly wider distributions of values compared to the Xavier initialization range ^1^. These large value initializations can lead to poor training performance due to saturated outputs in the network ^1^.

citations.title: On Initializing Transformers with Pre-trained Embeddings

Numerical Evaluation on Parametric Choices Influencing Segmentation Results in Radiology Images
GÇöA Multi-Dataset Study

sections.text: Another critical factor is how embedding initialization affects the interaction between token embeddings and positional encodings in transformers. Token embeddings are directly added to positional encodings to incorporate position information into the model ^1^. When the variance of word embeddings and positional encodings differ significantly, one type of information may dominate the other during this addition process. This phenomenon, referred to as "absorption," occurs when pre-trained embeddings with much higher variance effectively "absorb" the positional encoding values when added together, resulting in the loss of crucial position information ^1^. Since positional information is fundamental to transformer performance, this absorption effect can severely compromise model effectiveness.

citations.title: On Initializing Transformers with Pre-trained Embeddings

sections.text: Random initialization also provides better training stability during the pre-training phase. Research on large language model pre-training has shown that improper initialization can lead to loss spikes and training instability ^3^. The carefully calibrated variance of random initialization methods helps prevent these issues by ensuring that gradient norms remain stable throughout training. Furthermore, the training dynamics of transformers have been shown to rely on the specific properties of random initialization. Studies of gradient flow in transformers reveal that random initialization enables the model to naturally progress through distinct training phases, with different components (attention layers, MLP layers) contributing at different stages of training ^4^. This natural progression may be disrupted by the use of pre-trained embeddings that don't conform to the expected parameter distribution.

citations.title: Spike No More: Stabilizing the Pre-training of Large Language Models
Training Dynamics of Transformers to Recognize Word Co-occurrence via Gradient Flow Analysis

sections.text: Empirical studies have confirmed these theoretical predictions. Research comparing various initialization methods has found that pre-trained word embeddings from GloVe and sub-word embeddings from T5 and mT5 perform significantly worse than random initialization when training transformers from scratch ^1^. However, there are notable exceptions: BERT and multilingual BERT embeddings have been shown to perform better than random initialization, likely because their parameter distributions are closer to the Xavier initialization range ^1^. Importantly, when pre-trained embeddings are standardized to match the Xavier initialization distribution (by adjusting their mean and standard deviation), they can achieve substantial performance gains, sometimes matching or exceeding random initialization ^1^. This finding supports the theory that parameter distribution, rather than the lack of semantic information, is the primary factor limiting pre-trained embedding effectiveness.

citations.title: On Initializing Transformers with Pre-trained Embeddings

sections.text: From a practical standpoint, random initialization also offers several advantages: 1. Consistency: Random initialization provides a consistent starting point regardless of the specific pre-training task or domain. 2. Computational efficiency: There's no need to load, process, or adapt pre-trained embeddings, simplifying the training pipeline. 3. Flexibility: Random initialization allows the model to learn representations that are optimally suited to the specific pre-training objective and data distribution.

The preference for random initialization over pre-trained embeddings in transformer pre-training is primarily driven by the need to maintain proper parameter distributions for effective gradient flow and training stability. The interaction between embeddings and positional encodings further reinforces this choice, as pre-trained embeddings can interfere with crucial positional information. While pre-trained embeddings can be effective when properly standardized, random initialization provides a more robust and consistent approach that has proven successful across diverse transformer architectures and pre-training objectives.

question: Why do quadruped robots typically use 3 degrees of freedom for each leg?  What would be the disadvantages of 2 dof?

sections.text: Quadruped robots have become increasingly sophisticated over the past decades, with their leg design being a critical factor in determining their locomotion capabilities, stability, and versatility. The majority of successful quadruped robots employ a 3-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) configuration for each leg, which has become the standard in the field. This report examines the reasons behind this design choice and analyzes the disadvantages of using 2-DOF legs.

sections.text: The standard 3-DOF configuration for quadruped robot legs consists of three rotational joints that provide comprehensive mobility. Generally, quadruped robots have three DOFs in each leg and two DOFs in their hip joints (1). These hip joints are used to achieve lateral crossing and forward/backward swinging of the robot (1). The typical arrangement includes:1. Hip abduction/adduction joint (lateral movement)2. Hip flexion/extension joint (forward/backward movement) 3. Knee flexion/extension joint (vertical movement)This configuration allows each leg to perform complex three-dimensional movements essential for dynamic locomotion. The leg mechanism includes three degrees of freedom (DOF): hip joint side swing, hip joint front swing, and knee joint front swing (2).### Workspace and Mobility AdvantagesThe 3-DOF configuration provides several critical advantages for quadruped locomotion:**Large Workspace**: The workspace of the leg mechanism of the quadruped robot refers to the set of spatial position points that can be reached by the reference point of the foot end, which is a key parameter used to evaluate the feasibility and efficiency of the leg mechanism (3). Research has shown that the leg mechanism with 3-DOF has a large workspace, can achieve a step height of more than 200 mm, and has a large step length (3).**Versatility in Terrain Navigation**: The 3-DOF design enables quadruped robots to traverse complex terrain effectively. These robots can perform in response to external stimulation in an accurate and ideal manner of conditioned reflection and have the natural advantages of trafficability and agility on complex outdoor terrain (4).**Dynamic Stability**: The three degrees of freedom allow for precise control of foot placement and body posture, which is essential for maintaining stability during dynamic gaits and when traversing uneven surfaces.

sections.text: The primary disadvantage of 2-DOF legs is their significantly restricted workspace and mobility compared to 3-DOF systems. While some planar quadruped robots can realize pronking and jumping using parallel legs with two degrees of freedom (DOF), which combines the advantages of a large load capacity and good structural stability (4), they suffer from several limitations.### Constraint in Movement Patterns2-DOF legs impose severe constraints on the types of movements a quadruped robot can perform. For example, one study found that because the leg mechanism has only one active DOF, it is difficult to achieve a rich foot trajectory, and the foot trajectory formed during the movement is affected by the robot's weight and the terrain (5). This limitation extends to 2-DOF systems, which, while more capable than 1-DOF systems, still cannot match the versatility of 3-DOF configurations.### Singular Configuration IssuesA critical problem with 2-DOF legs is their susceptibility to singular configurations. Research has shown that robots with fewer DOFs can encounter situations where they become trapped in singular configurations, significantly limiting their mobility. When in such configurations, the robot can only move along limited axes, severely restricting its ability to navigate complex environments (6).### Reduced Adaptability to Terrain2-DOF legs have limited ability to adapt to varied terrain conditions. The reduced degrees of freedom mean that the robot cannot independently control all necessary parameters for optimal foot placement, body orientation, and load distribution. This limitation is particularly problematic when dealing with uneven surfaces, obstacles, or when precise foot positioning is required.### Control Complexity vs. Capability Trade-offWhile 2-DOF systems might appear simpler from a control perspective, they often require more complex strategies to achieve basic locomotion tasks that 3-DOF systems can perform more naturally. The motion performance of robots with fewer DOFs is hindered by their poor steering capabilities and inability to carry out transverse motion (7).

The three degrees of freedom allow for comprehensive control of leg positioning and orientation, enabling complex locomotion patterns, effective terrain navigation, and dynamic stability. question: In recommendation systems, how are new methods that optimize diversity typically evaluated?

sections.text: The evaluation of diversity-optimized recommendation systems is a multi-faceted challenge that requires consideration of both traditional accuracy metrics and novel diversity-specific measures. This report synthesizes current research to provide a comprehensive overview of how new methods that optimize diversity in recommendation systems are typically evaluated.

The most widely adopted approach for measuring diversity in recommendation systems relies on distance-based metrics that calculate pairwise dissimilarity between items in a recommendation list [1]. The two primary paradigms are Intra-List Average Distance (ILAD) and Intra-List Minimal Distance (ILMD), which originated from extending the intra-list similarity metrics proposed by Ziegler et al. [2]. Intra-List Diversity (ILD) measures the average distance between every pair of items in a recommendation list, typically using cosine distance between item embeddings [3]. The ILD metric has been extensively applied across different domains, with researchers reporting ILD scores ranging from 0.616 to 0.65 in practical implementations [4,5]. Coverage-based metrics evaluate diversity from a different perspective by measuring the breadth of item categories or catalog coverage. Category Coverage (CC) measures how many different categories appear in the top-K recommendation items [6]. Catalog Coverage (C-Coverage) quantifies the proportion of unique items that can be retrieved or recommended in the system by considering the union of all lists produced during measurement [7]. Recent research has identified critical limitations in existing diversity metrics, particularly their inability to distinguish between diversity improvements from effective versus ineffective recommendations [8]. To address this gap, new accuracy-aware metrics have been proposed, including DCC (Diversity with Correct Coverage), FDCC (Feature Distribution Correct Coverage), and DILAD (Diversity in List of Accurate Decisions) [8].

sections.text: Offline evaluation remains the predominant methodology for assessing diversity-optimized recommendation systems. These approaches can be categorized into three main strategies [9]: Pre-processing Strategies: These involve defining user types, establishing sampling strategies, and setting ground truth labels. While broadly applicable, their necessity varies depending on the model's loss function, with pair-wise loss models potentially benefiting more from sampling strategies than point-wise loss models [9]. In-processing Approaches: These treat diversity either as regularization or directly within the scoring function. Although intuitively aligned with list-wise loss models, these approaches can be adapted for pair-wise and point-wise models through creative adaptations [9]. Post-processing Strategies: These stand out for their universal compatibility, enabling the integration of diversity enhancements after model training while maintaining efficacy across all types of models [9]. While offline evaluation is prevalent, researchers increasingly recognize the limitations of purely offline approaches and advocate for online evaluation methods such as A/B testing [10]. Online evaluation through A/B testing has been demonstrated to provide more accurate assessments of diversity improvements in real-world applications, with some studies reporting successful 10-day A/B tests that confirmed diversity improvements in production systems [11]. User studies play a crucial role in validating diversity metrics and understanding user perception of diversity. Research involving over 500 participants has revealed that while ILS (Intra-List Similarity) can be a valid proxy for user-perceived diversity, the particularities matter significantly [12]. Different metric implementations can result in varying diversity perceptions, and what works well in one domain may not necessarily work well in another [12].

sections.text: Evaluating diversity-optimized systems requires careful consideration of the trade-off between accuracy and diversity. Research has shown that diversity improvements are often primarily contributed by ineffective recommendations, which do not positively contribute to user satisfaction [8]. This finding has led to the development of harmonic metrics like F-score to evaluate the balance between accuracy and diversity performance [13]. Modern evaluation frameworks incorporate multiple dimensions of assessment: Accuracy Metrics: Traditional measures like Recall@K, NDCG@K, Hit Rate, and Mean Reciprocal Rank continue to be essential [14]. Diversity Metrics: Including ILD, Category Coverage, and newly proposed accuracy-aware metrics [8]. Novelty and Serendipity Metrics: Such as Mean Self-Information (MSI) for measuring novelty, with reported values around 0.628 indicating novel recommendations [5]. Coverage Metrics: Both catalog coverage and prediction coverage to assess system-level diversity [15].

sections.text: A significant challenge in diversity evaluation is the lack of validated metrics that align with human perception. Research has revealed that algorithms are often assessed with anecdotal evidence or metrics that don't align with human perception [16]. This has led to calls for more robust evaluation methods that include controlled user studies to validate chosen diversity metrics [17]. When comparing diversity-optimized algorithms, especially in offline evaluations, there are fairness concerns. A recommender that seeks to diversify may use an objective function that is the same as, or closely related to, the metric used to measure diversity, leading to biased comparisons [18]. The evaluation becomes more challenging when dealing with multi-objective systems that must balance relevance and diversity. Traditional evaluation approaches that treat these objectives separately may not provide adequate insights into overall system performance [18].

sections.text: Recent research has introduced comprehensive evaluation frameworks specifically designed for diversity-enhanced recommendations. These frameworks provide standardized evaluation protocols that can be consistently applied across different approaches [19]. Evaluation methods are being adapted for specific domains and applications. For example, in sequential recommendation systems, diversity is evaluated for successive items with metrics like ILALD (Intra-List Average Local Distance) and ILMLD (Intra-List Minimal Local Distance) [20]. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) in recommendation systems introduces new considerations for diversity evaluation. While diversity metrics remain applicable, the direct application of diversity approaches to LLM-based recommendation systems may require novel evaluation methodologies [9].

sections.text: Current best practices recommend using multiple metrics to comprehensively evaluate diversity-optimized systems. This includes combining accuracy metrics (Recall@K, NDCG@K), diversity metrics (ILD, Category Coverage), and user-centric metrics validated through user studies [21]. Given the limitations of purely computational metrics, validation through user studies is increasingly recognized as essential. These studies should examine the correlation between computational diversity metrics and user-perceived diversity [12]. Evaluation should consider temporal aspects and decision contexts in user preference modeling, moving beyond simple train/test splits to more realistic evaluation scenarios [22].

sections.text: The evaluation of diversity-optimized recommendation systems requires a comprehensive approach that combines multiple metrics, evaluation methodologies, and validation techniques. While traditional distance-based and coverage-based metrics remain important, there is a growing recognition of the need for accuracy-aware diversity metrics and user-validated evaluation approaches. Future research should focus on developing more robust evaluation frameworks that can accurately assess the real-world impact of diversity optimizations while maintaining fairness in algorithmic comparisons. The field is moving toward more sophisticated evaluation practices that consider the multi-objective nature of diversity-optimized systems and the importance of user perception in determining the effectiveness of diversity enhancements. As recommendation systems continue to evolve, particularly with the integration of large language models, evaluation methodologies must adapt to ensure they provide meaningful insights into system performance and user satisfaction.

question: What are the latest techniques for ensuring the reliability of a P2P storage system?

sections.text: Peer-to-peer (P2P) storage systems have emerged as a critical component of modern distributed computing infrastructure, offering scalability, decentralization, and cost-effectiveness. However, ensuring reliability in these systems presents unique challenges due to the dynamic nature of peer participation, node failures, and the absence of centralized control. This report examines the latest techniques for enhancing P2P storage system reliability, focusing on recent advances in redundancy mechanisms, fault tolerance, consensus protocols, and data integrity verification.

Recent research has focused on optimizing erasure coding techniques for P2P storage systems. Erasure coding provides superior fault tolerance compared to traditional replication by generating redundant data that can reconstruct the original information even when some storage nodes fail (Arafa et al., 2018). The latest developments include:

citations.title: Erasure Coding Based Optimization in Decentralized Distributed Storage Systems

sections.text: **Adaptive Erasure Coding**: Song et al. (2023) proposed an environment-adaptive erasure coding scheme that dynamically adjusts encoding parameters based on network conditions. Their Environment-adaptive Parameters Algorithm (EAPA) and Optimal Repair Cost Parameters Algorithm (ORCPA) can significantly increase durability levels while reducing repair bandwidth costs and repair time in multi-peer failure scenarios (Song et al., 2023).**Tunable Erasure Coding**: Modern storage systems now support tunable erasure coding that allows efficient switching between different coding schemes based on system requirements. question: What principles of interactive machine teaching can be applied to interactively curating social media feeds?

sections.text: The application of interactive machine teaching (IMT) principles to social media feed curation represents a promising approach to addressing the limitations of current black-box algorithmic curation systems. This report examines how IMT's core principles	at—including iterative human-AI interaction, user agency, and interpretable feedback mechanisms	at—can be adapted to create more personalized and controllable social media experiences.

Social media feeds serve as deeply personal spaces that reflect individual values and preferences, yet current algorithmic curation systems often fail to provide users with meaningful control over their content experiences (Feng et al., 2024). Top-down, platform-wide content algorithms can reduce users' sense of agency and fail to account for nuanced experiences and values, leading to user frustration and attempts to "game" the system through strategic interactions (Feng et al., 2024).Interactive machine teaching (IMT) offers a human-centered approach to building machine-learned models that places the human-in-the-loop as a teacher who iteratively guides algorithmic learning (Ramos et al., 2020). This paradigm is particularly relevant for social media feed curation because it emphasizes user agency, interpretability, and the ability to adapt to individual preferences without requiring machine learning expertise.

citations.title: Interactive machine teaching: a human-centered approach to building machine-learned models
Mapping the Design Space of Teachable Social Media Feed Experiences

sections.text: The foundational principle of IMT is maintaining human agency in the teaching process. Unlike traditional machine learning approaches that treat users as passive data sources, IMT positions users as active teachers who can articulate their preferences and see immediate responses from the system (Ramos et al., 2020). This principle directly addresses the lack of user control in current social media feed systems.IMT systems operate through iterative processes where users provide feedback, observe system responses, and refine their teaching based on the results. This creates a continuous learning cycle that allows for dynamic adaptation to changing user preferences (Ramos et al., 2020). In social media contexts, this could enable real-time feed personalization based on user teaching interactions.A key advantage of IMT is the creation of interpretable models that users can understand and debug. This transparency is crucial for building user trust and enabling effective teaching (Ramos et al., 2020). For social media feeds, this means providing clear explanations of why certain content appears and how user actions influence future recommendations.

sections.text: Research has shown that users rely on diverse signals to evaluate content value in their feeds, including content relevance, source credibility, social validation, and temporal factors (Feng et al., 2024). IMT principles can be applied to allow users to explicitly teach these preferences to feed algorithms through structured feedback mechanisms.Five key design principles emerge from applying IMT to social media feed curation:1. Signal Taxonomies: Organizing user feedback into interpretable categories that the system can learn from2. Iterative Refinement: Allowing users to continuously adjust their teaching based on feed performance3. Transparent Explanations: Providing clear reasons for content inclusion or exclusion4. User Control: Maintaining user agency over the teaching process5. Adaptive Learning: Enabling the system to learn from minimal user input while providing maximum personalizationPractical implementation of teachable feed experiences can include: - Contextual Feedback Mechanisms: Allowing users to provide specific feedback on why content is relevant or irrelevant - Preference Articulation Tools: Interfaces that help users express complex preferences in teachable formats - Real-time Adaptation: Systems that immediately reflect user teaching in feed content - Explanation Interfaces: Clear visualizations of how user teaching influences feed curation

IMT applications to social media feeds must account for these biases through debiasing techniques and diverse feedback collection methods.Implementing IMT principles at social media scale requires efficient algorithms that can process user teaching in real-time. This includes developing lightweight models that can be updated frequently without significant computational overhead (He et al., 2023).

question: What kinds of coverage motion planning algorithms are effective for floor-cleaning robots?

sections.text: Floor-cleaning robots have become increasingly prevalent in both domestic and industrial environments, necessitating sophisticated coverage motion planning algorithms to ensure effective and efficient cleaning operations. Coverage path planning (CPP) algorithms are essential for enabling these robots to systematically traverse and clean entire floor areas while minimizing energy consumption and maximizing coverage completeness (Nair, 2024). This report examines the various types of coverage motion planning algorithms that have proven effective for floor-cleaning robots, analyzing their strengths, limitations, and applications.

citations.title: Efficient Path Planning Algorithm for Mobile Robots Performing Floor Cleaning Like Operations

sections.text: Boustrophedon-based coverage algorithms represent one of the most widely used approaches in floor-cleaning robotics. These algorithms utilize a back-and-forth sweeping motion pattern that systematically covers the entire area. The boustrophedon cellular decomposition method has been extensively modified to accommodate vehicle dynamics and environmental constraints (Yang et al., 2022). This approach provides good coverage completeness and is particularly effective for rectangular spaces with minimal obstacles.However, traditional boustrophedon algorithms can be limiting for reconfigurable robots due to their rigid motion patterns. Samarakoon et al. (2022) demonstrated that combining boustrophedon motion with adaptive algorithms like A* can significantly improve area coverage performance, particularly in narrow spaces that are inaccessible to fixed-morphology robots.Spiral-based algorithms offer smoother motion patterns compared to boustrophedon approaches, reducing aggressive accelerations and decelerations that result from sharp turns. Hassan et al. (2020) introduced the Squircular-CPP algorithm, which creates smooth spiral paths within fitted shapes. This algorithm can fit shapes between circles and squares, or ellipses and rectangles, without requiring preselection of the target shape. The spiral approach demonstrates superior performance in terms of motion smoothness and energy efficiency compared to traditional boustrophedon methods.

citations.title: Coverage Path Planning for Autonomous Road Sweepers in Obstacle-cluttered Environments

sections.text: Spanning Tree Coverage algorithms represent a sophisticated approach that combines exploration and coverage phases. Nair (2024) developed an efficient STC-based algorithm that operates under the assumption that the environment is initially unknown to the robot. The algorithm alternates between exploration and coverage phases, using local mapping to construct an STC tree that guides subsequent cleaning operations. This approach offers several advantages: the robot returns to its initial position upon completion, minimizing battery usage, and sensors are only active during exploration phases.The STC algorithm is classified as an offline-online scheme, providing both completeness of coverage and energy efficiency. Experimental validation using VRep/MATLAB environments and real-time implementations with Turtlebot in ROS-Gazebo environments have demonstrated the algorithm's effectiveness and non-repetitive nature.

Safety considerations are crucial for floor-cleaning robots operating in environments with hazardous components. Wijegunawardana et al. (2023) introduced a Failure Mode and Effect Analysis (FMEA) based coverage path planning strategy that trades off between area coverage and robot safety. This approach uses predefined hazard maps to classify risks and implement safety-ensured coverage processes.The FMEA method defines risk factors for environmental points, serving as key parameters to assess path safety. Rather than relying on expensive additional sensors, this approach uses intelligent path planning to navigate around hazards while maintaining coverage effectiveness. Experimental results with the hTetro mobile robot demonstrated significant reductions in high-risk robot movements compared to existing methods.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for adaptive coverage path planning. Noh et al. (2022) developed an adaptive coverage policy using deep reinforcement learning with an actor-critic model. This approach focuses on minimum energy path generation, demonstrating superior energy efficiency compared to rule-based and other learning-based algorithms when tested on the LG R9 cleaning robot.The reinforcement learning approach enables robots to learn optimal coverage strategies through interaction with their environment, adapting to different layouts and conditions. This adaptability is particularly valuable for commercial cleaning robots that must operate in diverse environments with varying layouts and obstacles.Advanced RL implementations incorporate multiple objectives simultaneously. Apuroop et al. (2021) proposed a complete area coverage planning module for the modified hTrihex robot using deep reinforcement learning. Their framework combines convolutional neural networks (CNN) with long short-term memory (LSTM) layers, trained using the actor-critic experience replay (ACER) algorithm. This approach simultaneously generates tiling shapes and trajectories while minimizing overall cost.The system outperformed traditional methods including zigzag, spiral, and greedy search schemes, as well as TSP-based approaches using genetic algorithms and ant colony optimization. The RL-based approach generated paths with minimized cost in significantly less time than conventional methods.

Hybrid algorithms combine multiple coverage strategies to leverage the advantages of different approaches. Li et al. (2023) proposed a hybrid path planning method for glass cleaning robots that combines contour-parallel paths with method-parallel paths to achieve full-coverage planning. This approach integrates convolutional neural networks for image recognition to determine glass cleanliness levels, enabling adaptive cleaning processes based on contamination assessment.The hybrid approach effectively improves cleaning efficiency and resource utilization by adapting cleaning intensity based on surface conditions. This demonstrates the potential for intelligent coverage algorithms that adjust their behavior based on real-time environmental assessment.Traditional optimization algorithms remain relevant for coverage path planning, particularly in hybrid implementations. Le et al. (2021) developed a coverage path planning system for the hTetran robot using TSP-based reinforcement learning optimization. The system incorporates both genetic algorithm and ant colony optimization approaches, demonstrating that hybrid optimization methods can effectively address the coverage problem while considering multiple constraints.The comparison between genetic algorithms, ant colony optimization, and particle swarm optimization for robot scheduling indicates that ant colony optimization demonstrates consistent performance with minimal processing times, making it suitable for real-time applications (Wu et al., 2024).

citations.title: Evaluation of Particle Swarm Optimization, Genetic Algorithms, and Ant Colony Optimization in Autonomous Mobile Robots Scheduling: A Comparative Study

sections.text: For cleaning robots operating on curved surfaces, specialized algorithms are required. Sakata and Suzuki (2023) developed a coverage motion planning algorithm based on 3D model curved shapes for home cleaning robots. This approach uses 3D models to generate cleaning actions more efficiently than point cloud-based methods, representing surfaces as simple graphs that can be solved as traveling salesman problems.The algorithm determines optimal end-effector postures based on surface shape and establishes coordinate systems for each node. Experimental results showed that this approach achieves similar cleaning results to previous methods while requiring less than one-tenth of the computational time.Reconfigurable robots present unique opportunities for coverage optimization. Kalimuthu et al. (2023) developed a framework using metaheuristic algorithms to determine optimal robot shapes for maximizing coverage while minimizing energy consumption. The approach uses Speed-constrained Multi-Objective Particle Swarm Optimization (SMPSO) and Strength Pareto Evolutionary Algorithm2 (SPEA2) to generate optimal configurations.This framework implements footprint-based path planning that adapts to all robot configurations, demonstrating the potential for morphologically adaptive coverage strategies. The results indicate that optimal morphology selection can significantly improve both coverage effectiveness and energy efficiency.

Recent developments in collaborative perception show promise for multi-robot cleaning systems. Nair (2024) explored collaborative perception frameworks where multiple robots share sensor data to construct comprehensive environmental representations. This approach improves task efficiency, coverage completeness, and safety through enhanced coordination and information sharing.Novel bio-inspired approaches continue to emerge. Champagnie et al. (2024) introduced Greedy Entropy Maximization (GEM), a hybrid approach that combines reward-based and pheromone-based methods. This algorithm maximizes entropy of deposited pheromones while maintaining superior generalization and adaptation capabilities in unknown environments.

Coverage motion planning algorithms for floor-cleaning robots have evolved significantly, encompassing traditional geometric approaches, advanced tree-based methods, safety-aware strategies, and adaptive learning systems. The most effective algorithms demonstrate several key characteristics:1. Completeness: Ensuring full area coverage without missed regions2. Efficiency: Minimizing energy consumption and cleaning time3. Adaptability: Adjusting to different environments and obstacles4. Safety: Incorporating risk assessment and hazard avoidance5. Optimality: Balancing multiple objectives including coverage, energy, and timeThe trend toward hybrid approaches combining multiple algorithmic strategies appears most promising, as these systems can leverage the strengths of different methods while mitigating individual limitations. Reinforcement learning-based approaches show particular promise for adaptive coverage in dynamic environments, while safety-aware algorithms address critical practical concerns for real-world deployment.Future research directions include enhanced collaborative multi-robot systems, bio-inspired algorithms, and integration of advanced perception capabilities for intelligent coverage adaptation. The continued evolution of these algorithms will be crucial for improving the effectiveness and efficiency of autonomous cleaning systems in increasingly complex environments.

question: What are good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots?

sections.text: The evaluation of mobile robot obstacle avoidance strategies requires a comprehensive approach that considers multiple performance dimensions, standardized benchmarks, and appropriate simulation environments. This report synthesizes current research to provide guidance on effective benchmarking methodologies and evaluation frameworks for comparing obstacle avoidance algorithms.

### 1.1 Navigation Performance MetricsThe foundation of obstacle avoidance evaluation lies in quantifying navigation performance through standardized metrics. Success Rate (SR) serves as the primary indicator, measuring the percentage of navigation tasks completed successfully without collisions (1). This metric is typically defined as reaching the target location within a specified distance threshold while maintaining collision-free movement.Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) provides a more nuanced evaluation by incorporating path efficiency into the success measurement (2). The SPL metric is calculated as the harmonic mean of success rate and path optimality, where path optimality is the ratio of shortest path length to actual path length taken. This metric effectively balances task completion with navigation efficiency.Path Length Optimality quantifies the efficiency of the generated path by comparing the actual distance traveled to the theoretically shortest path (3). This metric is crucial for evaluating whether obstacle avoidance strategies generate unnecessarily long or convoluted paths.### 1.2 Safety and Collision MetricsSafety evaluation represents a critical dimension that extends beyond simple success rates. Collision Rate (CR) measures the frequency of collisions during navigation tasks, providing insight into the safety characteristics of different algorithms (4). However, researchers have identified limitations in using raw collision counts, as they may not accurately reflect safety performance across scenarios with varying path lengths.Minimum Obstacle Distance tracks the closest approach distance to obstacles during navigation, offering insight into the safety margins maintained by different algorithms (5). This metric is particularly valuable for assessing the conservative or aggressive nature of obstacle avoidance behaviors.A newer metric, Success weighted by collision-Free Path Length (SFPL), addresses the limitations of traditional collision metrics by weighting collision occurrences against path length, enabling more accurate safety comparisons across different navigation scenarios (6).### 1.3 Temporal Performance MetricsNavigation Time measures the total time required to complete navigation tasks, serving as a direct indicator of algorithm efficiency (7). This metric is often analyzed in conjunction with success rates to provide comprehensive performance assessment.Time Optimality Ratio compares actual navigation time to the theoretical minimum time required, similar to path length optimality but focusing on temporal efficiency (8). This metric helps identify algorithms that may achieve path optimality but at the cost of increased navigation time.

sections.text: ### 2.1 Dedicated Obstacle Avoidance BenchmarksAvoidBench represents a significant advancement in standardized obstacle avoidance evaluation, providing a high-fidelity vision-based benchmarking suite specifically designed for multi-rotor vehicles (9). This platform addresses the lack of shared consensus in obstacle avoidance algorithm testing by offering large datasets and proper evaluation metrics, similar to established benchmarks in computer vision and natural language processing.BARN (Benchmark for Autonomous Robot Navigation) provides a comprehensive testbed for ground robot navigation in metric environments (10). The benchmark includes 300 navigation environments ordered by difficulty metrics, enabling systematic and objective performance comparison. The platform supports prediction of navigation difficulty for new environments and can serve as a curriculum for both planning-based and learning-based navigation systems.### 2.2 Simulation Environment PlatformsGazebo emerges as the most widely adopted simulation platform for robotics research, providing realistic physics engines, high-quality graphics rendering, and extensive sensor model support (11). Its integration with the Robot Operating System (ROS) creates a seamless development and testing environment that facilitates the transition from simulation to real-world deployment.ROS/Gazebo Integration enables researchers to conduct controlled experiments with standardized interfaces, allowing for fair comparison of different algorithms under identical conditions (12). This integration supports headless operation for performance-constrained systems and provides extensive command-line tools for parameter manipulation and data collection.### 2.3 Environment Complexity GradationEffective benchmarking requires systematic progression of environment complexity. Research indicates that optimal benchmarking protocols should include four distinct complexity levels: free linear motion, single obstacle scenarios, multiple obstacle configurations, and complex dynamic environments (13).Static Obstacle Configurations typically progress from single obstacles to parallel and perpendicular arrangements, providing controlled assessment of basic obstacle avoidance capabilities (14). These configurations allow for systematic evaluation of algorithm performance across varying obstacle densities and spatial arrangements.Dynamic Obstacle Scenarios introduce temporal complexity through moving obstacles with different behavioral patterns, including passing, crossing, and overtaking maneuvers (15). These scenarios are essential for evaluating real-world applicability of obstacle avoidance algorithms.

sections.text: ### 3.1 Experimental Design PrinciplesRigorous evaluation requires systematic experimental design with appropriate statistical sampling. Research demonstrates that meaningful performance assessment typically requires a minimum of 100 trials per test condition to achieve statistical significance (16). This sample size ensures adequate power for detecting performance differences between algorithms while accounting for inherent variability in robot navigation tasks.Multi-Environment Testing is essential for comprehensive evaluation, as algorithm performance often varies significantly across different environmental conditions (17). Best practices include testing across environments with varying obstacle densities, spatial layouts, and dynamic characteristics to assess algorithm robustness and generalizability.### 3.2 Comparative Analysis FrameworksAlgorithmic Parameter Analysis should systematically examine the impact of different algorithmic parameters, controller architectures, and learning environments on performance (18). This approach enables identification of performance bottlenecks and ensures robust algorithm development.

question: What is a good Ontology semantic similarity measure that considers multiple inheritance cases of concepts?

sections.text: Based on my research, I'll now generate a comprehensive report on ontology semantic similarity measures that handle multiple inheritance cases.

Ontology semantic similarity measures are essential tools for comparing concepts within structured knowledge representations. While traditional measures often treat ontologies as trees, many real-world ontologies exhibit multiple inheritance patterns, where concepts can have multiple parent classes. This creates a challenge for similarity computation, as standard measures may not properly account for the rich semantic relationships present in these complex hierarchical structures.Multiple inheritance occurs when a concept inherits properties from more than one parent concept in an ontology's directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure (Yang et al., 2015). This phenomenon is particularly common in biomedical ontologies such as Gene Ontology (GO) and SNOMED CT, where concepts often belong to multiple taxonomic branches simultaneously.

citations.title: An Ontology-Based Semantic Similarity Measure Considering Multi-Inheritance in Biomedicine

sections.text: The primary challenges in handling multiple inheritance for semantic similarity computation include:1. Path Ambiguity: When multiple paths exist between two concepts, traditional measures may select only one path, potentially losing important semantic information (Pesquita et al., 2009).2. Parallel Interpretations: Concepts sharing multiple common ancestors through different inheritance paths may represent stronger semantic relationships than those sharing only single paths (Pesquita et al., 2009).3. Computational Complexity: Exhaustive exploration of all inheritance paths can lead to exponential computational complexity, making measures impractical for large ontologies (Pesquita et al., 2009).

citations.title: Disjunctive shared information between ontology concepts: application to Gene Ontology

sections.text: ### 1. DiShIn (Disjunctive Shared Information)DiShIn represents the most effective approach for handling multiple inheritance in semantic similarity computation. This method addresses the limitations of earlier approaches by redefining how shared information content is calculated between concepts with multiple inheritance paths (Pesquita et al., 2009).Key Features:- Efficiently incorporates multiple inheritance by considering disjunctive common ancestors- Maintains linear computational complexity O(n), making it practical for large ontologies- Can be integrated into any existing similarity measure that depends on shared information content- Outperforms traditional approaches in correlation with sequence similarity benchmarksAlgorithm: DiShIn identifies disjunctive ancestors based on the difference in the number of distinct paths from concepts to their common ancestors. An ancestor is considered disjunctive if the path difference to that ancestor differs from more informative ancestors, representing distinct parallel interpretations (Pesquita et al., 2009).### 2. Enhanced Superconcept-Based MeasureYang et al. (2015) propose a similarity measure that combines superconcepts consideration with common specificity features. This approach specifically addresses multiple inheritance by incorporating all superconcepts of evaluated concepts rather than just the most informative common ancestor.Key Features:- Takes into account all superconcepts of evaluated concepts to handle multiple inheritance- Combines depth-based specificity with comprehensive ancestor analysis- Demonstrates improved correlation with human similarity judgments- Computationally efficient and simple to implement### 3. GOGO AlgorithmThe GOGO algorithm represents a hybrid approach that combines benefits of information content-based and topology-based methods while considering multiple inheritance scenarios (Zhao & Wang, 2018).Key Features:- Considers the number of children nodes in DAG structures when calculating semantic contributions- Does not require external corpus statistics for information content calculation- Maintains computational efficiency while preserving semantic accuracy- Particularly effective for Gene Ontology applications### 4. Fusion-Based Semantic SimilarityAl-hassan et al. (2024) developed a fusion-based approach that comprehensively captures semantic knowledge by exploiting all possible shared semantics between instances in domain ontologies.Key Features:- Analyzes hierarchical relationships among instances comprehensively- Considers both features of instances and their relationships to other instances- Demonstrates superior performance in collaborative filtering applications- Achieves 6% reduction in Mean Absolute Error compared to benchmark techniques

While GraSM exhibits non-linear computational complexity leading to execution times approximately 3 times higher than basic measures, DiShIn maintains linear complexity close to traditional approaches (Pesquita et al., 2009).### Accuracy ImprovementsExperimental evaluations show that measures specifically designed for multiple inheritance consistently outperform traditional single-path approaches:- DiShIn achieves statistically significant higher correlation coefficients between semantic and sequence similarity- Enhanced superconcept-based measures show improved correlation with human similarity judgments- GOGO demonstrates accurate gene clustering based on functional similarities

This approach allows researchers to enhance existing measures without complete reimplementation (Pesquita et al., 2009).### Domain SpecificityWhile these measures were primarily developed and evaluated in biomedical contexts, their principles apply to any domain ontology exhibiting multiple inheritance patterns. The measures have shown particular effectiveness in:- Gene Ontology applications- SNOMED CT medical terminology- General domain ontologies with complex inheritance structures

The fusion-based approach shows promise for applications requiring comprehensive semantic knowledge exploitation.Future developments in this area will likely focus on extending these approaches to handle more complex ontology features beyond simple subsumption relationships, and developing better evaluation standards that are not biased by structural features.

question: Suggest some ways in which precise positioning and context-aware networking can be achieved in 6G mobile communication?

sections.text: The evolution toward 6G mobile communication systems necessitates unprecedented precision in positioning capabilities and intelligent context-aware networking solutions. This report examines the technological approaches that can enable centimeter-level positioning accuracy and adaptive networking in 6G systems, addressing key challenges such as multipath propagation, dynamic environments, and the integration of multiple sensing modalities. The solutions range from advanced antenna systems and intelligent reflecting surfaces to artificial intelligence-driven optimization and multi-sensor fusion techniques.

### 1.1 Machine Learning-Based Channel State Information (CSI) Fingerprinting One of the most promising approaches for precise indoor positioning in 6G systems involves leveraging AI-enabled CSI fingerprinting techniques. CSI fingerprinting utilizes the unique characteristics of wireless channels at different locations to create location-specific "fingerprints" that can be used for positioning (Kaur et al., 2023). This approach demonstrates superior precision compared to traditional heuristic methods like Direction of Arrival (DOA) estimation, particularly in complex indoor environments where multipath propagation and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions are prevalent. The integration of machine learning algorithms with CSI fingerprinting enables the system to adapt to dynamic indoor environments and improve positioning accuracy over time. The spatial distribution of cellular networks makes them particularly suitable for localization services, enabling context-aware networking that can customize services based on user location (Kaur et al., 2023). ### 1.2 Channel Knowledge Maps for Environment-Aware Communications A paradigm shift from environment-unaware to environment-aware communications is enabled through Channel Knowledge Maps (CKM). This approach addresses the challenge of acquiring channel state information in real-time for dense 6G infrastructures by exploiting location-tagged channel data from various sources (Zeng et al., 2023). The CKM framework enables proactive beamforming, resource allocation, and network optimization based on predicted channel conditions at specific locations. This environment-aware approach is particularly beneficial for 6G systems that will feature large antenna arrays, wide bandwidth, and enhanced intelligence capabilities. The integration of positioning methods with communication systems creates opportunities for more efficient spectrum utilization and improved service delivery (Zeng et al., 2023).

sections.text: ### 2.1 RIS-Assisted Environment-Aware Positioning Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces have emerged as a key technology for enhancing positioning performance in 6G networks. RIS-assisted positioning systems can achieve high-precision localization by creating smart radio environments that optimize signal propagation paths (Mondal & Biswas, 2023). These systems take into account the incident planar wavefront on the RIS to achieve accurate positioning of users within the network. The optimal placement and configuration of RIS elements within the network is crucial for achieving desired positioning accuracy. Research demonstrates that RIS can significantly enhance positioning performance through strategic deployment and intelligent phase optimization (Mondal & Biswas, 2023). ### 2.2 Compressive Sensing for Near-Field Localization For multipath RIS-aided environments, compressive sensing techniques offer solutions for single-anchor localization that account for both near-field propagation and multipath conditions. These systems achieve more than one order of magnitude improvement in localization accuracy compared to RIS with non-optimized phases (Rinchi et al., 2022). The approach addresses issues associated with near-field localization and model mismatches through tailored compressed sensing algorithms. ### 2.3 IRS-Empowered 6G Network Architecture The integration of IRS technology with other 6G enabling technologies creates synergistic effects for positioning and networking. IRS-empowered 6G networks combine artificial intelligence, integrated terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks, multi-access edge computing, and terahertz/millimeter wave communications (Naeem et al., 2022). This integration enables enhanced energy efficiency, spectrum efficiency, and physical layer security while supporting precise positioning capabilities.

sections.text: ### 3.1 Massive MIMO and Extreme Beamforming The positioning and sensing requirements of 6G networks can be met through systems that support extreme massive MIMO configurations with enhanced signal processing capabilities. Low-complexity position estimation methods using massive MIMO-OFDM systems can achieve centimeter-level positioning accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency (Masal et al., 2024). These systems support both downlink angle of departure (DL-AoD) and uplink angle of arrival (UL-AoA) techniques. The proposed angle-based position estimation methods can achieve 90th percentile positioning accuracy requirements of 20 cm for outdoor scenarios and 3 m for indoor factory environments, as specified in 3GPP releases 16 and 17 (Masal et al., 2024). ### 3.2 Cooperative Multi-Monostatic Sensing Cooperative sensing frameworks using multiple base stations enable passive target localization and positioning in bandwidth-limited scenarios. These systems introduce fusion-based estimation processes that mitigate multipath effects by assigning appropriate weights to range estimations from each base station (Figueroa et al., 2023). The approach is particularly effective in Frequency Range 1 (FR1) operations where bandwidth constraints limit traditional localization techniques. ### 3.3 Beam Management for mmWave and THz Communications Advanced beam management techniques are essential for maintaining robust positioning and communication in mmWave and THz frequency bands. These systems require sophisticated initial access and beam tracking capabilities to overcome the challenges of narrow beams and high measurement overhead (Xue et al., 2023). The integration of artificial intelligence, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, and integrated sensing and communications creates new opportunities for efficient beam management.
